Can you explain Article 325 of the Philippine Civil Code about property given to a minor for education?

Article 325 states that if property or income is donated, bequeathed, or devised to an unemancipated child for the expenses of his education and instruction, the child owns it and has the usufruct (right to use and enjoy the fruits). However, the father or mother shall administer the property, unless the donation or testamentary provision states otherwise. In short, the child is the owner, but the parents manage it for the child's benefit, unless the giver specified a different arrangement.

Can you explain Article 1253 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when it says payment of principal is not deemed made until interests are covered?

Article 1253 provides that if a debt bears interest, any payment made by the debtor is applied first to the interest due. The principal is not considered paid until all accrued interest has been fully satisfied. This means that partial payments are credited to interest before any reduction of the principal amount.

Can you explain Article 530 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 530 states that only things and rights that can be appropriated, meaning they can be owned or possessed exclusively by a person, may be the object of possession. Things that are not susceptible of appropriation, such as common things like air or the open sea, or things outside the commerce of man, cannot be legally possessed.

Can you explain Article 285 of the Philippine Civil Code about recognition of natural children?

Article 285 states that an action for recognition of natural children must generally be filed during the lifetime of the presumed parents. However, there are two exceptions: (1) if the father or mother died while the child was still a minor, the child can file the action within four years from reaching the age of majority; (2) if after the death of the parent, a document is discovered that recognizes the child, the action must be commenced within four years from the finding of that document.

=== PRIMARY STATUTORY AUTHORITY: PHILIPPINE CIVIL CODE (REPUBLIC ACT NO. 386) ===

[Statutory Article 1]
SOURCE TYPE: PHILIPPINE CIVIL CODE ARTICLE
PROVISION: Article 183 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK I - PERSONS > TITLE VI.—PROPERTY RELATIONS BETWEEN - HUSBAND AND WIFE > CH 4 - CONJUGAL PARTNERSHIP OF GAINS > SEC 7.— Liquidation of the Conjugal Partnership > Art. 183
STATUTORY TEXT: The deductions from the inventoried property having been made as provided in the two preceding articles, the remainder of said property shall constitute the credit of the conjugal partnership.

My husband and I are separated and we are liquidating our conjugal partnership. We have inventoried all our properties, but I'm confused about what amount will actually be divided between us. After listing everything, how do we compute the 'credit' of the conjugal partnership as mentioned in Article 183? For example, we have a house worth 5 million, a car worth 1 million, but we also have outstanding loans of 1.5 million and other obligations. Does the entire 6 million get divided, or do we first subtract the loans? Please explain.

Therefore, you do not divide the entire 6 million; you first deduct all legitimate debts and charges, and only the balance is subject to division.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 183, after the inventory of all conjugal properties has been made, the deductions provided in the two preceding articles (Articles 181 and 182) must first be made. These deductions typically include debts, charges, and obligations of the conjugal partnership. [Art. 183].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your scenario, the total inventoried property is 6 million (house worth 5 million plus car worth 1 million). From this amount, you must subtract the outstanding loans and other obligations of 1.5 million. The remainder, which is 4.5 million, constitutes the credit of the conjugal partnership. This net amount is what will be divided between you and your husband according to the rules on liquidation.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 183, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Petition for Judicial Liquidation and Partition of Conjugal Partnership Properties

Can you explain Article 1278 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean?

Article 1278 of the Philippine Civil Code states that compensation takes place when two persons are both creditors and debtors of each other in their own right. This means that if Person A owes Person B a debt, and Person B also owes Person A a debt, then these two obligations may be offset or extinguished up to the amount that corresponds to both, provided each acts as a creditor and debtor in their own name—not as a representative or agent of another. Compensation effectively cancels the debts to the extent that they are equal.

Ano po ang nakasaad sa Artikulo 93 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa kalayaan sa relihiyon sa pagpapakasal?

Ang Artikulo 93 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay nagsasaad na dapat igalang ng mga pampublikong opisyal ang kalayaan sa relihiyon kapag nag-iisyu ng awtorisasyon na magkasal. Dahil dito, hindi maaaring tanungin o siyasatin ng sinumang pampublikong opisyal ang katotohanan o bisa ng anumang doktrinang panrelihiyon na pinaniniwalaan ng aplikante o ng kanyang simbahan. Sa madaling salita, ang gobyerno ay hindi dapat makialam sa mga paniniwalang panrelihiyon at hindi maaaring gamitin ang doktrina bilang batayan sa pagbibigay o pagtanggi ng awtorisasyon.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 204 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa mga utang na ginawa ng isang asawa nang walang pahintulot ng isa pa.

Ayon sa Artikulo 204, kung ang isang asawa ay nagkaroon ng utang nang walang pahintulot ng kanyang asawa, ang utang na iyon ay maaaring singilin laban sa komunidad (ang mga karaniwang ari-arian ng mag-asawa) hanggang sa halaga lamang na nakinabang ang pamilya. Ibig sabihin, ang pinagkakautangan ay maaaring habulin ang pondo o ari-arian ng komunidad kung ang utang ay ginamit para sa bagay na nakinabang ang pamilya. Kung ang utang ay para sa personal na gamit at hindi nakinabang ang pamilya, hindi mananagot ang komunidad; tanging ang asawang nag-utang ang personal na mananagot. Ang pananagutan ng komunidad ay limitado sa halaga ng benepisyong natanggap ng pamilya.

=== PRIMARY STATUTORY AUTHORITY: PHILIPPINE CIVIL CODE (REPUBLIC ACT NO. 386) ===

[Statutory Article 1]
SOURCE TYPE: PHILIPPINE CIVIL CODE ARTICLE
PROVISION: Article 1163 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE I.—OBLIGATIONS > CH 2 - NATURE AND EFFECT OF OBLIGATIONS > Art. 1163
STATUTORY TEXT: Every person obliged to give something is also obliged to take care of it with the proper diligence of a good father of a family, unless the law or the stipulation of the parties requires another standard of care.

I sold my car to my neighbor and we agreed he would pick it up next week. Meanwhile, I left the car parked on the street and it got damaged by a storm. Am I liable for the damage? What does the law say about my duty to take care of the car before delivery?

Otherwise, the default standard applies, and liability for the damage will depend on whether your care of the car met the standard of a good father of a family.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1163 of the Civil Code, since you are obliged to deliver a specific car to the buyer, you have the duty to take care of it with the diligence of a good father of a family until delivery. This means you should have taken reasonable steps to protect the car, such as parking it in a safe, covered area if possible, especially if a storm was expected. If leaving it on the street was not what a prudent person would do under the circumstances, then you failed to exercise the required diligence and may be liable for the resulting damage. [Art. 1163].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, if the contract between you and the buyer set a different standard (e.g., the buyer agreed to bear the risk of loss from the moment of sale), that agreement would control.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1163, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1163 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 563 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa kung paano nalilikha ang usufruct.

Ayon sa Artikulo 563, ang usufructo — ang karapatang gamitin at pakinabangan ang ari-arian ng iba at kunin ang mga bunga nito, habang pinapanatili ang mismong bagay — ay maaaring malikha sa tatlong paraan: (1) sa bisa ng batas, kapag itinakda mismo ng batas ang usufructo; (2) sa kagustuhan ng mga pribadong tao, na ipinahayag sa pamamagitan ng mga gawaing inter vivos (tulad ng kontrata o donasyon habang buhay) o sa pamamagitan ng huling habilin at testamento; at (3) sa pamamagitan ng preskripsiyon, kung saan nakukuha ang karapatan sa pamamagitan ng pag-aari at paggamit bilang usufructuario sa loob ng panahon at mga kondisyong itinakda ng batas.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1302 ng Civil Code tungkol sa legal subrogation.

Ang Artikulo 1302 ng Civil Code ay nagtatakda ng mga pagkakataon kung kailan ipinapalagay na may legal subrogation. Ang legal subrogation ay ang pagkakalipat ng karapatan ng orihinal na pinagkakautangan sa taong nagbayad ng utang. May tatlong sitwasyon: (1) Kapag ang isang pinagkakautangan ay nagbayad sa ibang pinagkakautangan na may mas mataas na karapatan, kahit hindi alam ng may utang; (2) Kapag ang isang ikatlong tao na walang interes sa obligasyon ay nagbayad na may pahintulot ng may utang, hayagan man o tahimik; (3) Kapag ang isang taong may interes sa pagtupad ng obligasyon ay nagbayad, kahit walang kaalaman ang may utang, ngunit hindi ito nakakaapekto sa epekto ng confusion sa kanyang bahagi. Sa mga kasong ito, ang nagbayad ay pumapalit sa karapatan ng orihinal na pinagkakautangan.

STATUTORY TEXT: Succession may be:
(1) Testamentary;
(2) Legal or intestate; or
(3) Mixed.
My father passed away and left a will that only covers half of his properties. The other half is not mentioned in the will. How will his estate be distributed among us, his children, and our mother?

This results in mixed succession, where part of the estate is governed by the will and part by the law.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 778 of the Civil Code, succession may be testamentary, legal or intestate, or mixed. [Art. 778].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In this scenario, your father's will covers only part of his estate. The portion covered by the will will be distributed according to the will's provisions (testamentary succession). The portion not covered by the will will be distributed according to the rules on legal or intestate succession, meaning the law will determine the heirs, typically the compulsory heirs such as the surviving spouse and children.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

What does Article 370 of the Philippine Civil Code say about how a married woman can use her surname?

Article 370 allows a married woman to choose from three options for her name: (1) use her maiden first name and maiden surname, then add her husband's surname (e.g., Maria Santos Cruz); (2) use her maiden first name and her husband's surname (e.g., Maria Cruz); or (3) use her husband's full name with a prefix like 'Mrs.' (e.g., Mrs. Juan Cruz). She is not forced to adopt only her husband's full name.

Can you explain what Article 306 of the Philippine Civil Code means about funerals?

Article 306 states that every funeral should be in keeping with the social position of the deceased. This means that the funeral arrangements, including the type of service, casket, and other expenses, should be appropriate for the person's status in life. It implies that a person of high social standing would have a more elaborate funeral, while someone of modest means would have a simpler one. The law recognizes that funeral expenses should reflect the deceased's social position, but this is generally interpreted to mean that the expenses should be reasonable and not excessive beyond what is customary for someone of that standing.

I bought a used smartphone from a reputable merchant's store in Manila. I have been in continuous possession of it for over three years, believing the seller was the rightful owner. What about the rules for items bought from a merchant's store?

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1132 of the Civil Code, ownership of movables may be acquired through uninterrupted possession for four years in good faith, or through uninterrupted possession for eight years without any other condition. However, the same article also states that for movables acquired from a merchant's store, the provisions of Article 1505 (and Article 559) shall be observed. Article 1505 generally provides that if the owner has entrusted the property to a merchant who deals in similar goods, a buyer in good faith from that merchant in the ordinary course of business acquires valid title to the property, and the original owner is left to seek remedy against the merchant. ### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, you purchased the smartphone from a reputable merchant's store, presumably in good faith and in the ordinary course of business. If the store was a merchant dealing in such items, your title may be protected under Article 1505, and the original owner cannot recover the phone from you; instead, they must go after the merchant. What does Article 1549 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 1549 of the Philippine Civil Code states that in a contract of sale, the buyer is not required to appeal a court decision that results in eviction (loss of the property to a third party claiming a better right) in order for the seller to become liable under the warranty against eviction. Can you explain Article 1080 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about partition of estate?

Article 1080 states that if a person partitions his estate through a deed during his lifetime (act inter vivos) or through a will, that partition must be respected, provided it does not reduce the legitime (forced share) of compulsory heirs. This allows the parent to assign the business to one child and pay the others their legitime in money, as long as their legitime is fully satisfied.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

If the court finds your proof sufficient, it will deduct the amount of damages from the rent you owe, thereby reducing or possibly eliminating your liability for unpaid rent.

Yes, under Article 676, you may demand an easement of drainage over a contiguous property if your yard is surrounded by other houses and it is not possible to give an outlet through your own house. This is a legal easement, meaning it can be imposed even without the neighbor's consent, but you must strictly comply with the conditions set by law. First, you must choose the point of egress on the adjacent lands or tenements where the water can flow out most easily. Second, you must construct the drainage conduit in such a manner as to cause the least damage to the servient estate (the neighbor's property). Third, you must pay proper indemnity to the owner of the servient estate for the use of their land and any damage caused. [Art. 676].

The easement does not give you unlimited rights; it is limited to what is necessary for drainage, and you must minimize the burden on the neighbor.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Can you explain Article 743 of the Philippine Civil Code about donations to incapacitated persons?

Article 743 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that any donation made to a person who is legally incapacitated to receive donations is void from the beginning. This means the donation has no legal effect and cannot transfer ownership. The law also prevents circumvention by declaring that even if the donation is disguised as another type of contract, such as a sale or a loan, or if it is made through an intermediary person who receives the donation on behalf of the incapacitated person, the donation is still void. The purpose is to ensure that the legal incapacity of the donee cannot be bypassed through simulation or interposition.

Can you explain Article 975 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 975 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with inheritance by nephews and nieces (children of brothers or sisters of the deceased) in intestate succession. It covers two situations: (1) If the deceased's siblings (uncles or aunts of the nephews/nieces) are still alive, the nephews and nieces inherit by right of representation. This means they step into the shoes of their deceased parent (the sibling of the deceased) and receive the share that parent would have received. (2) If no siblings of the deceased survive (i.e., only nephews and nieces survive), they inherit in equal portions, meaning each nephew or niece gets an equal share, not by representation.

Article 925 allows a testator (the person making a will) to impose charges or obligations on the gifts (legacies for personal property, devises for real property) given to compulsory heirs or other beneficiaries (legatees and devisees). Can you explain what are the ways a person can lose possession of a thing under Article 555 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Under Article 555 of the Philippine Civil Code, a possessor may lose possession in four ways: (1) by abandoning the thing, meaning voluntarily giving up possession; (2) by assigning it to another, whether by sale (onerous title) or by donation (gratuitous title); (3) by the destruction or total loss of the thing, or because it is taken out of commerce (like becoming illegal to possess); and (4) by another person's possession, provided that the new possession lasts longer than one year, but the real right of possession is not lost until after ten years.

Can you explain Article 503 of the Philippine Civil Code about private ownership of waters?

Article 503 lists the types of waters that are considered private property. These include: (1) springs or streams that rise on private land and flow through that same land; (2) lakes and lagoons, including their beds, that are naturally formed on private land; (3) underground water found on private land; (4) rainwater that falls on private land as long as it stays within the property boundaries; and (5) the beds of streams or brooks that are formed by rainwater and cross lands that are not public property. Additionally, when a drain or aqueduct is built, the water, bed, banks, and floodgates are considered part of the land or building that the water is intended for. Owners of lands crossed by an aqueduct cannot claim ownership over the aqueduct or any right to use its bed or banks unless they have a legal title that specifically grants such ownership or right.

Can you explain Article 719 of the Philippine Civil Code about finding lost movable property?

Article 719 provides rules for a person who finds a lost movable property that is not treasure. The finder must return it to its previous possessor if that person is known. If the previous possessor is unknown, the finder must immediately deposit the item with the mayor of the city or municipality where the item was found. The mayor must publicly announce the finding for two consecutive weeks in whatever manner he deems best. If the item cannot be kept without deterioration, or if keeping it would involve expenses that considerably reduce its value, it may be sold at public auction eight days after the publication. If no owner appears within six months from the publication, the item or its value is awarded to the finder. The finder and the owner, as the case may be, are obliged to reimburse the expenses.

Can you explain Article 1016 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about the right of accretion in testamentary succession?

Article 1016 states the conditions for the right of accretion to apply in testamentary succession. Accretion means that if two or more heirs are instituted to the same inheritance or to the same portion of it without specific division (pro indiviso), and one of them cannot or will not take the inheritance because he died before the testator, renounced the inheritance, or is legally incapacitated to receive it, then the share of that heir is added to the shares of the other co-heirs. This right is automatic and does not require the consent of the remaining heirs. It ensures that the testator's intent to give the property collectively to the group is respected, rather than allowing the vacated share to pass through other modes like intestate succession or substitution.

STATUTORY TEXT: The husband may dispose of the conjugal partnership property for the purposes specified in articles 161 and 162.

My husband recently sold our conjugal car without my consent. He said he used the money to pay off a personal debt he had before we got married. Is that allowed under Article 171 of the Civil Code? I thought conjugal property cannot be disposed of without my consent.

Note that if the debt had redounded to the benefit of the family, the disposition would be valid even without your consent, because Article 171 grants the husband administrative power for those legitimate purposes.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 171 of the Civil Code, the husband may dispose of conjugal partnership property only for the purposes specified in Articles 161 and 162. Article 161 lists the obligations for which the conjugal partnership is liable. One of those obligations is the payment of personal debts contracted by either spouse before the marriage, but only insofar as those debts have redounded to the benefit of the family. [Art. 171].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the debt was a personal debt of your husband incurred before marriage. If that debt did not benefit the family (for example, it was not used for household expenses, family support, or any conjugal purpose), then the conjugal partnership is not liable for it, and your husband had no authority under Article 171 to use conjugal property to pay it. Disposing of conjugal property for an unauthorized purpose is not valid. Therefore, the sale of the car to pay that personal debt is not allowed, and you may have legal remedies to recover the property or its value.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 171, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.

Can you explain what Article 1476 of the Philippine Civil Code says about sale by auction?

Article 1476 of the Philippine Civil Code provides rules for sales by auction. First, if goods are put up for auction in lots, each lot is considered a separate contract of sale. Second, an auction sale is perfected when the auctioneer announces its perfection, usually by the fall of the hammer or another customary manner. Until that announcement, any bidder may retract their bid, and the auctioneer may withdraw the goods from sale unless the auction has been announced to be without reserve. Third, the seller may expressly reserve a right to bid, unless otherwise provided by law or stipulation. Fourth, if no notice has been given that the sale is subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, it is unlawful for the seller to bid themselves or to employ or induce any person to bid on their behalf, and the auctioneer is likewise prohibited from employing or inducing any person to bid on behalf of the seller or knowingly taking any bid from the seller or their agent. Any sale contravening this rule may be treated as fraudulent by the buyer.

In that case, you could only dispose of the free portion—the part of your estate not covered by the legitime—to your friend.

Can you explain Article 1210 of the Philippine Civil Code about the relationship between indivisibility and solidarity?

Article 1210 states that indivisibility and solidarity are distinct concepts. Indivisibility refers to the nature of the prestation or object—if it cannot be performed in parts, such as delivering a specific car. Solidarity refers to the relationship between multiple debtors or creditors—if each debtor is liable for the entire obligation or each creditor can demand the whole performance. An obligation can be indivisible without being solidary: for example, two debtors owe one car, but since they are not solidary, each is liable only for his share; however, because the car is indivisible, the creditor must demand performance from both collectively, or one debtor may voluntarily deliver the whole car and then seek reimbursement from the other. Conversely, an obligation can be solidary but divisible: for example, three solidary debtors owe P90,000; due to solidarity, any one of them can be compelled to pay the entire P90,000, even though money is divisible. The article clarifies that one characteristic does not automatically give rise to the other.

Can you explain Article 1461 of the Philippine Civil Code about selling things that do not exist yet?

Article 1461 of the Philippine Civil Code states that things which have a potential existence may be the object of a contract of sale. This means you can sell something that does not yet exist at the time of the sale, as long as it is expected to come into existence in the future. For example, you can sell the future harvest of a farm or the expected offspring of an animal. The sale of a mere hope or expectancy is valid, but it is subject to the condition that the thing will actually come into existence. If the thing never comes into existence, the sale is ineffective. However, if the hope or expectancy is vain, meaning there is no reasonable possibility that the thing will exist, the sale is void from the beginning.

The reduction is done in accordance with the rules on collation and reduction under the Civil Code, which generally aims to ensure that the legitimes of all compulsory heirs (including legitimate children) are not impaired. What does Article 308 of the Philippine Civil Code mean? Can you explain it simply?

Article 308 of the Philippine Civil Code states that no human remains shall be retained, interred, disposed of, or exhumed without the consent of the persons mentioned in Articles 294 and 305. This means that before anyone can keep a body unburied, bury it, cremate or otherwise dispose of it, or dig up already buried remains, they must first obtain the consent of the relatives who are authorized to make funeral arrangements. These authorized persons are determined under Article 294, which generally gives priority to the spouse, descendants, ascendants, and other relatives in a specific order. Article 305 also requires their consent for exhumation. Essentially, the law protects the wishes and rights of the family regarding the deceased's remains.

Can you explain Article 877 of the Philippine Civil Code about conditions in a will?

Article 877 of the Civil Code deals with conditional dispositions in a will where the condition is casual (dependent on chance or the will of a third person) or mixed (dependent partly on the heir's will and partly on chance or a third person). It states that for such conditions, it is sufficient if the condition happens or is fulfilled at any time before or after the testator's death, unless the testator provided otherwise. If the condition already existed or was fulfilled at the time the will was executed and the testator was unaware of it, it is considered as complied with. However, if the testator had knowledge of its prior fulfillment, the condition is only considered fulfilled if it is of such a nature that it can no longer exist or be fulfilled again (i.e., it cannot happen a second time).

Can you explain Article 82 of the Philippine Civil Code? What marriages are considered void under this article?

Article 82 of the Philippine Civil Code lists marriages that are void from the beginning due to certain relationships by affinity or adoption. All these marriages are void ab initio, meaning they are considered invalid from the start.

STATUTORY TEXT: The inheritance of a person includes not only the property and the transmissible rights and obligations existing at the time of his death, but also those which have accrued thereto since the opening of the succession.

My father died last month leaving a rental apartment. At the time of his death, there was unpaid rent from a tenant for the month before he died. After his death, the tenant continued to pay rent for the following months. Do these unpaid rent before death and the rent paid after death form part of my father's inheritance?

Both amounts should be included in the estate for proper distribution among the heirs.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, under Article 781 of the Civil Code, the inheritance includes all property and transmissible rights and obligations existing at the time of death, including the right to collect unpaid rent that accrued before your father died. Additionally, the rent that accrues after death—from the date of death until the estate is settled—also forms part of the inheritance because those are fruits that accrue to the estate since the opening of succession. [Art. 781].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, the unpaid rent due before death is a right that existed at the time of death and is part of the estate, while the rent paid after death is an accrual to the estate and also belongs to the heirs.

My uncle passed away and left a will. In the will, he gave his house and lot to his best friend, and his car and bank savings to his neighbor. He did not mention his two children at all. I want to understand who are considered heirs, devisees, and legatees in this situation.

Under Article 782 of the Civil Code, an heir is a person called to succession either by a will or by operation of law. The best friend who receives the house and lot is a devisee because that is a gift of real property given by will. [Art. 782].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The neighbor who receives the car and bank savings is a legatee because those are gifts of personal property given by will.

SUBSECTION 3.—Illegitimate Children

My father died without a will. His parents are both deceased. He is survived by his paternal grandfather, his maternal grandmother, and his maternal grandfather. No other relatives. How will his estate be divided under Philippine law?

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Per the article, when ascendants of equal degree come from different lines, the estate is split equally between the paternal and maternal lines. Thus, one-half of the estate goes to the paternal line, and since there is only one paternal ascendant, the paternal grandfather receives that entire one-half share. [Art. 987].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The other one-half goes to the maternal line, and since there are two maternal ascendants, they divide it per capita, meaning each receives one-fourth of the total estate.

(1) When the spouse has been convicted of an attempt against the life of the testator, his or her descendants, or ascendants;
(2) When the spouse has accused the testator of a crime for which the law prescribes imprisonment of six years or more, and the accusation has been found to be false;

My husband had an affair and we are now separated. I am making my will and I want to exclude him from inheriting anything. I heard that under Article 921 of the Civil Code, I can disinherit him if he gave cause for legal separation. Is adultery considered a cause for legal separation, and can I use that to disinherit him?

Make sure to specify the cause clearly in your will, and if possible, gather evidence of the adultery to support your action.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, you can disinherit your husband based on Article 921(4) of the Civil Code. The law states that a spouse may be disinherited if he or she has given cause for legal separation. Adultery, or sexual infidelity, is a ground for legal separation under the Family Code of the Philippines. Therefore, if your husband committed adultery and you can prove it, it qualifies as a sufficient cause for disinheritance. However, to be effective, the disinheritance must be made in a valid will, and the cause must be stated in the will and must be true. [Art. 921].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the disinherited spouse contests the will, the burden is on the heirs to prove the truth of the cause for disinheritance.

What does Article 1341 of the Philippine Civil Code mean? It says that a mere expression of opinion does not signify fraud unless made by an expert and the other party has relied on the former's special knowledge.

Article 1341 clarifies the distinction between an opinion and fraud. Generally, expressing an opinion—even if it turns out to be incorrect—does not amount to fraud. However, there is an exception: if the opinion is given by a person who is an expert in the relevant field, and the other party relies on that opinion because of the expert's special knowledge, then that opinion may be considered fraud. In short, a layperson's wrong opinion is not fraud, but an expert's wrong opinion that is relied upon can be the basis for fraud.

Pakisabi kung ano ang nakasaad sa Artikulo 1522 ng Civil Code tungkol sa paghahatid ng maling dami o halo-halong kalakal.

Ang Artikulo 1522 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas ay tumatalakay sa mga sitwasyon kung saan naghatid ang nagbebenta ng dami ng kalakal na iba sa napagkasunduan. Kung mas kaunti ang inihatid, maaaring tanggihan ng mamimili ang mga kalakal. Ngunit kung tinanggap o iningatan ng mamimili ang mga kalakal na alam niyang hindi na kukumpletuhin ng nagbebenta ang kontrata, dapat niyang bayaran ang mga tinanggap na kalakal sa napagkasunduang presyo. Kung ginamit o ipinagbili ng mamimili ang mga kalakal bago niya nalaman na hindi tutuparin ng nagbebenta ang buong kontrata, mananagot lamang siya sa makatwirang halaga ng mga kalakal na natanggap. Kung mas marami ang inihatid, maaaring tanggapin ng mamimili ang mga kalakal na kasama sa kontrata at tanggihan ang sobra, o tanggapin ang lahat at bayaran ang lahat sa napagkasunduang presyo. Kung ang inihatid ay hinaluan ng ibang uri ng kalakal na hindi kasama sa kontrata, maaaring tanggapin ng mamimili ang mga kalakal na naaayon sa kontrata at tanggihan ang iba pa. Kung hindi mahahati ang paksa, maaaring tanggihan ng mamimili ang buong delivery. Ang mga tuntuning ito ay napapailalim sa kaugalian sa kalakalan, espesyal na kasunduan, o nakagawiang pakikitungo ng mga partido.

STATUTORY TEXT: The effects of a conditional obligation to give, once the condition has been fulfilled, shall retroact to the day of the constitution of the obligation. Nevertheless, when the obligation imposes reciprocal prestations upon the parties, the fruits and interests during the pendency of the condition shall be deemed to have been mutually compensated. If the obligation is unilateral, the debtor shall appropriate the fruits and interests received, unless from the nature and circumstances of the obligation it should be inferred that the intention of the person constituting the same was different.
In obligations to do and not to do, the courts shall determine, in each case, the retroactive effect of the condition that has been complied with.

I sold my land to my neighbor under a condition that his bank loan would be approved. While waiting for the approval, I harvested rice from the land and earned P50,000. He also had the purchase money in a savings account earning interest. The loan was approved last month. Now he is asking for the harvested crops and interest. What does the law say?

Thus, his demand for the crops or interest is not supported by law.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1187 of the Civil Code, in a conditional obligation to give, once the condition is fulfilled (here, the loan approval), the effects retroact to the day the obligation was constituted. However, because your contract is a reciprocal obligation—both parties have prestations (you to deliver the land, him to pay the price)—the fruits and interests during the pendency of the condition are deemed mutually compensated. This means that you are entitled to keep the value of the rice you harvested (P50,000), and he is entitled to keep the interest earned on his money. Neither of you can claim from the other. [Art. 1187].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This rule applies unless there is a contrary stipulation or clear intention showing otherwise.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

I am making a last will and testament. My neighbor is one of my three witnesses, and I also want to leave him a small cash gift in the will. Is that allowed? Will he still receive the gift?

In your case, your neighbor is a witness and you want to give him a cash gift. Since there are only two other witnesses besides him (not three other competent witnesses), the gift to him would be void. He can still act as a witness, but he will not receive the cash gift.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 949 of the Philippine Civil Code, since the bequest of 100 sacks of rice is a generic or quantity bequest (not a specific and determinate thing), the general rule is that you, as the legatee, would not be entitled to the fruits and interests from the time of your father's death. Therefore, you are entitled to any fruits, profits, or interests that the 100 sacks of rice (or its monetary equivalent, if applicable) may have produced from the moment of your father's death until actual delivery. Can you explain Article 1429 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Under Philippine law, when a person dies, their heirs inherit their property but also their debts. However, an heir is only liable for the decedent's debts up to the value of the property they actually received from the estate. Article 1429 deals with a situation where an heir voluntarily pays a debt of the decedent that is greater than the value of the property they inherited. The article states that such payment is valid and cannot be rescinded. In other words, even though the heir was not legally obligated to pay beyond what they received, if they voluntarily choose to pay more, they cannot later demand a refund or cancellation of that payment. This is considered a natural obligation: not legally enforceable but morally binding. The law recognizes the heir's voluntary act and upholds it.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Since you transferred your car to your friend as payment for a debt in money, this is a dation in payment under Article 1245 of the Civil Code. This transaction is governed by the law on sales, meaning you are considered the seller and your friend the buyer. Under the law on sales, you may be liable for hidden defects that render the car unfit for its intended use or diminish its value. If the engine defect was hidden and existed at the time of transfer, he may have the right to rescind the sale or demand a reduction in price, but only if the defect is serious and he was unaware of it. The debt is considered extinguished upon delivery, subject to any warranty claims.

The donation shall be inofficious in all that it may exceed this limitation.

My father donated a large piece of land to my brother, leaving almost nothing for me and my other siblings. He said that since he is still alive, he can give his property to anyone he wants. Is that true? Can we question the donation?

The donation may be reduced to the extent that it impairs your legitime, ensuring that your father's property is distributed according to the rules on forced heirship.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 752 of the Civil Code, your father cannot donate more than what he could give by will. This means that even though he is alive and can generally dispose of his property, donations are subject to the same limitations as testamentary dispositions, particularly the protection of the legitime of compulsory heirs. [Art. 752].

### 💡 Application to Facts
As a compulsory heir, you and your siblings have a reserved share in your father's estate that cannot be impaired by donations. If the donation to your brother exceeds the disposable free portion (the part your father could freely give by will), the donation is considered inofficious to the extent of the excess. In your situation, if the donated land effectively deprives you and your other siblings of your legitime, you have the right to question the donation and file an action for reduction.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 1532 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa stoppage in transitu?

Ipinaliliwanag ng Artikulo 1532 kung paano maaaring gamitin ng hindi pa nababayarang nagbebenta ang karapatan ng stoppage in transitu. Maaaring makuha ng nagbebenta ang aktwal na pagmamay-ari ng mga kalakal o magbigay ng abiso sa carrier o bailee na may hawak ng mga kalakal. Ang abiso ay maaaring ibigay sa taong aktwal na may hawak o sa kanyang principal. Kung sa principal ibinigay, dapat itong ibigay sa oras at sitwasyon na maaaring mapigilan ng principal ang paghahatid sa mamimili. Kapag naibigay na ang abiso, dapat ibalik ng carrier ang mga kalakal sa nagbebenta o ayon sa direksyon nito. Ang gastos sa paghahatid ay sasagutin ng nagbebenta. Ngunit kung may negotiable document of title na inilabas, hindi obligado ang carrier na ibigay ang mga kalakal sa nagbebenta maliban kung isusuko muna ang dokumento para kanselahin.

STATUTORY TEXT: The action for annulment of marriage must be commenced by the parties and within the periods as follows:
(1) For causes mentioned in number 1 of article 85, by the party whose parent or guardian did not give his or her consent, within four years after attaining the age of twenty or eighteen years, as the case may be; or by the parent or guardian or person having legal charge, at any time before such party has arrived at the age of twenty or eighteen years;
(2) For causes mentioned in number 2 of article 85, by the spouse who has been absent, during his or her lifetime; or by either spouse of the subsequent marriage during the lifetime of the other;
(3) For causes mentioned in number 3 of article 85, by the sane spouse, who had no knowledge of the other's insanity; or by any relative or guardian of the party of unsound mind, at any time before the death of either party;
(4) For causes mentioned in number 4, by the injured party, within four years after the discovery of the fraud;
(5) For causes mentioned in number 5, by the injured party, within four years from the time the force or intimidation ceased;
(6) For causes mentioned in number 6, by the injured party, within eight years after the marriage.
I got married in 2020, and just last month I discovered that my spouse lied to me about being pregnant with my child to get me to marry her. Now I want to have the marriage annulled. Is it too late?

You should consult a lawyer to assess the strength of your case and ensure proper filing.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 87(4) of the Civil Code, for annulment based on fraud (a ground under Article 85), the injured party must file the action within four years after the discovery of the fraud. [Art. 87].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you discovered the fraud last month, so the four-year period has just started. You are still well within the allowed time to file for annulment of marriage. However, you must be able to prove that the fraud existed at the time of marriage and that it was of such a nature as to have prevented you from freely giving consent to the marriage. Note that the specific acts constituting fraud are defined by law, and not every lie qualifies.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 87, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 87 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

The seller's failure to disclose the tax sale origin of his title is a breach of warranty, and he must indemnify you if you lose the property.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1551 of the Civil Code, if the property was sold for nonpayment of taxes due and this fact was not made known to the vendee before the sale, the vendor is liable for eviction. [Art. 1551].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the seller acquired the property through a tax sale, which is a sale for nonpayment of taxes. Since the seller did not disclose this to you before the sale, he is liable for eviction. This means that if you are evicted from the property because the previous owner successfully redeems it or because the tax sale is invalidated, you can hold the seller liable. You may demand that the seller return the price you paid, pay for damages, and answer for the eviction as provided by the law on warranty against eviction (Articles 1548, 1555, and related provisions).

I donated a piece of land to my nephew a few years ago. Recently, I had a legitimate child of my own. I want to revoke the donation because of the birth of my child. In your case, since it was sold, your remedy is to demand from your nephew the value of the land as it was worth at the date of the donation.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 762, since you are revoking the donation due to the birth of a legitimate child, the donated property should be returned to you. However, because your nephew sold the land, you cannot recover the land itself from the buyer; instead, you are entitled to the value of the property from your nephew. The value is determined as of the time of the donation, not the time of sale or revocation. [Art. 762].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the land was mortgaged when your nephew sold it, you would have the right to redeem the mortgage by paying the guaranteed amount and then recover that amount from your nephew.

Based on your situation, if you and the alleged father were living together (cohabiting) at the time the child was conceived, then under Article 283(3) of the Civil Code, he is obliged to recognize the child as his natural child. [Art. 283].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This means that the law compels him to acknowledge paternity because the child was conceived during the period of cohabitation. You may present evidence of your cohabitation, such as proof of shared residence, testimonies, or other documents, to establish this fact. Can you explain Article 1365 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1365 provides that if two parties agree to enter into a mortgage or pledge of real or personal property, but the written instrument they execute states that the property is sold absolutely or with a right of repurchase, the instrument may be reformed. This means that the court can order the correction of the document to reflect the true intention of the parties, which was to create a mortgage or pledge, not a sale. The remedy of reformation is available because the written contract does not express the real agreement due to mistake, fraud, inequitable conduct, or accident.

What is the rule under Article 917 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the burden of proof in disinheritance?

Can you explain what Article 1355 of the Civil Code means about lesion or inadequacy of cause not invalidating a contract?

Article 1355 states that, except when the law provides otherwise, a contract cannot be set aside merely because the price or consideration is inadequate, or because the cause is insufficient. In other words, if someone sells something for less than its true value, that alone does not make the contract void. However, if there was fraud, mistake, or undue influence involved, then the contract may be invalidated. So the general rule is that inadequacy of price or cause does not invalidate a contract; only when combined with fraud, mistake, or undue influence does it become a ground for invalidation.

Can you explain Article 853 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when the shares of instituted heirs exceed the whole inheritance?

Article 853 provides that if a testator gives each instituted heir an aliquot part (a fraction) of the inheritance, and the sum of those fractions exceeds the whole inheritance or the whole free portion (after deducting legitimes of compulsory heirs), each share shall be reduced proportionally so that the total does not exceed what the testator could validly dispose of. Each share is then multiplied by 2/3, resulting in 1/3 each. This ensures the shares fit within the available estate.

Can you explain Article 1132 of the Philippine Civil Code about ownership of movable property through prescription?

Article 1132 provides two ways to acquire ownership of movable (personal) property by prescription: (1) through uninterrupted possession for four years in good faith, and (2) through uninterrupted possession for eight years without any other condition (meaning even without good faith). Can you explain what Article 791 of the Civil Code says about interpreting the words of a will?

Article 791 provides two rules for interpreting a will. First, the words should be interpreted to give effect to every expression, if possible, rather than making any part meaningless or inoperative. Second, if there are two possible interpretations, the one that prevents intestacy (i.e., the person dying without a valid will covering that property) should be preferred. This is because the law presumes that the testator intended to dispose of all his or her property by will, and not leave any part to be distributed by the rules on intestate succession.

Article 283 of the Philippine Civil Code lists four situations where a father is legally obliged to recognize a child as his natural child. These are: (1) when the child was conceived as a result of rape, abduction, or seduction, and the period of the offense roughly coincides with the time of conception; (2) when the child has been continuously treated as the child of the alleged father, either by the father himself or by his family; (3) when the child was conceived during a time when the mother and the supposed father were living together (cohabiting); and (4) when there is any evidence or proof that the defendant is the father. In these cases, the father cannot simply deny paternity; he is compelled by law to acknowledge the child.

Article 102 of the Philippine Civil Code sets two time limits for filing an action for legal separation. Can you explain Article 867 of the Philippine Civil Code? What kinds of testamentary substitutions are considered void?

Article 867 of the Philippine Civil Code lists four types of provisions in a will that shall not take effect: (1) Fideicommissary substitutions that are not made expressly, either by using the term 'fideicommissary' or by imposing on the fiduciary heir an absolute obligation to deliver the property to a second heir; (2) Provisions that prohibit the heir from selling or disposing of the property forever, or even for a temporary period longer than allowed by Article 863; (3) Provisions that require the heir to pay a certain income or pension to several persons successively beyond the limit set by Article 863; and (4) Provisions that leave property to a person with secret instructions from the testator on how to apply or invest it. These are considered void because they either circumvent the limits on fideicommissary substitutions, impose excessive restrictions on property, or rely on undisclosed instructions.

STATUTORY TEXT: When a creditor whose claim is not mentioned in article 243 obtains a judgment in his favor, and he has reasonable grounds to believe that the family home of the judgment debtor is worth more than the amount mentioned in article 231, he may apply to the Court of First Instance for an order directing the sale of the property under execution.

I owe money to a creditor who got a court judgment against me. The debt is not one of those that are exempt from being collected from a family home. The creditor is now saying that our family home is worth more than the maximum amount allowed for exemption, and they want to ask the court to order the sale of our home. Can they do this? What are their rights and what should I expect?

It is advisable to consult a lawyer to protect your interests in the court proceedings.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 247 of the Philippine Civil Code, a creditor who has obtained a judgment in their favor and whose claim is not mentioned in Article 243 may apply to the court (now the Regional Trial Court) for an order directing the sale of your family home under execution if they have reasonable grounds to believe that the property's value exceeds the maximum amount allowed for exemption under Article 231. This means the creditor can indeed seek to have your family home sold if they can satisfy the court that (1) their claim is not among those listed in Article 243, which are debts that may be enforced against the family home despite its general exemption, and (2) the family home is worth more than the exempt limit. If the court finds these conditions met, it may issue an order for the sale of the property under execution to satisfy the judgment. However, the exemption still protects the portion of the home's value up to the limit in Article 231; only the excess value can be used to pay the creditor. [Art. 247].

### 💡 Application to Facts
As the debtor, you have the right to challenge the creditor's valuation or argue that the claim falls under Article 243 or that the value does not exceed the limit.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 247, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 247 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

I paid my brother's debt to a bank without his knowledge because I wanted to help him. The bank had a mortgage on his house as collateral for the loan. You only have a personal right to be reimbursed by your brother for the amount you paid, based on the principle of quasi-contract (e.g., negotiorum gestio or solutio indebiti). [Art. 1237].

### 💡 Application to Facts
You cannot demand that the mortgage be transferred to you, and you cannot foreclose on the house yourself.

STATUTORY TEXT: The contract of sale is perfected at the moment there is a meeting of minds upon the thing which is the object of the contract and upon the price.

I agreed to buy my neighbor's car for ₱500,000. We shook hands and he said it's a deal, but we didn't sign any written contract. The next day, he sold the car to someone else. Under Article 1475, a contract of sale is perfected at the moment there is a meeting of minds on the object and the price. [Art. 1475].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you and your neighbor agreed on the car and the price of ₱500,000, so the contract of sale was perfected even without a written agreement. From that moment, you could demand performance, meaning he should deliver the car upon your payment. However, Article 1475 also states that the right to demand performance is subject to the provisions of the law governing the form of contracts. For the sale of goods with a price of at least ₱500, the Statute of Frauds under Article 1403(2)(d) requires that the agreement be in writing, or that the buyer accepts and receives part of the goods, or gives earnest or part payment. Since your agreement involved a car priced at ₱500,000, and you did not put it in writing, did not pay any amount, and did not take delivery, the contract, while perfected, may be unenforceable in court. Your neighbor is not entirely correct that the sale is not valid; it is a perfected contract, but you may not be able to compel him through court action for specific performance unless you can prove the agreement and fall under an exception to the Statute of Frauds, such as having a written note or memorandum signed by him, or showing partial performance. What does Article 872 of the Philippine Civil Code mean regarding conditions on legitimes?

Article 872 of the Philippine Civil Code states that a testator (the person making a will) cannot impose any charge, condition, or substitution on the legitimes of compulsory heirs. Legitimes are portions of the estate that the law reserves for compulsory heirs, such as children or spouse, and they are protected from any burden. Can you explain what Article 1258 of the Philippine Civil Code says about consignation?

Article 1258 of the Civil Code outlines the procedure for consignation, which is a way for a debtor to fulfill an obligation when the creditor refuses to accept payment without valid reason. The debtor must deposit the thing or money due with the court (judicial authority). Before doing so, the debtor must prove that a valid tender of payment was made, if tender is required (for example, when the creditor simply refuses to accept). In cases where tender is not required (such as when the creditor is absent, unknown, or incapacitated), the debtor instead announces the consignation to the court. After the deposit is made, the interested parties must be notified about the consignation.

Can you explain Article 1020 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1020 states that when an heir renounces the inheritance or is unable to receive it, the share that would have gone to that heir passes to the other heirs by right of accretion. Can you explain what Article 564 of the Philippine Civil Code says about usufruct?

Article 564 states that usufruct can be constituted over the whole or just a part of the fruits of a thing, in favor of one or more persons, either simultaneously or successively, and it may be set from or until a certain day, purely or conditionally. Can you explain Article 5 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 5 states that acts executed against the provisions of mandatory or prohibitory laws shall be void, except when the law itself authorizes their validity. This means that if a law requires something (mandatory) or prohibits something (prohibitory), any act that violates such law is void and has no legal effect. However, the law itself may provide exceptions that allow the act to be valid despite the violation. In essence, the general rule is voidness, but the law can create exceptions to preserve validity.

Can you explain Article 269 of the Philippine Civil Code about legitimated children?

Article 269 states that only natural children can be legitimated. Natural children are those born outside wedlock to parents who, at the time of the child's conception, were not disqualified by any legal impediment to marry each other. Article 626 states that the owner of the dominant estate (the property that benefits from the easement) cannot use the easement except for the specific purpose for which it was originally established. Ang Artikulo 1378 ay nagbibigay ng mga patakaran sa pagbibigay-kahulugan sa mga kontrata kapag may natitirang pagdududa matapos gamitin ang mga naunang alituntunin. Kung ang pagdududa ay tungkol sa mga incidental na pangyayari ng isang gratuitous na kontrata (walang kapalit), ang interpretasyon na naglilipat ng pinakamaliit na karapatan at interes sa tumatanggap ang dapat manaig. Can you explain what Article 1061 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 1061 requires every compulsory heir (such as children or the surviving spouse) who inherits together with other compulsory heirs to include in the computation of the estate any property or right they received from the deceased during the deceased's lifetime by donation or any other gratuitous transfer. This process is called collation. Its purpose is to determine the legitime (the portion of the estate reserved by law for compulsory heirs) and to ensure a fair partition. The value of the donated property is added to the total estate, and it is considered an advance on the heir's inheritance. If the donation exceeds the heir's share, they may have to return the excess; if it is less, they can still receive additional property from the estate to complete their share.

Can you explain Article 295 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding support obligations when there are multiple persons obliged to give support or multiple recipients?

Article 295 of the Philippine Civil Code addresses situations involving multiple parties in support obligations. It has three main rules: First, if two or more persons are obliged to give support, the payment is divided among them in proportion to their financial resources. Second, in cases of urgent need and special circumstances, a judge may order only one of them to provide support provisionally. That person can later claim reimbursement from the other obligors for their respective shares. Third, if two or more recipients claim support from one person who lacks sufficient means to support all, the order of priority set in Article 294 applies. However, if the competing claimants are the spouse and a child subject to parental authority, the child is given priority.

Can you explain what Article 537 of the Philippine Civil Code means about possession?

Article 537 states that acts merely tolerated, done clandestinely without the possessor's knowledge, or committed through violence do not affect possession. This means such acts cannot change or interrupt a person's possession because true possession must be open, continuous, and peaceful. For example, if someone uses your land with your permission, that is merely tolerated and does not give them possession. If someone secretly enters your property without your knowledge, that secret act does not affect your possession. If someone takes your property by force, that violent act also does not affect your possession. Possession remains with the original possessor despite these acts.

Can you explain what Article 32 of the Philippine Civil Code is about?

Article 32 of the Philippine Civil Code makes any public officer or employee, or any private individual, liable for damages if they directly or indirectly obstruct, defeat, violate, or in any way impede or impair certain fundamental rights and liberties of another person. These rights include freedom of religion, speech, press, freedom from arbitrary detention, right to due process, right against unreasonable searches and seizures, and many others listed in the article. The law allows the aggrieved party to file a separate civil action for damages even if the act is also a criminal offense. This civil action proceeds independently of any criminal prosecution and only requires proof by preponderance of evidence. The damages may include moral damages and exemplary damages. However, judges are not liable under this article unless their act or omission constitutes a violation of the Penal Code or other penal statute.

STATUTORY TEXT: The titles of ownership, or of other rights over immovable property, which are not duly inscribed or annotated in the Registry of Property shall not prejudice third persons.

I bought a parcel of land from a seller and we signed a deed of sale. However, we never registered the sale with the Registry of Deeds. A few months later, I discovered that the same seller sold the land to another person, and that second buyer was able to register the sale. Now the second buyer is claiming ownership and wants me to vacate. Can I use my earlier deed of sale to claim the land? What are my rights?

The law requires registration to give notice to the public; without it, you bear the risk of losing to a subsequent buyer who registers in good faith.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 709 of the Civil Code, titles of ownership or other rights over immovable property that are not duly inscribed or annotated in the Registry of Property shall not prejudice third persons. [Art. 709].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, your purchase was not registered, so your unregistered right cannot be used to defeat the claim of the second buyer, who is a third person. The second buyer, having registered the sale, obtains a right that is protected against your unregistered claim. This means you cannot assert your earlier purchase to take the property from the second buyer. Your remedy would be to file a case against the seller for breach of contract or damages, but you cannot recover the land itself from the second buyer.

Can you explain what Article 343 of the Philippine Civil Code means regarding the inheritance rights of an adopted child when the adopter also has legitimate parents or ascendants?

Under Article 343 of the Civil Code, if an adopter dies and is survived by legitimate parents or ascendants (such as parents, grandparents) and also by an adopted person (the adopted child), the adopted person's inheritance rights are limited. The adopted person cannot receive more than what an acknowledged natural child (an illegitimate child who has been recognized by the parent) would receive. This means the adopted child is treated as an acknowledged natural child for succession purposes, not as a legitimate child, in that specific situation where legitimate parents or ascendants survive. This provision protects the rights of the adopter's blood relatives. Consequently, the adopted child will only get the share of an acknowledged natural child, which is generally less than that of a legitimate child.

Under Article 1178, all rights acquired in virtue of an obligation are transmissible if there has been no stipulation to the contrary, subject to the laws. [Art. 1178].

Ang pribadong kasulatan ay sapat na upang patunayan ang kasunduan. Ayon sa Artikulo 1403(2), ang pagbebenta ng lupa ay kailangang nasa sulat upang maipatupad, ngunit hindi kinakailangang notaryado para sa bisa. Ang notarization ay kailangan lamang para sa pagpaparehistro sa Registry of Deeds at upang maging epektibo laban sa mga ikatlong tao. [Art. 1358].

Samakatuwid, maaari mong pilitin ang nagbebenta na lumagda sa isang pampublikong dokumento sa pamamagitan ng paghahain ng kaso sa korte para sa specific performance.

STATUTORY TEXT: The donation shall be revoked at the instance of the donor, when the donee fails to comply with any of the conditions which the former imposed upon the latter.

My aunt donated a piece of land to her nephew with the condition that he would build a house for her on that land within two years. He did not build anything. The action may also be transmitted to the donor's heirs and can be exercised against the donee's heirs if necessary.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 764, because the donee failed to comply with the condition imposed by the donor (building a house within two years), the donor may revoke the donation. Upon revocation, the donated land must be returned to the donor. The mortgage taken by the donee on the land is generally void, but this is subject to the rights of third parties under the Mortgage Law and Land Registration laws. If the mortgagee is a third person in good faith and the mortgage is duly registered, the mortgagee's rights may be protected. [Art. 764].

Can you explain Article 957 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 957 states that a legacy or devise (a gift of property in a will) will have no effect in three situations: (1) If the testator changes the thing given so much that it no longer keeps its original form or name; (2) If the testator sells, donates, or otherwise transfers the thing, or any part of it. If only a part is transferred, the legacy or devise is ineffective only for that part. If the thing later returns to the testator, even if the transfer is declared void, the legacy or devise will not become valid again, unless the testator got it back by exercising a right of repurchase; (3) If the thing is completely lost during the testator's lifetime, or after his death without the fault of the heir. However, if the thing was not determinate as to its kind, the person obliged to deliver the legacy or devise may still be liable for eviction under Article 928.

STATUTORY TEXT: No declaration for the extrajudicial establishment of the family home shall be recorded in the Registry of Property if the estimated actual value of the building and the land exceeds the amount stated in article 231.

### 💡 Application to Facts
The extrajudicial route is only available for properties whose value is within the limit set by Article 231.

STATUTORY TEXT: The legitime of legitimate children and descendants consists of one-half of the hereditary estate of the father and of the mother.
The latter may freely dispose of the remaining half, subject to the rights of illegitimate children and of the surviving spouse as hereinafter provided.

My father passed away recently. He left a will giving half of his estate to his best friend. He has two legitimate children (including me) and one illegitimate child. He is also survived by his wife, our mother. According to the lawyer, legitimate children are entitled to one-half of the estate, and the other half is free for him to give away. But the illegitimate child and our mother also claim they have rights. How should the estate be divided under the law? Please explain based on Article 888.

If the free portion is insufficient to cover both the friend's bequest and the legitimes of the illegitimate child and spouse, the bequest to the friend will be reduced or invalidated to the extent necessary to protect those legitimes.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 888 of the Civil Code, the legitime of legitimate children and descendants is one-half of the hereditary estate of the father and mother. This means that, as legitimate children, you and your sibling are collectively entitled to one-half of your father's estate as your legitime, and this cannot be reduced by the will. The remaining one-half is the 'free portion' which the testator may dispose of as he wishes. However, the law expressly states that this free portion is 'subject to the rights of illegitimate children and of the surviving spouse.' Therefore, before the best friend can receive anything from the free portion, the legitimes of the illegitimate child and of the surviving spouse must first be satisfied. The illegitimate child is entitled to a legitime equal to one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child (computed from the one-half reserved for legitimate children), and your mother, as surviving spouse, has a legitime equal to that of a legitimate child. These legitimes are charged against the free portion, thereby reducing what can be given to the friend. [Art. 888].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In practice, the estate must be allocated: first, the one-half legitime of legitimate children; then, from the remaining half, the legitimes of the illegitimate child and spouse are taken; whatever remains after those are satisfied is the true free portion that can be given to the friend.

Article 638 establishes legal easements relating to waters. First, the banks of rivers and streams, even if privately owned, are subject to a 3-meter easement of public use along their margins. STATUTORY TEXT: Acquisitive prescription of dominion and other real rights may be ordinary or extraordinary.
Ordinary acquisitive prescription requires possession of things in good faith and with just title for the time fixed by law.

I have been in continuous possession of a parcel of agricultural land for 15 years. I bought the land from a person I believed was the owner, and I have a notarized deed of sale, so I thought everything was proper. However, recently another person came forward claiming to be the true owner, saying that the person I bought from had no right to sell. I have been paying real property taxes and have been openly occupying and cultivating the land. I want to know if I can acquire ownership through prescription. I heard that under Article 1117 of the Civil Code, there are two kinds of acquisitive prescription: ordinary and extraordinary. Ordinary requires good faith and just title. Since I have a deed of sale but from a non-owner, does that count as just title? And if my good faith is questionable because maybe I should have checked the title, can I still acquire by extraordinary prescription if the required period is longer? Please explain how this article applies to my situation.

Based on the facts you described, if you can prove good faith and that your deed of sale constitutes a just title, you may be on track for ordinary acquisitive prescription, provided the required period has already lapsed.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1117, acquisitive prescription may be ordinary or extraordinary. Ordinary acquisitive prescription requires possession in good faith and with just title for the time fixed by law. [Art. 1117].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, a notarized deed of sale from a person you believed to be the owner may qualify as a just title, because a just title is one that would have transferred ownership if the transferor had been the true owner. Good faith means that at the time you acquired the property, you honestly believed the seller was the rightful owner and had no knowledge of any defect in the title. If you possessed the land openly, continuously, exclusively, and peacefully for the period required by law for ordinary prescription (typically shorter than for extraordinary, but the exact period is determined by other provisions of the Civil Code), you can acquire ownership through ordinary acquisitive prescription. However, if either good faith or just title is lacking, you may still acquire through extraordinary prescription, which does not require these elements but generally requires a longer period of possession (usually 30 years for immovables). Article 1117 itself does not specify the periods; these are found in other articles.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 911 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa pagbabawas ng mga devises at legacies.

Ang Artikulo 911 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay nagtatakda ng mga patakaran sa pagbabawas ng mga pamana sa testamento kapag naaapektuhan nito ang legitime ng mga compulsory heirs. Matapos matukoy ang legitime, kung ang testator ay nagbigay ng higit sa maaaring malayang ipamana, ang pagbabawas ay gagawin sa ganitong pagkakasunud-sunod: (1) Ang mga devises o legacies sa testamento ang unang babawasan o aalisin upang matugunan ang legitime. Ang mga donasyon ay igagalang hangga't maaaring matugunan ang legitime sa pamamagitan ng pagbabawas ng mga devises o legacies. (2) Ang pagbabawas sa mga devises at legacies ay pro rata o pantay-pantay. Ngunit kung itinakda ng testator na ang isang partikular na devise o legacy ay uunahin sa pagbabayad, hindi ito mababawasan hangga't hindi pa lubos na nagagamit ang iba pa para matugunan ang legitime. (3) Kung ang devise o legacy ay isang usufruct o life annuity na ang halaga ay itinuturing na mas malaki kaysa sa disposable portion, ang mga compulsory heirs ay may pagpipilian: sumunod sa probisyon ng testamento o ibigay sa devisee o legatee ang bahagi lamang ng mana na malayang maaaring ipamana ng testator.

STATUTORY TEXT: The obligation to give a determinate thing includes that of delivering all its accessions and accessories, even though they may not have been mentioned.

I bought a house and lot from a seller. A house and lot is a determinate thing. The keys are an accessory necessary for the use and enjoyment of the house. The air conditioning units and built-in cabinets, if they are permanently attached or incorporated into the house, are considered accessions or accessories because they form part of the house or are intended for its proper use. Therefore, the seller is legally obligated to deliver them along with the house and lot, even though the deed of sale did not expressly list them.

Hello, I am a wife. My husband committed adultery and we are now legally separated. We have two children together, and he also has a child from a previous relationship.
