### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 176, since your husband is the guilty spouse due to adultery, he shall forfeit his share of the conjugal partnership profits. These profits will be awarded to your common children and his child from the previous relationship. However, the forfeiture does not apply if the conjugal partnership property came mostly or entirely from his work, industry, wages, salaries, or the fruits of his separate property. [Art. 176].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the profits came from both his salary and your business. If his salary did not constitute the main source of the conjugal partnership property, then the forfeiture will apply and his share will be given to the children. But if his salary was the primary source, then he may not forfeit his share. Since you mentioned both sources, the determination will depend on which source contributed more to the conjugal partnership property.

Under Article 817 of the Philippine Civil Code, a will made in the Philippines by a citizen or subject of another country, which is executed in accordance with the law of the country of which he is a citizen or subject, and which might be proved and allowed by the law of his own country, shall have the same effect as if executed according to the laws of the Philippines. This provision ensures that foreigners can validly dispose of their property by will while in the Philippines, even if they do not follow the specific execution formalities required by Philippine law, as long as their will is valid under the law of their home country. However, it is important that the will is indeed valid under Japanese law and can be proved and allowed in Japan, as the Philippine courts will rely on that foreign law.

If for some reason the term becomes impossible (e.g., your brother passes away before 30), then administration ends accordingly.

STATUTORY TEXT: The husband must be joined in all suits by or against the wife, except:
(1) When they are judicially separated;
(2) If they have in fact been separated for at least one year;
(3) When there is a separation of property agreed upon in the marriage settlements;

(7) When the action is upon the civil liability arising from a criminal offense;
(8) If the litigation is incidental to the profession, occupation or business in which she is engaged;

(10) In an action upon a quasi-delict.

Hello. I am a married woman, a dentist by profession. A patient filed a civil case for damages against me, claiming negligence during a dental procedure. Hence, you may properly face the lawsuit alone.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, based on Article 113 of the Civil Code, specifically exception (8), which provides that the husband need not be joined when the litigation is incidental to the wife's profession, occupation, or business. Since the case against you arises from your dental practice, it is directly incidental to your profession. Therefore, your husband does not need to be joined as a party defendant. Additionally, exception (10) may also apply because the action is based on a quasi-delict. However, note the last paragraph of Article 113: in cases under exceptions 7 to 10, the husband must be joined as a defendant if the third paragraph of Article 163 is applicable. Article 163, third paragraph, generally makes the husband liable for the wife's obligations arising from her profession or industry if the conjugal partnership has been benefited. [Art. 113].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, since your dental practice is your exclusive property and your husband is not involved or benefited, that provision does not apply.

Can you explain Article 105 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding legal separation and the care of minor children?

Article 105 provides that during the pendency of legal separation proceedings, the court is required to make arrangements for the care of minor children based on the circumstances. Mahalagang suriin ang mga tiyak na pangyayari at ebidensya upang matukoy ang tamang aplikasyon ng batas.

STATUTORY TEXT: The expenses, costs and liabilities in suits brought with regard to the usufruct shall be borne by the usufructuary.

I inherited a usufruct over a piece of agricultural land from my mother, while my sister owns the naked title. Recently, my sister filed a court case claiming that I am not allowed to harvest the mango fruits because she says my usufruct is limited to the house only. I believe my usufruct covers the entire property including the trees. Who is responsible for paying the lawyer's fees and court costs in this case?

Your sister, as the naked owner, is not liable for those litigation costs because the lawsuit concerns the usufruct itself and not the naked ownership.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 602 of the Philippine Civil Code, the expenses, costs, and liabilities in suits brought with regard to the usufruct shall be borne by the usufructuary. [Art. 602].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the court case filed by your sister directly questions the extent of your usufruct—specifically whether it includes the right to harvest mango fruits. This is clearly a suit 'with regard to the usufruct.' Therefore, as the usufructuary, you are responsible for bearing the lawyer's fees, court costs, and any other litigation expenses or liabilities arising from that case. Even if you win the case, the costs of the litigation are your responsibility under the law, unless the court awards costs in your favor under the Rules of Court or another provision, but Article 602 establishes the general rule that the usufructuary shoulders these expenses.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 602, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.

You may file a case for reduction to the extent necessary to protect your legitime.

Can you explain Article 1516 of the Civil Code? What warranties does a person who transfers a document of title give?

Article 1516 of the Civil Code provides that when a person transfers a document of title (like a warehouse receipt or bill of lading) for value, either by indorsement or delivery, or assigns for value a claim secured by such a document, that person makes certain implied warranties to the transferee. These warranties are: (1) the document is genuine; (2) the transferor has a legal right to negotiate or transfer it; (3) the transferor has no knowledge of any fact that would impair the validity or worth of the document; and (4) the transferor has the right to transfer title to the goods, and the goods themselves are merchantable or fit for a particular purpose, but only to the same extent as if the contract had been to transfer the goods directly without a document of title. These warranties protect the person receiving the document by ensuring they can rely on its authenticity and the transferor's authority.

STATUTORY TEXT: Responsibility arising from negligence in the performance of every kind of obligation is also demandable, but such liability may be regulated by the courts, according to the circumstances.

I hired a contractor to renovate my kitchen. He was negligent and left the electrical wiring exposed, which caused a fire that damaged my property. I want to claim damages from him for all the losses I suffered. Can the court reduce his liability? How does Article 1172 apply to my situation?

Ultimately, while you can hold the contractor responsible, the exact compensation may be adjusted by the court to achieve a fair result under the facts of your case.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1172, the contractor's negligence in performing his obligation to renovate your kitchen properly makes him liable for the damages you suffered from the fire. You have the right to demand compensation. However, the court is not obligated to award the full amount of your claimed damages. Article 1172 allows the courts to regulate the liability according to the circumstances. The court may consider the degree of negligence—whether it was simple or gross—any contributory negligence on your part, the foreseeability of the harm, and other equitable factors. [Art. 1172].

### 💡 Application to Facts
For example, if the contractor's negligence was gross and the fire was a direct and foreseeable consequence, the court may hold him fully liable. But if there were mitigating circumstances, such as you having some fault or the damage being partly due to an unforeseen event, the court may reduce the amount of damages.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

I had a debt that was already prescribed, so the creditor couldn't sue me anymore. Without my knowledge, a friend paid that debt for me. Later, I voluntarily reimbursed my friend. Now I regret it and want to get my money back. Can I recover what I paid to my friend?

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1425 of the Civil Code, when a third person pays a debt that has prescribed without the debtor's knowledge or against the debtor's will, the debtor is not legally bound to reimburse the third person. However, if the debtor later voluntarily reimburses the third person, the debtor cannot recover what he has paid. [Art. 1425].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the debt was already prescribed, and your friend paid it without your knowledge. You then voluntarily reimbursed your friend. This voluntary reimbursement is considered a fulfillment of a natural obligation, which is binding in conscience. Therefore, you cannot recover the amount you paid to your friend.

Can you explain Article 1526 of the Philippine Civil Code about the rights of an unpaid seller?

Article 1526 lists the rights of a seller who has not been paid for goods. Regardless of whether ownership of the goods has already passed to the buyer, the unpaid seller has: (1) a lien on the goods, meaning the right to keep possession of them until the price is paid; (2) if the buyer becomes insolvent, the right to stop the goods while they are in transit, even after the seller has given up possession; (3) a right to resell the goods, subject to certain limitations in the law; and (4) a right to rescind or cancel the sale, also subject to limitations. If ownership has not yet passed to the buyer, the unpaid seller also has the right to withhold delivery, which is similar to the rights of lien and stoppage in transit that apply when ownership has passed.

The phrase 'my land' can be reasonably interpreted as referring to his own interest, but it does not clearly indicate an intention to give the whole land. Therefore, the legacy is presumed limited to his 50% share. You will only inherit his share, not the entire land. [Art. 929].

Puwede po bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 912 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa pagbabawas ng mga pamana kapag hindi mahahati ang ari-arian?

Ang Artikulo 912 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas ay tumatalakay sa sitwasyon kung saan ang isang devise (pamana ng real property sa testamento) ay kailangang bawasan dahil lumalabag ito sa legitime ng mga compulsory heirs, at ang property ay hindi madaling hatiin. Nakasaad dito: Kung ang kailangang bawasan ay mas mababa sa kalahati ng halaga ng property, mapupunta ang property sa devisee, ngunit dapat bayaran ng devisee ang mga compulsory heirs ng cash para sa kanilang bahagi. Bukod pa rito, kung ang devisee mismo ay isang compulsory heir na may karapatan sa legitime, maaari niyang panatilihin ang buong property kung ang halaga nito ay hindi lalampas sa disposable portion at sa kanyang sariling legitime.

STATUTORY TEXT: Any marriage subsequently contracted by any person during the lifetime of the first spouse of such person with any person other than such first spouse shall be illegal and void from its performance, unless:
(1) The first marriage was annulled or dissolved; or
(2) The first spouse had been absent for seven consecutive years at the time of the second marriage without the spouse present having news of the absentee being alive, or if the absentee, though he has been absent for less than seven years, is generally considered as dead and believed to be so by the spouse present at the time of contracting such subsequent marriage, or if the absentee is presumed dead according to articles 390 and 391. The marriage so contracted shall be valid in any of the three cases until declared null and void by a competent court.

My spouse has been missing for over seven years. I have not received any news that he is still alive. I plan to marry again. If I proceed, is my subsequent marriage valid, or will it be considered bigamous?

Therefore, your planned marriage would not be considered void from the start, but it would be voidable, subject to judicial declaration of nullity.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 83 of the Civil Code, your situation falls under the exception where the first spouse has been absent for seven consecutive years without the spouse present having news of the absentee being alive. In such a case, a subsequent marriage contracted by you will be valid from its performance. However, this validity is not absolute: the subsequent marriage remains valid only until a competent court declares it null and void. [Art. 83].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This means that while you can marry and the marriage will be recognized as valid initially, it is vulnerable to being annulled if it is later proven that your first spouse was actually alive at the time you contracted the second marriage.

Can you explain Article 1470 of the Philippine Civil Code about gross inadequacy of price?

Article 1470 states that gross inadequacy of price does not, by itself, affect the validity of a contract of sale. Even if the price is very low compared to the actual value of the thing sold, the sale remains valid and binding. However, there are two exceptions: first, if the gross inadequacy of price indicates a defect in the consent of one of the parties (such as fraud, mistake, intimidation, or undue influence), the contract may be annulled on that ground; second, if the price is so low that it shows the parties really intended a donation or some other act or contract, then the transaction will be treated according to their true intent. In other words, inadequate price alone is not a ground to invalidate a sale, but it can be a warning sign that the consent was flawed or that the parties did not truly intend a sale.

Can you explain Article 962 of the Philippine Civil Code about who inherits when there is no will?

Article 962 states that in legal or intestate succession, the relative nearest in degree to the deceased excludes more distant relatives. For example, children inherit before grandchildren, and siblings inherit before nieces or nephews, unless the right of representation applies (such as when a child predeceases the parent, and that child's own children take their place). Can you explain Article 144 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding property of unmarried couples living together?

Article 144 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that when a man and a woman live together as husband and wife but are not married, or their marriage is void from the beginning, any property acquired by either or both of them through their work or industry or their wages and salaries shall be governed by the rules on co-ownership. This means that such property is owned in common by both partners. The rules on co-ownership apply, so each partner has an undivided interest in the property, and they may demand partition or prove their respective shares. Unless proven otherwise, their shares are presumed equal.

I shipped a package worth P50,000 through a courier. The waybill I signed contained a clause stating that the carrier's liability is limited to P500 regardless of the actual value, unless a higher value is declared and an extra fee paid. I did not declare a higher value. The package was lost. Is that limitation clause valid under Philippine law?

Since you did not declare a higher value and presumably accepted the terms, the limitation may be upheld, but you may argue that it is unconscionable if P500 is extremely low compared to the value and you were not adequately informed.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1750 of the Civil Code, a contract fixing the sum that may be recovered for loss of goods is valid if it is reasonable and just under the circumstances and has been fairly and freely agreed upon. [Art. 1750].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the clause limiting liability to P500 may be valid if the carrier gave you a fair opportunity to declare a higher value by paying a reasonable extra charge, and the limitation was clearly communicated, not hidden in fine print, and you freely agreed to it. However, if the limitation is grossly disproportionate to the actual value, or if the carrier misrepresented the terms, or if you were not given a real choice, the clause may be considered unreasonable or not freely agreed upon and thus void. The court will weigh these factors.

Article 860 states that in a will, the testator can substitute two or more persons to take the place of a single heir, or substitute one person to take the place of two or more heirs. STATUTORY TEXT: When the obligee accepts the performance, knowing its incompleteness or irregularity, and without expressing any protest or objection, the obligation is deemed fully complied with.

I delivered 100 sacks of rice to a store as agreed. The owner accepted only 95 sacks and did not complain at the time of delivery. A week later, he is demanding that I deliver the missing 5 sacks or pay for them. Does he have the right to demand?

But based on the facts given, since he accepted without protest knowing the quantity was short, he has no right to demand.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1235 of the Civil Code, if the store owner accepted the delivery of 95 sacks knowing that the agreed quantity was 100 sacks (i.e., knowing the incompleteness), and did not express any protest or objection at the time of acceptance, then the obligation to deliver 100 sacks is deemed fully complied with. The owner's acceptance without objection constitutes a waiver of the deficiency. Therefore, he cannot later demand the missing 5 sacks or claim damages for the short delivery, because the obligation is considered extinguished. The key is that the acceptance must be made with knowledge of the incompleteness and without protest. [Art. 1235].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the owner did not actually know of the shortage at the time of acceptance (e.g., the shortage was concealed and only discovered later), Article 1235 would not apply, and he may still have a right to claim.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

That easement is attached to your land, not to the previous owner personally. When you bought the land, the easement automatically transferred to you as the new owner. Your neighbor cannot unilaterally revoke or block that right of way just because ownership changed. The easement continues to exist as long as the dominant estate needs it, and it binds the servient estate regardless of who owns it.

Can you explain Article 955 of the Philippine Civil Code about renouncing legacies and devises?

Article 955 governs how a legatee or devisee may renounce multiple legacies or devises given to them. If one legacy/devise is onerous (with a burden or condition) and the other is gratuitous (without burden), the legatee cannot accept the gratuitous one and renounce the onerous one; they must accept both or renounce both, unless the testator intended them to be inseparable. If both are onerous or both gratuitous, the legatee may freely accept or renounce both, or accept one and renounce the other. However, if the testator specified that the two legacies/devises are inseparable, then the legatee must accept or renounce both together. Additionally, a compulsory heir who is also given a legacy or devise may choose to waive their inheritance (their share as forced heir) and accept the legacy/devise, or renounce the legacy/devise and accept the inheritance, or accept or renounce both.

STATUTORY TEXT: The preterition or omission of one, some, or all of the compulsory heirs in the direct line, whether living at the time of the execution of the will or born after the death of the testator, shall annul the institution of heir; but the devises and legacies shall be valid insofar as they are not inofficious.
If the omitted compulsory heirs should die before the testator, the institution shall be effectual, without prejudice to the right of representation.

I am a widower with two legitimate children. I executed a will in 2020 where I instituted my second wife as my sole heir, and I also gave a specific parcel of land to a friend as a legacy. I did not mention my children in the will. Now I have passed away, and my children are contesting the will. What happens to the institution of my second wife as heir and to the legacy to my friend? My children are still alive. They say the will is invalid as to the heir, but what about the legacy? Please explain.

The right of representation does not apply here because the omitted compulsory heirs did not die before you.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 854 of the Philippine Civil Code, the omission of compulsory heirs in the direct line from a will constitutes preterition. [Art. 854].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In this scenario, your two legitimate children are compulsory heirs in the direct line, and they were alive at the time of execution of the will and at your death. Since you did not mention them in the will, preterition occurred. The effect is that the institution of your second wife as sole heir is annulled; she cannot inherit as an instituted heir. However, the legacy of the specific parcel of land to your friend remains valid insofar as it is not inofficious. This means the legacy is valid only if it does not impair the legitime of your children. The legitime of legitimate children is one-half of the entire estate, divided equally between them. The other half is the free portion that you may dispose of by will, including through legacies. If the value of the land given as legacy does not exceed the free portion, the legacy stands in full. If it exceeds the free portion, the legacy will be reduced to the extent of the inofficiousness. Since your children are alive, the institution of heir is void, but the legacy can be valid if it does not encroach on their legitime.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 555(4) of the Civil Code, a possessor may lose possession by the possession of another, provided the new possession has lasted longer than one year, subject to Article 537. [Art. 555].

Can you explain Article 559 of the Philippine Civil Code to me?

Article 559 states that the possession of movable property acquired in good faith is equivalent to a title. This means that if a person buys or acquires movable property (like a car, jewelry, or electronics) in good faith, not knowing that the seller is not the true owner, the possessor is treated as if he has a valid title to the property. However, there is an exception: if the property was lost by the original owner or the owner was unlawfully deprived of it (for example, through theft), the owner may recover it from the current possessor, even if the possessor acquired it in good faith. But if the current possessor bought the movable at a public sale (such as an auction) in good faith, the owner cannot recover the property without reimbursing the price paid by the possessor. This article balances the protection of good faith buyers with the rights of true owners.

However, this is subject to the rule on inofficious donations. [Art. 1062].

I have a loan with two co-borrowers. The loan agreement does not say that we are solidarily liable. The lender is now demanding that I pay the entire amount. Can they do that under Philippine law? Please explain Article 1207.

Your liability is limited to your proportionate part of the debt.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1207 of the Civil Code, when there are two or more debtors in one and the same obligation, the presumption is that the obligation is joint, not solidary. This means each debtor is bound to pay only his proportionate share of the debt, and the creditor cannot demand from one debtor the entire prestation unless solidarity is expressly stipulated, or required by law or the nature of the obligation. [Art. 1207].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, since the loan agreement does not provide for solidary liability, the obligation is joint. Therefore, the lender cannot legally demand that you alone pay the entire amount. The lender may only require you to pay your share of the loan, and must collect the other shares from the other co-borrowers separately.

STATUTORY TEXT: Real contracts, such as deposit, pledge and commodatum, are not perfected until the delivery of the object of the obligation.

Mario borrowed ₱100,000 from Juan. They signed a written agreement stating that Mario pledges his motorcycle as security for the loan. However, Mario never delivered the motorcycle to Juan because he continued using it. Later, Mario failed to pay the loan. Juan now claims he can foreclose on the motorcycle because the pledge was perfected by their written agreement. Mario insists there was no valid pledge because he never surrendered the motorcycle. Who is correct?

He may still pursue Mario for the unpaid loan based on the loan contract, but he cannot enforce the pledge over the motorcycle.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1316, a pledge is a real contract that is not perfected until the delivery of the object of the obligation. [Art. 1316].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In this case, although Mario and Juan had a written agreement stipulating that the motorcycle would serve as security, the motorcycle was never delivered to Juan. Therefore, the contract of pledge was never perfected. Without delivery, there is no valid pledge. Consequently, Juan cannot foreclose on the motorcycle as a pledgee because no real contract of pledge exists.

Can you explain Article 1140 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 1140 provides that the right to file a court case to recover possession of movable (personal) property prescribes, or expires, after eight years from the time the owner lost possession of the property. This means that if the owner does not sue within eight years from losing the item, the action is generally barred. However, there are exceptions: if the person currently in possession has already acquired ownership of the property through prescription in a shorter period (such as three years if in good faith and with just title, or six years without these conditions, as provided in Article 1132), then the owner's action is cut short even before the eight-year period ends. The article also states that this rule is without prejudice to other provisions, including Article 559 (which allows recovery from a good faith possessor under certain conditions, sometimes with reimbursement), Article 1505 (which deals with sales by non-owners and when a buyer may get valid title), and Article 1133 (which prevents a thief from acquiring ownership by prescription).

Can you explain what Article 220 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 220 of the Philippine Civil Code states that when there is any doubt or ambiguity in legal or factual matters concerning the family, the law presumes in favor of family solidarity and unity. This means that courts and authorities should lean towards upholding the family as a strong and stable unit. Specifically, the law provides that every interpretation of law or facts should favor: (1) the validity of marriage, so a marriage is presumed valid unless clearly proven otherwise; (2) the indissolubility of the marriage bonds, meaning marriage is intended to be permanent; (3) the legitimacy of children, so children born to a married couple are presumed legitimate; (4) the community of property during marriage, meaning spouses are presumed to own property jointly; (5) the authority of parents over their children, so parental authority is presumed; and (6) the validity of defense for any family member in case of unlawful aggression, meaning a family member acting to defend another is presumed to be acting lawfully. In short, the law resolves doubts in favor of protecting the family.

Can you explain Article 1271 of the Philippine Civil Code?

If a creditor voluntarily gives back to the debtor a private document that proves the debt (like a promissory note or IOU), it is presumed that the creditor is renouncing or forgiving the debt. This means the creditor loses the right to sue for collection. However, if someone claims that this renunciation is inofficious (meaning it is an excessive or illegal donation that prejudices heirs), the debtor and his heirs can defend the validity of the delivery by proving that the document was returned because the debt was actually paid. So, the return of the document can either be a remission (forgiveness) or evidence of payment, depending on what is proven.

Can you explain Article 1125 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when it says recognition interrupts possession?

Article 1125 states that if a person who is possessing a property (the possessor) acknowledges, either expressly (in words or writing) or tacitly (through actions implying recognition), that the property actually belongs to another person (the owner), then the possession is interrupted. This means the period of time for acquiring ownership through prescription stops running because the possessor is no longer claiming the property as their own in a way that is adverse to the owner. In short, recognizing the owner's right breaks the continuity of possession needed for adverse possession.

STATUTORY TEXT: The creditor has a right to the fruits of the thing from the time the obligation to deliver it arises. However, he shall acquire no real right over it until the same has been delivered to him.

I agreed to buy a mango farm from a seller. The contract was signed last month, but the seller will only turn over the property next month. The mangoes are being harvested now. Am I entitled to the mangoes even though I haven't received the property yet?

Thus, you can claim the mangoes as fruits, but ownership of the land transfers only upon delivery.

Under Article 1164 of the Civil Code, you, as the creditor (buyer), have the right to the fruits of the thing from the time the obligation to deliver it arises. In a contract of sale, the obligation to deliver generally arises upon the perfection of the contract, which typically occurs when there is a meeting of the minds on the object and the price. Since your contract was signed last month, the obligation to deliver the mango farm already arose at that time. Therefore, you are entitled to the mangoes harvested now, even though actual delivery of the property will happen next month. [Art. 1164].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, note that while you have a personal right to the fruits, you do not acquire a real right (ownership) over the farm itself until it is actually delivered to you.

Can you explain Article 91 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about damages in annulment or void marriages?

Article 91 of the Civil Code allows the court to award damages when a marriage is judicially annulled or declared void from the beginning, in specific situations where one party was at fault or concealed important facts. These situations include: (1) fraud, force, or intimidation in obtaining consent; (2) one party was physically incapable of entering into the married state and the other party was unaware; (3) the person solemnizing the marriage was not legally authorized, and one party knew but concealed it from the other; (4) a bigamous or polygamous marriage where the impediment was concealed by the disqualified party; (5) an incestuous marriage or other prohibited marriage under Article 82 where the relationship was known to only one party and not disclosed; (6) one party was insane and the other was aware at the time of marriage. In these cases, the innocent party may be entitled to damages.

Can you explain Article 1545 of the Philippine Civil Code about conditions and warranties in sales?

Article 1545 of the Civil Code states that if a party's obligation under a sales contract is subject to a condition that is not performed, that party may either refuse to proceed with the contract or waive the performance of the condition. If the other party promised that the condition would happen or be performed, the first party may also treat the non-performance of the condition as a breach of warranty. Additionally, if ownership of the thing has not yet passed to the buyer, the buyer may consider the seller's obligation to deliver the thing as described and as warranted (expressly or impliedly) as a condition of the buyer's own obligation to accept and pay for the thing.

STATUTORY TEXT: If the testator orders the payment of what he believes he owes but does not in fact owe, the disposition shall be considered as not written. If as regards a specified debt more than the amount thereof is ordered paid, the excess is not due, unless a contrary intention appears.
The foregoing provisions are without prejudice to the fulfillment of natural obligations.

My father passed away and left a will. In the will, he ordered us to pay his friend Juan a debt of PHP 100,000. But when we checked his records, we found out he only owed Juan PHP 50,000. He also ordered us to pay another person, Pedro, a debt of PHP 20,000, but we later discovered that he never actually owed Pedro anything. Do we have to follow these instructions in the will? What does the law say?

However, if the payment to Pedro or the excess to Juan is based on a natural obligation (a moral duty not legally enforceable but voluntarily performable), the law allows you to fulfill it if you choose to do so, but you are not legally compelled.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 939 of the Civil Code, the instruction to pay Pedro PHP 20,000 is considered not written because your father believed he owed a debt but in fact did not owe any. That provision in the will is void, and you are not legally required to pay Pedro. [Art. 939].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Regarding the payment to Juan, since the actual debt is only PHP 50,000 but the will orders payment of PHP 100,000, the excess PHP 50,000 is not due unless the will clearly shows that your father intended to give the extra amount as a gift or liberality. If there is no such contrary intention, you are only obligated to pay Juan the actual debt of PHP 50,000.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

Ang Artikulo 523 ay nagbibigay ng pangunahing kahulugan na maaaring gamitin sa iyong paghahabol, ngunit kailangan mong suriin ang iba pang probisyon tungkol sa prescription upang malaman kung ang iyong posesyon ay maaaring maging pagmamay-ari.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 523, ang posesyon ay ang paghawak ng isang bagay o ang pagtatamasa ng isang karapatan. [Art. 523].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Sa iyong sitwasyon, ang iyong paggamit ng lupa bilang daanan ay isang anyo ng posesyon: hawak mo ang bagay (ang lupa) sa pamamagitan ng aktwal na paggamit at kontrol dito, at tinatamasa mo ang karapatan ng pagdaan. Ang posesyon ay hindi nangangahulugang pagmamay-ari; ito ay isang katotohanang kalagayan. Gayunpaman, ang patuloy na posesyon sa loob ng mahabang panahon ay maaaring maging batayan para sa pagkuha ng pagmamay-ari sa pamamagitan ng acquisitive prescription, kung matutugunan ang mga kundisyon ng batas (halimbawa, posesyon sa konsepto ng may-ari, pampubliko, mapayapa, at walang patid).

Can you explain Article 1407 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1407 deals with contracts where both parties are incapable of giving consent, such as minors or persons of unsound mind. It states that if the parent or guardian of one party ratifies the contract, the contract is treated as if only one party was incapacitated. This means the contract becomes voidable – the incapacitated party whose guardian did not ratify may still seek annulment, but the other party is bound. If the parents or guardians of both parties ratify the contract, then the contract is validated from the very beginning, as if both parties had capacity from the start.

The owner may demand passage through neighboring estates after paying proper indemnity. If the easement is permanent and continuous, indemnity includes the value of the land occupied plus damages to the servient estate. If it is only a temporary passage for cultivation and gathering of crops without a permanent way, indemnity is limited to actual damages caused. However, this easement is not compulsory if the isolation was caused by the owner's own acts.

Can you explain Article 580 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding usufruct and set-off of improvements against damages?

Article 580 states that a usufructuary (a person who has the right to use and enjoy another's property) may offset the value of improvements he has made on the property against any damage he has caused to it. This means if the usufructuary improved the property (e.g., added useful or necessary repairs) and also caused some damage, he can use the value of the improvements to reduce or eliminate his liability for the damage. The set-off is not automatic but may be claimed. It is subject to the rules on usufruct, particularly the duty to preserve the property and not make alterations that reduce its value. The improvement must be legitimate and the damage must be compensable.

Can you explain Article 991 of the Philippine Civil Code about inheritance when there are illegitimate children and legitimate ascendants?

Article 991 applies when a person dies without a will (intestate) and leaves behind illegitimate children and legitimate ascendants (like parents or grandparents), but no legitimate children or descendants. In that case, the estate is divided into two equal halves: the illegitimate children as a group receive one-half of the estate, and the legitimate ascendants as a group receive the other half. The number of illegitimate children or ascendants does not change this 50-50 split. Within each group, the members share their respective half equally or according to the rules for ascendants.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 80 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas. Anong mga kasal ang walang bisa mula sa simula?

Ang Artikulo 80 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay naglilista ng mga kasal na walang bisa mula pa sa simula, ibig sabihin ay walang legal na epekto kahit kailan, parang hindi nangyari. Kabilang dito: (1) mga kasal kung saan ang lalaki ay wala pang 16 na taong gulang o ang babae ay wala pang 14, kahit may pahintulot ng mga magulang; (2) mga kasal na isinagawa ng taong hindi awtorisadong magkasal; (3) mga kasal na walang lisensya sa kasal, maliban sa mga pambihirang kaso na pinapayagan ng batas (tulad ng kasal sa artikulo mortis o sa malalayong lugar); (4) bigamous o polygamous na kasal na hindi saklaw ng mga eksepsyon sa Artikulo 83, bilang 2; (5) incestuous na kasal ayon sa Artikulo 81; (6) mga kasal kung saan ang isa o parehong partido ay nahatulan ng pagpatay sa asawa ng alinman sa kanila; at (7) mga kasal sa pagitan ng mga stepbrother at stepsister at iba pang tinukoy sa Artikulo 82. Ang mga kasal na ito ay void ab initio, kaya walang nabubuong legal na karapatan o obligasyon sa pagitan ng mga partido.

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, as co-heirs, you and your other siblings have the right to recover damages from your disqualified brother for the value of the property or any loss you suffered due to his act.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1599 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa mga remedyo ng buyer kapag may breach of warranty sa bilihan.

Ang Artikulo 1599 ay nagbibigay sa buyer ng ilang pagpipilian kapag nagkaroon ng breach of warranty ang seller. Maaaring: (1) itago ang mga kalakal at bawasan o alisin ang presyo; (2) itago ang mga kalakal at magsampa ng kaso para sa danyos; (3) tanggihan ang mga kalakal at magsampa ng kaso para sa danyos; o (4) ipawalang-bisa ang kontrata at ibalik ang mga kalakal (o mag-alok na ibalik ang mga ito) at mabawi ang anumang bayad. Kapag napili at naigawad na ang isang remedyo, hindi na maaaring lumipat sa iba, alinsunod sa Artikulo 1191. Hindi pinapayagan ang pagpapawalang-bisa kung tinanggap ng buyer ang mga kalakal na alam ang breach, hindi nag-abiso sa seller sa loob ng makatwirang panahon, o hindi naibalik ang mga kalakal sa halos parehong kondisyon (maliban kung ang pagkasira ay dulot ng breach). Kung valid ang pagpapawalang-bisa, hindi na mananagot ang buyer sa presyo, at dapat ibalik ng seller ang anumang bayad kapag naibalik o inalok na ibalik ang mga kalakal. Kung tumanggi ang seller na tanggapin ang pagbabalik, ang buyer ay magiging bailee na may lien para sa bayad na presyo. Para sa breach ng warranty sa kalidad, ang danyos ay karaniwang ang pagkakaiba ng halaga ng mga kalakal sa oras ng delivery at ang halaga sana kung sumunod ito sa warranty.

Can you explain Article 1473 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the fixing of price in a sale?

Article 1473 states that the fixing of the price in a contract of sale cannot be left to the discretion of only one of the contracting parties. This means that one party cannot unilaterally determine the price without the agreement of the other. However, there is an exception: if the price fixed by one party is accepted by the other party, the sale is perfected. In other words, the prohibition is against unilateral determination without consent, but if the other party agrees to the price, mutual consent is achieved and the contract becomes valid.

I bought a second-hand car from a neighbor who did not yet have the certificate of registration under his name. Based on Article 1459 of the Civil Code, the sale of the car is valid as long as the seller has the right to transfer ownership at the time of delivery. The law does not require that the seller be the owner at the time of the contract; it only requires that at the time the thing is delivered to you, he has the right to transfer its ownership. In your case, if your neighbor acquires the ownership (or obtains the authority to sell) by the time he delivers the car, then the sale is valid. The car is a licit object, so that requirement is satisfied. However, if he fails to acquire such right by the time of delivery, he cannot fulfill his obligation to transfer ownership, and he may be liable for breach of contract, but the sale itself is not automatically void just because he was not the owner at the time of the contract.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1544 of the Civil Code, when the same immovable property is sold to different buyers, the ownership belongs to the buyer who first records the sale in the Registry of Property, provided they acted in good faith. [Art. 1544].

Can you explain Article 492 of the Philippine Civil Code about co-ownership?

Article 492 states that when property is co-owned, decisions about its administration and better enjoyment are made by majority vote of the co-owners. However, majority is determined not by the number of co-owners but by the value of their shares—those who own more than half of the property's value must agree. If no such majority exists, or if the majority's decision is seriously harmful to the other co-owners, any interested co-owner can ask the court to step in. The court may then order appropriate measures, such as appointing an administrator. Also, if one co-owner exclusively owns a part of the property while the rest is co-owned, these rules apply only to the co-owned portion.

Can you explain Article 197 of the Philippine Civil Code about the wife being transferred administration of all property?

Under the system of absolute community, if the administration of all the property of the marriage is transferred to the wife, she has the same powers and responsibilities as the husband would have if he were the administrator. What does Article 331 of the Philippine Civil Code say about the suspension of parental authority?

Article 331 of the Civil Code states that parental authority is suspended (temporarily set aside) in the following situations: (1) when the father is judicially declared incapable, (2) when the father is judicially declared absent, (3) when the mother, in cases where she is the one exercising parental authority, is judicially declared incapable or absent, and (4) when the parent is under civil interdiction. Suspension means the parent temporarily loses the right to exercise parental authority over the child, but this can be restored if the condition ends (e.g., the parent reappears or regains capacity).

In your case, you borrowed ₱100,000 in 1980 when that amount had significant purchasing power. This means you cannot simply pay ₱100,000; instead, you must pay an amount that reflects the original purchasing power of ₱100,000 in 1980, unless you and your friend had agreed otherwise.

In summary, your prenuptial donation is limited to 1/5 of your current assets, and any future property must be left by will.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

This means you can give her a portion of your current house and savings, but the total value of the donation cannot exceed 1/5 of your present assets. However, you cannot donate your future inheritance or any future property in the marriage settlement. The law specifically states that with respect to future property, donations can only be made in the event of death, and only to the extent allowed by the rules on testamentary succession. Therefore, you cannot promise to give her a share of your future inheritance in the prenuptial agreement. If you want to provide for her from your future property, you must do so through a will, subject to the limitations on testamentary dispositions, including the legitime of forced heirs.

What does Article 909 of the Philippine Civil Code say about donations and how they affect the legitime and disposable portion of an estate?

Article 909 provides that donations given to children are considered advances on their legitime, meaning the value of such donations is deducted from the child's share of the reserved portion of the estate. Donations made to strangers (those who are not compulsory heirs) are charged against the disposable free portion—the part of the estate that the testator could freely dispose of by will. If any such donations are inofficious (i.e., they exceed the disposable portion), they must be reduced according to the rules on inofficious donations under the Civil Code. This ensures that the legitime of compulsory heirs is protected.

Can you explain Article 203 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the payment of debts of spouses?

Article 203 of the Civil Code states that debts contracted by both spouses, or by one spouse with the consent of the other, are considered common debts. These debts must be paid from the community property (the common assets of the spouses). If the community property is insufficient to cover these common debts, the creditors can enforce payment against the separate property of each spouse. In that case, both spouses are equally liable, meaning each spouse is responsible for an equal share of the debt.

STATUTORY TEXT: Expenses for pure luxury or mere pleasure shall not be refunded to the possessor in good faith; but he may remove the ornaments with which he has embellished the principal thing if it suffers no injury thereby, and if his successor in the possession does not prefer to refund the amount expended.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 548 of the Civil Code, as a possessor in good faith, you cannot demand reimbursement for expenses incurred for pure luxury or mere pleasure, such as the crystal chandelier and expensive wall paintings. Can you explain Article 1424 of the Philippine Civil Code about natural obligations?

Article 1424 states that if a creditor's right to sue on a civil obligation has already lapsed due to extinctive prescription (meaning the legal action is barred), and the debtor still voluntarily fulfills the obligation, the debtor cannot later recover what he delivered or the value of the service rendered. In other words, even though the obligation can no longer be enforced in court, voluntary performance turns it into a natural obligation, and the law prevents the debtor from demanding restitution.

Can you explain Article 1441 of the Philippine Civil Code about trusts?

Article 1441 states that trusts are either express or implied. An express trust is created by the clear intention of the trustor (the person creating the trust) or the parties involved. An implied trust, on the other hand, arises not from an explicit agreement but by operation of law, typically to prevent unjust enrichment or to enforce equity. So, if someone explicitly sets up a trust, it's express; if the law creates a trust due to circumstances, it's implied.

Can you explain Article 939 of the Philippine Civil Code about a testator ordering payment of a debt he believes he owes?

Article 939 says that if a person making a will (testator) orders payment of a debt that he thinks he owes but actually does not owe, that part of the will is considered void or not written. I lent money to a friend and he signed a note saying he will pay when his means permit him to do so. It's been two years and he hasn't paid anything, always saying he still doesn't have the means. What can I do? Can I demand payment now? Under Article 1180, what are my rights?

You cannot unilaterally demand immediate payment unless it can be shown that his means already permit him to pay, but you can file a case in court to have a period fixed, and if he fails to pay within that period, you can enforce the obligation.

STATUTORY TEXT: Unless otherwise agreed, the buyer of goods is not bound to accept delivery thereof by instalments.
Where there is a contract of sale of goods to be delivered by stated instalments, which are to be separately paid for, and the seller makes defective deliveries in respect of one or more installments, or the buyer neglects or refuses without just cause to take delivery of or pay for one or more instalments, it depends in each case on the terms of the contract and the circumstances of the case, whether the breach of contract is so material as to justify the injured party in refusing to proceed further and suing for damages for breach of the entire contract, or whether the breach is severable, giving rise to a claim for compensation but not to a right to treat the whole contract as broken.

I ordered 1,000 sacks of rice from a supplier, to be delivered in four instalments of 250 sacks each, with each instalment paid upon delivery. The first two instalments were fine. In the third instalment, 50 sacks were infested with weevils and not usable. I refused to accept the third instalment and told the supplier I am cancelling the whole contract and want a refund for the defective sacks plus damages for the entire contract. The supplier says the contract is still valid and I should just get a replacement or credit for the 50 sacks. What does the law say about my right to cancel the whole contract?

Absent such circumstances or agreement, you would generally not be justified in cancelling the whole contract; you must accept the remaining instalments and seek remedy only for the defective portion.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1583, your right to cancel the entire contract depends on whether the defective delivery in the third instalment constitutes a material breach of the whole contract. Since the contract provides for delivery in four instalments with separate payments, the breach in one instalment may be treated as severable if it does not substantially impair the value of the entire contract. [Art. 1583].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Here, only 50 out of 250 sacks in the third instalment were defective, and the first two instalments were properly delivered. This suggests the defect is likely limited and severable, allowing you to claim compensation for the defective sacks (e.g., replacement or price reduction) but not necessarily to terminate the entire contract. However, if the infestation indicates a systemic problem that would affect future instalments or if the contract expressly provides that any defect in one instalment allows cancellation, then the breach could be considered material.

STATUTORY TEXT: To be of sound mind, it is not necessary that the testator be in full possession of all his reasoning faculties, or that his mind be wholly unbroken, unimpaired, or unshattered by disease, injury or other cause.

My father is 78 years old and was recently diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's disease. He sometimes forgets recent events but still knows his properties and recognizes all his children. He wants to make a will now. Is he allowed to do so? I'm worried his will might be contested because of his condition.

It is advisable, however, to ensure that the will is executed properly and perhaps have a medical evaluation close to the time of execution to support his capacity if ever challenged.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 799 of the Civil Code, a testator does not need to be in full possession of all reasoning faculties, nor must the mind be wholly unbroken or unimpaired by disease. It is sufficient if at the time of making the will, the testator was able to know: (1) the nature of the estate to be disposed of, (2) the proper objects of his bounty (the persons who would normally inherit), and (3) the character of the testamentary act (that he is making a will). [Art. 799].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your father's case, if despite his early-stage Alzheimer's he can still identify his properties, recognize his children as his natural heirs, and understand that he is executing a will, then he has the requisite testamentary capacity. The fact that he sometimes forgets recent events does not automatically disqualify him. As long as these three elements are present at the time of making the will, the will may be valid.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 134 of the Philippine Civil Code, a donation made by a spouse during the marriage to the children of the other spouse by another marriage is voidable at the instance of the donor's heirs after his death. [Art. 134].

You may file the case in court to have the donation declared void and the property returned to your father's estate, subject to the rules on prescription and other legal requirements. The purpose of Article 134 is to protect the donor's own heirs from having their inheritance diminished by donations made to stepchildren or to persons who might be heirs of the other spouse, presumably due to the influence of that spouse.

Under Article 1123 of the Civil Code, civil interruption is produced by judicial summons to the possessor. [Art. 1123].

In your situation, when the registered owner filed a case against you and you were served with the summons, that service constitutes civil interruption of the prescriptive period you are claiming. This means that the running of the 30-year period for extraordinary prescription is stopped from the moment you received the summons. Consequently, you cannot continue counting your possession after that date. The previous 15 years of possession may be considered lost or at least interrupted, and you cannot rely on it to complete the prescriptive period.

Can you explain Article 305 of the Philippine Civil Code about the duty and right to make funeral arrangements for a relative?

This ensures that funeral arrangements are handled by the closest family members according to a legal hierarchy.

Can you explain Article 1165 of the Philippine Civil Code to me?

Article 1165 deals with obligations to deliver a thing. If the thing to be delivered is determinate (specific), the creditor can compel the debtor to make the delivery, in addition to claiming damages under Article 1170. If the thing is indeterminate or generic, the creditor can ask that the obligation be complied with at the debtor's expense. This means that even if the thing is destroyed by an unforeseeable event, the debtor remains liable because of his delay or double promise.

Can you explain Article 983 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 983 states that if a person dies without a will (intestate) and is survived by both legitimate and illegitimate children, the inheritance share of each illegitimate child must be computed using the proportion set in Article 895. Under Article 895, the share of an illegitimate child is one-half of the share of each legitimate child. So, for example, if each legitimate child receives ₱100,000, each illegitimate child will receive ₱50,000. This rule ensures that illegitimate children get a smaller share than legitimate children when both classes of children inherit together.

PROVISION: Article 1370 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 5 - INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS > Art. 1370
STATUTORY TEXT: If the terms of a contract are clear and leave no doubt upon the intention of the contracting parties, the literal meaning of its stipulations shall control.
If the words appear to be contrary to the evident intention of the parties, the latter shall prevail over the former.

I signed a written contract for the sale of a parcel of land. The contract clearly states that the purchase price is ₱500,000. However, the seller is now claiming that our actual agreement was for ₱600,000, and he says we had a verbal understanding before signing that the price would be higher. He is demanding that I pay the additional ₱100,000. The written contract is clear on the price. What should I do? Will the court enforce the written amount or the alleged verbal agreement?

Thus, you are generally entitled to rely on the written contract unless the seller successfully proves that the written words were not the true agreement.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1370 of the Civil Code, if the terms of a contract are clear and leave no doubt upon the intention of the parties, the literal meaning of its stipulations shall control. [Art. 1370].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the written contract states a purchase price of ₱500,000, which appears clear and unambiguous. Therefore, the literal meaning of that stipulation should prevail. However, the second paragraph provides that if the words appear to be contrary to the evident intention of the parties, the latter shall prevail over the former. This means that if the seller can present strong evidence that the true intention of both parties was actually ₱600,000, and the written words do not reflect that intention (for example, due to mistake, fraud, or other compelling circumstances), then the court may give effect to the intention. Can you explain what Article 1410 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 1410 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that the action or defense for the declaration of the inexistence of a contract does not prescribe. This means that there is no time limit for a person to ask a court to declare a contract void (inexistent) from the beginning, or to raise the nullity of the contract as a defense in a legal dispute. My father passed away last month. In his will, he left me his specific farm which includes a mango orchard and a pregnant cow. At the time of his death, there were mangoes still growing on the trees, the cow had not yet given birth, and there was rental income from a tenant for the month before his death that was due but not yet paid. There was also rent due for the month after his death which has not been collected yet. Who is entitled to these items, and if the cow dies after his death, who bears the loss?

Regarding the cow, since the risk of loss or deterioration passed to you from the moment of death, if the cow dies after your father's death, you bear that loss, unless there is fault on the part of the executor or administrator.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 948 of the Civil Code, because the farm is a specific and determinate thing given to you as a legacy, you became the owner of the farm immediately upon your father's death. This ownership extends to the growing mangoes (growing fruits) and the unborn calf (unborn offspring of animals). You are also entitled to the rental income that accrued after your father's death, even if it has not yet been collected, because it is uncollected income arising after death. [Art. 948].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, you are not entitled to the rent that was due and unpaid before your father's death; that belongs to the estate.

If there are other surviving siblings (full or half-blood), the half-brother's share would be one-half the share of a full-blood sibling under Article 1007, but if the half-brother is the only sibling (or only sibling line), his children take the entire estate per stirpes.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, the children of your uncle's deceased half-brother are entitled to inherit. Under Article 1008 of the Civil Code, children of brothers and sisters of the half blood shall succeed per capita or per stirpes, in accordance with the rules laid down for brothers and sisters of the full blood. Since your uncle had no descendants, spouse, or parents, and his half-brother predeceased him, the half-brother's children (your uncle's nephews/nieces) inherit by right of representation of their deceased parent. Under Article 1006, which governs full-blood siblings, if the deceased is survived by siblings and nephews/nieces (children of deceased siblings), the siblings inherit per capita while the nephews/nieces inherit per stirpes. Article 1008 extends this to half-blood siblings: their children inherit per stirpes. [Art. 1008].

Can you explain Article 598 of the Philippine Civil Code about usufruct over a whole patrimony and debts?

Article 598 applies when a usufruct is constituted over the entire estate (patrimony) of a person. If the owner has outstanding debts at that time, the law applies the rules on donations with reservation of usufruct (Article 758) and donations subject to payment of debts (Article 759). This means: (1) the usufruct remains valid and is governed by the rules on usufruct; and (2) the usufructuary is obligated to pay the owner's debts, but only up to the value of the property received in usufruct, unless the parties agree otherwise. The same rule applies if the owner is bound to make periodical payments (like pensions) even without a known capital amount.

Ang mga walang kasalanan na may utang ay may karapatang maningil o maghabol sa nagkasala o nagpabayang kasama. Bukod dito, kung ang pagkawala o imposibilidad ay dulot ng fortuitous event (aksidente o kalamidad) ngunit nangyari ito matapos na ang isa sa mga solidary debtors ay nagkaroon ng delay (naantala) dahil sa demand ng pinagkakautangan, ang patakaran sa may kasalanan ay ilalapat — lahat ng solidary debtors ay mananagot para sa presyo at danyos.

Under Article 1471 of the Civil Code, if the price in a sale is simulated, the sale is void. [Art. 1471].

Can you explain Article 1156 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1156 of the Philippine Civil Code defines an obligation as a juridical necessity to give, to do, or not to do. This means that once an obligation exists, the person bound by it (the obligor or debtor) must comply with what is required—whether it is to deliver something (to give), to perform an act (to do), or to refrain from doing something (not to do). If the obligor fails to fulfill the obligation, the law provides remedies to the obligee (creditor) to compel performance or seek damages. The term 'juridical necessity' emphasizes that the obligation is enforceable by legal processes, distinguishing it from purely moral or social duties.

Ang Artikulo 1403 ay naglilista ng mga kontratang hindi maipatutupad (unenforceable) maliban kung ratipikado. Kabilang dito ang: (1) mga kontratang pinasok ng isang tao para sa iba nang walang awtoridad o lumampas sa kanyang kapangyarihan; (2) mga kontratang hindi sumusunod sa Statute of Frauds, na nangangahulugang ang ilang kasunduan ay dapat nakasulat at nilagdaan ng partidong sinisingil o ng kanyang ahente upang maipatupad. Can you explain Article 1285 of the Philippine Civil Code about compensation in assignment of rights?

Article 1285 governs the debtor's right to claim compensation (set-off) when the creditor assigns his credit to a third person. The rule depends on the debtor's involvement and knowledge:

1. If the debtor consented to the assignment, he cannot set up compensation against the assignee, unless he reserved that right at the time of consent and notified the assignor.
2. If the creditor notified the debtor of the assignment but the debtor did not consent, the debtor may set up compensation for debts owed to him by the assignor that existed before the assignment, but not for debts that arose after the assignment.
3. If the assignment was made without the debtor's knowledge, the debtor may set up compensation for all credits he had against the assignor prior to the assignment, and also for credits that arose after the assignment but before he learned of the assignment.

Can you explain what Article 709 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 709 states that if you have a title of ownership or other rights over real property (like land or buildings) but you do not have it duly inscribed or annotated in the Registry of Property, then that unregistered right will not affect third persons. In simpler terms, if you fail to register your ownership or claim, you cannot use it against someone else who deals with the property based on the public records. Registration gives notice to everyone, and those who rely on the registry are protected.

Can you explain Article 890 of the Philippine Civil Code about the legitime of parents and ascendants?

Article 890 provides the rules for dividing the legitime (forced share) reserved for legitimate parents and ascendants. If both legitimate parents survive the testator, this legitime is divided equally between them. If one parent has predeceased the testator, the entire legitime goes to the surviving parent. If both parents are deceased, the legitime goes to the ascendants: if the surviving ascendants are of equal degree in both the paternal and maternal lines, the legitime is divided equally between the two lines. If the ascendants are of different degrees, the legitime goes entirely to the nearest ascendant(s) in degree, regardless of line.

Can you explain Article 1583 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding delivery of goods by instalments?

Article 1583 provides that, unless otherwise agreed, a buyer of goods is not obligated to accept delivery by instalments. However, if there is a contract for delivery by stated instalments, each separately paid for, and a breach occurs in one or more instalments—such as the seller making defective deliveries or the buyer unjustifiably failing to take or pay for an instalment—the effect depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances. If the breach is so material that it defeats the purpose of the whole contract, the injured party may treat the entire contract as broken and sue for damages for total breach. If the breach is severable, the injured party may only claim compensation for that particular instalment, without the right to terminate the whole contract.

Can you explain Article 934 of the Philippine Civil Code about legacies and devises of pledged or mortgaged property?

Article 934 states that if a testator leaves a specific thing (such as a car, land, or jewelry) that is pledged or mortgaged as security for a debt, the estate is generally required to pay off that debt so the recipient (legatee or devisee) receives the thing free from the pledge or mortgage. This applies whether the pledge or mortgage was made before or after the will was executed, unless the will clearly shows a different intention. However, for any other type of charge or burden on the thing (like an easement, usufruct, or other lien), that burden is not paid by the estate; it remains attached to the property and passes to the recipient along with the thing.

The heir or estate must determine the just value, which may require a valuation by an expert if disputed.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 931 of the Philippine Civil Code, if a testator orders that a thing belonging to another be acquired to be given to a legatee or devisee, the heir or the estate must acquire it and give it to the legatee or devisee. [Art. 931].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the heir or the estate is obligated to acquire the vintage car from its owner and give it to you. However, if the owner refuses to sell the car or demands an excessive price, the obligation of the heir or estate is converted into a monetary obligation: they are only required to give you the just value of the vintage car. You cannot compel the owner to sell against his will. Instead, you are entitled to receive from the heir or estate the fair market value of the car at the time of compliance. This means you will get the monetary equivalent, not the car itself.

Under Article 1297 of the Civil Code, if the parties enter into a new obligation intended to replace an old one, but the new obligation is void or invalid, the original obligation remains in force. Based on Article 1602 of the Civil Code, your transaction is presumed to be an equitable mortgage, not a true sale with right to repurchase. As an equitable mortgage, the transaction is treated as a loan secured by your land. [Art. 1602].

This means you retain ownership subject to the mortgage and can redeem the property by paying the principal debt and lawful interest, even after the stated repurchase period has lapsed, because the period is not controlling when the contract is actually a mortgage.

Can you explain Article 1287 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1287 provides exceptions to the general rule on compensation of obligations. Compensation is a mode of extinguishing obligations where two persons are mutually debtor and creditor of each other, and both debts are due, liquidated, and demandable. However, this article states that compensation shall not be proper in two situations: (1) when one of the debts arises from a depositum (a deposit for safekeeping) or from the obligations of a depositary or of a bailee in commodatum (a borrower of a thing for use without pay); and (2) when the creditor has a claim for support due by gratuitous title (i.e., support given without any consideration, such as legal support). The second exception is without prejudice to paragraph 2 of Article 301, which allows compensation of support in arrears (past due support) but not current or future support. The law thus protects the return of deposited or loaned items and the right to receive support from being set off by other debts.

Can you explain Article 410 of the Philippine Civil Code to me? What does it mean when it says the civil register books are public documents and prima facie evidence?

Article 410 provides that all books and documents in the civil register, such as birth certificates, marriage certificates, and death certificates, are considered public documents. Being public documents means they are official records kept by the government. Furthermore, they are considered 'prima facie evidence' of the facts they contain. This means that when you present a certified copy of a civil registry document in court or any proceeding, it is accepted as true unless the other party can prove otherwise. The document itself is enough to establish the facts stated, like date of birth or place of marriage, and the burden shifts to the other party to present contrary evidence. In short, these documents are reliable and authoritative unless successfully challenged.

Can you explain Article 288 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean that minor children mentioned in the preceding article are under the parental authority of the mother?

Article 288 of the Philippine Civil Code states that minor children who are classified as illegitimate under Article 287 (whether natural or spurious) are placed under the parental authority of their mother. This means that the mother has the sole right and duty to care for them, make decisions about their upbringing, education, and welfare, and exercise legal custody. The father of an illegitimate minor child does not automatically share parental authority; his rights are limited, though he may have obligations such as support. The mother's authority is the default rule, and any change must be obtained through a court order based on the best interest of the child.

Can you explain Article 1403 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding unenforceable contracts?

Article 1403 lists contracts that are unenforceable unless they are ratified. These include: (1) contracts entered into by a person without authority or beyond their powers on behalf of another; (2) contracts that do not comply with the Statute of Frauds, meaning certain agreements must be in writing and signed by the party charged or their agent to be enforceable. These agreements include: (a) those not to be performed within one year; (b) a promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another; (c) an agreement made in consideration of marriage other than a mutual promise to marry; (d) sale of goods, chattels, or things in action priced at 500 pesos or more, unless there is acceptance and receipt of part of the goods or payment of part of the price, or a sufficient memorandum by an auctioneer; (e) lease of real property for more than one year or sale of real property or an interest therein; (f) a representation as to the credit of a third person. (3) contracts where both parties are incapable of giving consent. These contracts may be ratified, which would make them enforceable.

Can you explain what Article 60 of the Philippine Civil Code says about the documents needed to prove age when applying for a marriage license?

Article 60 requires the local civil registrar, upon receiving a marriage license application, to ask for the original baptismal or birth certificates of the contracting parties, or certified copies attested by the custodians. These certificates or copies need not be sworn to and are exempt from documentary stamp tax. The signature and official title of the issuing person are sufficient proof of authenticity. If a party cannot produce these because the original is lost or destroyed, or if an affidavit shows the certificate has been requested at least 15 days prior but not yet received, the party may instead provide a residence certificate for the current or previous years to show age, or, in the absence of that, an instrument drawn up and sworn to before the local civil registrar or any authorized officiant. This instrument must contain the sworn declarations of two witnesses of lawful age, of either sex, stating the party's full name, profession, residence, parents' names if known, and place and date of birth. The nearest of kin are preferred as witnesses; if they are unavailable, persons known for honesty and good repute in the locality may be used. (2) When he is incapacitated to receive the payment at the time it is due;

I borrowed money from a friend. When I tried to pay him back on the due date, he refused to accept the payment without any reason. He just said he didn't want to receive it. I'm worried that he might later claim I never paid. What can I do under the law? Can I deposit the money somewhere to be free from the debt?

But in your situation, since you have already made a tender and he refused, you can proceed directly with consignation.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1256 of the Civil Code, if you have made a valid tender of payment and the creditor (your friend) refuses to accept it without just cause, you can be released from your obligation by consigning the amount due with the proper court. This means you deposit the money with the court or other authorized depository, following the legal procedure for consignation. After a valid consignation, your obligation is extinguished, and the creditor cannot later claim non-payment. [Art. 1256].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, since you tried to pay and he refused without reason, you should make a formal tender (offer of payment) and then file a consignation case in court, depositing the money. The court will then notify the creditor, and if the consignation is found proper, you will be freed from the debt. Note that if the creditor is absent or one of the other enumerated circumstances (like refusal to give a receipt) exists, consignation alone may be sufficient even without prior tender.

Can you explain what Article 1137 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 1137 states that ownership and other real rights over immovable property (like land or buildings) can be acquired through prescription after uninterrupted adverse possession for thirty years. This means that if a person possesses an immovable property openly, continuously, and exclusively as if they were the owner for at least 30 years, and their possession is adverse to the true owner's rights, then that person acquires ownership by law. Importantly, this type of prescription does not require the possessor to have a title (a legal document proving ownership) or to be in good faith (i.e., believing they have a right to possess). It is called extraordinary acquisitive prescription.

The spouse receives one-fourth (1/4) of the total estate, and the illegitimate children collectively receive the other one-fourth (1/4). Therefore, your grandparents together receive 1/2, your stepmother receives 1/4, and you (as the only illegitimate child) receive 1/4 of your father's estate.
