Can you explain Article 744 of the Civil Code about donations of the same thing to multiple donees?

Article 744 states that if a donor gives the same thing to two or more different donees, the rules that apply are the same as those governing the sale of the same thing to two or more different persons. In a double sale, ownership is determined by priority: first, the one who first takes possession in good faith; if no possession, the one who first registers in good faith; if neither, the one with the oldest title in good faith. Thus, for donations, the same priority rules apply to determine which donee gets the property.

Can you explain Article 903 of the Philippine Civil Code about the legitime of parents of an illegitimate child?

Article 903 of the Civil Code governs the legitime (the portion of the estate reserved by law) of the parents of an illegitimate child who dies. The rule depends on who else survives the deceased. If the illegitimate child leaves no legitimate descendants, no surviving spouse, and no illegitimate children, the parents are entitled to a legitime of one-half (1/2) of the hereditary estate. (6) If it is improved at the expense of the debtor, he shall have no other right than that granted to the usufructuary.

I signed a contract to sell my farm lot to my cousin if he passes the agriculture licensure exam. While waiting for the exam results, a landslide destroyed a portion of the lot. I had no control over the landslide. Am I still obligated to deliver the full lot? What are my rights under the law?

In your case, since only a portion was damaged, you are not at fault and no liability arises; the impairment is on the buyer.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1189, since your obligation to deliver the farm lot is subject to a suspensive condition (your cousin passing the exam), the rules on loss or deterioration apply while the condition is pending. Paragraph (3) provides that when the thing deteriorates without the fault of the debtor, the impairment is to be borne by the creditor. This means your cousin, as the creditor, will bear the loss in value; you are not liable for damages or for restoring the destroyed portion. You are still obligated to deliver the lot in its deteriorated state if the condition is fulfilled, but your cousin cannot demand compensation or rescission based on that no-fault deterioration. However, if the landslide had completely destroyed the lot or made it impossible to recover, that would be loss under paragraph (1), and your obligation would be extinguished.

Can you explain Article 1199 of the Philippine Civil Code about alternative obligations? What does it mean that the creditor cannot be compelled to receive part of one and part of the other undertaking?

Article 1199 states that when a person is alternatively bound by different prestations (meaning he owes one of several possible obligations), he must completely perform one of them. He cannot split the obligation by performing part of one prestation and part of another. The creditor, on the other hand, cannot be forced to accept a combination of partial performances from different prestations. The debtor generally has the right to choose which prestation to perform, but once he chooses, he must fulfill that chosen prestation in full.

Can you explain what Article 166 of the Philippine Civil Code says?

Article 166 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that a husband cannot sell, mortgage, or otherwise dispose of real property belonging to the conjugal partnership without the wife's consent. This article does not apply to conjugal partnership property acquired before the effectivity of the Civil Code.

What are the grounds for disinheriting a spouse under Article 921 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 921 of the Philippine Civil Code lists six sufficient causes for disinheriting a spouse: (1) the spouse was convicted of attempting to kill the testator, his/her descendants, or ascendants; (2) the spouse falsely accused the testator of a crime punishable by at least six years imprisonment; (3) the spouse caused the testator to make or change a will through fraud, violence, intimidation, or undue influence; (4) the spouse gave cause for legal separation; (5) the spouse gave grounds for loss of parental authority; (6) unjustifiable refusal to support the children or the other spouse. If any of these causes exists and is properly stated in the will, the testator may validly disinherit the spouse.

Can you explain Article 1348 of the Civil Code? What does it mean that impossible things or services cannot be the object of contracts?

Article 1348 states that for a contract to be valid, its object (the thing or service) must be possible. If the thing or service is impossible at the time the contract is made, the contract is void because there is no valid object. Impossible things or services cannot be legally contracted. For example, selling a car that has already been destroyed, or promising a service that is physically impossible to perform. The law requires that the object be within the commerce of men, and impossible things are not.

STATUTORY TEXT: The thing bequeathed shall be delivered with all its accessions and accessories and in the condition in which it may be upon the death of the testator.

I inherited a specific car from my deceased uncle through his will. When he died, the car had a cracked windshield and was missing its spare tire. The executor now insists that I must pay for the repairs before I can take possession, saying the car is damaged and I should cover the cost. I thought the law says the car should be given as it was at his death. What does Article 951 actually require?

Any attempt to charge you for repairs would be contrary to Article 951.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 951 of the Civil Code, when a specific thing is bequeathed, it must be delivered with all its accessions and accessories, and in the condition it is in at the moment of the testator's death. [Art. 951].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the car is the specific thing bequeathed. The executor has no right to demand payment for repairs; the law obliges delivery of the car in the exact state it was when your uncle died, including any damage. You, as the beneficiary, must accept the car with the cracked windshield and without the spare tire if that was the condition at his death. The spare tire is an accessory, but since it was already missing at the time of death, it is not required to be provided. The executor must deliver the car as-is, without imposing any repair costs on you.

Can you explain Article 114 of the Philippine Civil Code about a wife acquiring property by gratuitous title?

Article 114 provides that a wife cannot accept property by gratuitous title (such as a donation) without the consent of her husband, except when the donor is her ascendant, descendant, parent-in-law, or collateral relative within the fourth degree. ### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Since your aunt, as usufructuary, has the right to enjoy the property and collect its fruits (such as rental income), she is the one obligated to pay the real property tax during the existence of the usufruct, not you as the owner. [Art. 596].

This obligation continues as long as her usufruct lasts.

Can you explain Article 303 of the Philippine Civil Code about when support obligations cease?

Article 303 lists the situations when a person no longer has to provide support. The obligation to give support ceases: (1) upon the death of the recipient; (2) when the resources of the person giving support have been reduced to the point where he cannot give support without neglecting his own needs and those of his family; (3) when the recipient may engage in a trade, profession, or industry, or has obtained work, or has improved his fortune in such a way that he no longer needs the allowance for his subsistence; (4) when the recipient, whether a forced heir or not, has committed an act which gives rise to disinheritance; and (5) when the recipient is a descendant, brother or sister of the obligor and the need for support is caused by his or her bad conduct or by lack of application to work, so long as this cause subsists.

Article 994 of the Philippine Civil Code applies to intestate succession (dying without a will) of an illegitimate child. ### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Specifically, one-half of its value (or the property itself if so required) is brought into your father's estate and the other half into your mother's estate. This means that when computing the hereditary shares, your brother's advancement is considered as having been taken partly from each parent. The collation ensures that your brother does not receive more than his legitimate share from either parent's inheritance.

As for your sister's baby girl, she was conceived before your father's death but born after. Article 1025 expressly provides that a child already conceived at the time of the decedent's death is capable of succeeding provided it be born later under the conditions prescribed in Article 41. Assuming the baby was born alive and met those conditions (complete delivery from the mother's womb, and if she had an intra-uterine life of less than seven months, she must have survived at least 24 hours after complete delivery), she is also capacitated to inherit.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 895 ng Civil Code tungkol sa legitime ng mga illegitimate children.

Itinatakda ng Artikulo 895 ng Civil Code ang mga patakaran para sa legitime (sapilitang bahagi) ng mga illegitimate children. Ayon dito: (1) Ang bawat acknowledged natural child at natural child by legal fiction ay may karapatan sa legitime na katumbas ng kalahati ng legitime ng isang legitimate child. (2) Ang illegitimate child na hindi acknowledged natural o hindi natural child by legal fiction ay may legitime na apat-na-limang bahagi (4/5) ng legitime ng isang acknowledged natural child, na katumbas ng dalawang-ikalima (2/5) ng legitime ng isang legitimate child. Ngunit ang kabuuang legitime ng mga illegitimate children ay hindi maaaring lumampas sa free portion na iyon, at ang legitime ng surviving spouse ay dapat munang ganap na masiyahan bago sila.

Article 538 of the Philippine Civil Code states that possession as a fact cannot be recognized in two different persons at the same time, except in cases of co-possession. If there is a dispute about who is the actual possessor, the following rules apply: first, the present possessor (the one currently holding or occupying the property) is preferred. If there are two claimants who are both considered possessors, the one who has been in possession longer is preferred. If they have been in possession for the same length of time, the one who can present a title (a document proving ownership or right) is preferred. If all these conditions are equal, the property will be placed in judicial deposit (under the custody of the court) until the issue of possession or ownership is resolved through proper legal proceedings.

What does Article 1382 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 1382 states that if a debtor is already insolvent (unable to pay debts) and voluntarily pays an obligation that he was not legally required to pay at that time (for example, a debt that is not yet due, or a natural obligation that cannot be enforced), that payment can be rescinded or cancelled. This is to protect other creditors because the insolvent debtor's assets should be distributed fairly among all creditors. Paying one creditor ahead of others when not legally compelled to do so is unfair, so the law allows rescission of such payments.

I have a family home that was judicially constituted by the court. I owe some unpaid real property taxes on it. I also have a personal loan from a friend, but that loan is not secured by any mortgage on my house. My friend is threatening to have my house sold to pay my personal loan. Can he do that? In your situation, only the tax liability can be enforced against your family home; the unsecured personal loan cannot.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 232 of the Civil Code, your family home is exempt from execution, forced sale, or attachment, except for two cases: nonpayment of taxes and debts secured by a mortgage on the property (whether the mortgage was constituted before or after the family home was established). Your personal loan from a friend is unsecured, meaning it is not backed by a mortgage on your house. Therefore, your friend cannot force the sale of your family home to satisfy that personal loan. However, the government can enforce collection of unpaid real property taxes, which may eventually lead to the sale of the property if the taxes remain unpaid. [Art. 232].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If you had a mortgage on the property from another debt (e.g., a bank loan), that creditor could also enforce a judgment against the family home.

Thus, D can claim the full value of the car from A, B, and C jointly (since the obligation is indivisible and they are all liable for the price), but for damages beyond the value of the car, D can only claim from C.

You must secure the required parental consent from your parents under Philippine law before you can validly marry.

Can you explain what Article 756 of the Philippine Civil Code means about donating ownership and usufruct separately?

Article 756 allows a donor to give the ownership of a property to one person and the usufruct (the right to use and enjoy the property) to another person or persons, as long as all the donees (recipients) are living at the time of the donation. STATUTORY TEXT: The principles of estoppel are hereby adopted insofar as they are not in conflict with the provisions of this Code, the Code of Commerce, the Rules of Court and special laws.

I sold a parcel of land to my friend and we signed a deed of sale, but it was not notarized. Later, I discovered that the land actually belonged to my brother because of a previous inheritance, and my brother is now claiming it. My friend is saying that I cannot deny that I owned it because I sold it to him, citing estoppel. Does Article 1432 of the Civil Code apply here? I need to understand if I am estopped from denying ownership.

The buyer may have a cause of action against you for damages, but he cannot acquire ownership from a non-owner simply because of estoppel, because that would conflict with the fundamental rule that no one can transfer a better title than he has, and with laws on property ownership and succession.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1432 of the Civil Code, the principles of estoppel are adopted as part of Philippine law, but only to the extent they do not conflict with existing statutes like the Civil Code itself, the Code of Commerce, the Rules of Court, and special laws. [Art. 1432].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the question is whether you are estopped from denying that you owned the land you sold to your friend. Estoppel arises when a person, by his own act, representation, or silence, intentionally or through culpable negligence, induces another to believe certain facts to exist and such other person relies and acts on that belief to his detriment. If you executed a deed of sale and represented that you were the owner, and your friend relied on that representation in good faith and paid you, you may be estopped from later denying your ownership as against your friend. This means you cannot defeat your friend's claim by asserting that you never owned the land, because it would be unfair to allow you to profit from your own misrepresentation. However, this estoppel does not operate against your brother, who is the true owner, unless he also did something that led your friend to believe you had authority to sell or that he ratified the sale. Your brother's right to claim the property remains unless he is estopped by his own conduct. Therefore, while you might be personally liable to your friend for breach of warranty or fraud, the estoppel under Article 1432 cannot override your brother's legal title.

What does Article 467 of the Philippine Civil Code mean? How do we determine which is the principal thing when two movable things are joined?

Article 467 provides that when two movable things are incorporated or united, the principal thing is deemed to be the one to which the other has been united as an ornament, for its use, or for its perfection. This means you look at the purpose of the attachment: if one thing is attached to another to decorate it, to make it more useful, or to complete or improve it, then the thing being decorated, used, or perfected is the principal thing. For example, a diamond set in a ring is an ornament, so the ring is principal; a motor installed in a car is for the car's use, so the car is principal. This rule is important for determining ownership under accession.

Can you explain Article 1071 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding collation of donations?

Article 1071 provides that when collation of a donation is required, the donated property itself is not returned to the estate. Instead, only its value at the time of donation is added to the estate of the deceased for the purpose of computing the shares of the heirs. Any increase or decrease in value after donation, or even total loss or destruction, is for the benefit or risk of the donee. So the donee keeps the property, but its value at donation is accounted for in the division of the estate.

I bought a second-hand car from a private seller. The seller told me that the car was in excellent condition and had never been involved in any accident. I relied on that statement and bought the car. Later, I discovered that the car had been in a major accident and had hidden frame damage. Can I hold the seller liable for breach of warranty under Article 1546 of the Civil Code?

You may pursue legal remedies for breach of warranty under the Civil Code.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1546, an express warranty arises when the seller makes an affirmation of fact or promise relating to the thing sold, and that affirmation naturally induces the buyer to purchase, and the buyer relies on it. [Art. 1546].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the seller's statement that the car was in excellent condition and had never been in an accident is an affirmation of fact, not merely an opinion or a statement of value. This statement would naturally induce a buyer to purchase the car, and you relied on it when deciding to buy. Therefore, the seller made an express warranty. Statements of opinion or value are generally not warranties, but here the seller did not express a mere opinion; he asserted a factual condition of the car. Thus, the seller may be held liable for breach of express warranty if the car's actual condition contradicts the affirmation.

Can you explain Article 570 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about usufruct on rents, pensions, and business profits?

Article 570 clarifies that when a usufruct is constituted over the right to receive rent, a periodical pension, or interest on bonds or securities payable to bearer, each payment that becomes due is considered as the proceeds or fruits of that right. This means the usufructuary is entitled to receive those payments during the usufruct period, regardless of when the right to receive them accrued. Similarly, if the usufruct consists in the enjoyment of benefits from a participation in any industrial or commercial enterprise, and the distribution dates are not fixed, such benefits are likewise treated as civil fruits. Can you explain Article 540 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean that only possession in the concept of owner can serve as title for acquiring dominion?

Article 540 of the Civil Code states that for possession to lead to acquiring ownership through prescription, the possession must be in the concept of an owner. Can you explain Article 1504 of the Philippine Civil Code? I'm confused about when the risk of loss transfers in a sale.

Article 1504 states that goods remain at the seller's risk until ownership transfers to the buyer. Once ownership transfers, the risk of loss shifts to the buyer even if actual delivery has not yet been made. However, there are two exceptions: (1) If the goods have been delivered to the buyer or to a bailee for the buyer, and the seller retained ownership only to secure the buyer's performance (like retaining title until full payment), then the risk is on the buyer from the time of delivery. (2) If actual delivery was delayed due to the fault of either the buyer or the seller, the risk is on the party at fault.

Under Article 1131 of the Civil Code, for the purposes of prescription, just title must be proved; it is never presumed. This means that if you are claiming ownership through ordinary prescription (which requires possession in good faith and with just title for the period required by law), you have the burden of proving that you had a just title, such as a deed of sale, donation, or other valid legal basis for acquiring the property. The law will not assume that you have such a title simply because you have been in possession. Since you mentioned that you misplaced the deed of sale, you must present other evidence to prove the existence of the sale transaction, such as witness testimony, tax declarations, proof of payment, or any other documentary evidence that can establish that you acquired the property through a valid title. If you cannot prove just title, you cannot rely on ordinary prescription. [Art. 1131].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, you should also be aware that Philippine law provides for extraordinary prescription under Article 1137, which may allow acquisition of ownership through uninterrupted adverse possession for thirty years without need of title or good faith.

(2) If either party was, at the time of the marriage, physically incapable of entering into the married state, and the other party was unaware thereof;

(4) If a bigamous or polygamous marriage was celebrated, and the impediment was concealed from the plaintiff by the party disqualified;
(5) If in an incestuous marriage, or a marriage between a stepbrother and a stepsister or other marriage prohibited by article 82, the relationship was known to only one of the contracting parties but was not disclosed to the other;

STATUTORY TEXT: In the line, as many degrees are counted as there are generations or persons, excluding the progenitor.
In the direct line, ascent is made to the common ancestor. Thus, the child is one degree removed from the parent, two from the grandfather, and three from the great-grandparent.
In the collateral line, ascent is made to the common ancestor and then descent is made to the person with whom the computation is to be made. Thus, a person is two degrees removed from his brother, three from his uncle, who is the brother of his father, four from his first cousin, and so forth.

My father passed away without a will. I'm trying to figure out if my first cousin can inherit from him. I read that inheritance depends on degrees of relationship. Can you explain how to count the degrees between my father and my first cousin? I'm confused about the rules.

This is consistent with the general rule that an uncle/aunt and nephew/niece are three degrees apart.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
To compute the degree of relationship between your father and your first cousin, we apply the rule in Article 966. In the collateral line, you first go up to the common ancestor, then go down to the other person. Your father and your first cousin share a common ancestor: your grandparent (your father's parent and your cousin's grandparent). Starting from your father, you go up one degree to his parent (your grandparent). Then from that common ancestor, you go down to your first cousin: down one degree to your father's sibling (your cousin's parent), and another degree down to your cousin. Total: 1 (up) + 2 (down) = 3 degrees. [Art. 966].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, your father and your first cousin are three degrees apart in the collateral line.

Can you explain Article 1005 of the Philippine Civil Code about inheritance when siblings and nephews/nieces are involved?

Article 1005 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with intestate succession when the deceased is survived by brothers and sisters, and also by nephews and nieces who are children of the deceased's other brothers or sisters of the full blood. In this case, the living siblings inherit per capita, meaning each sibling gets an equal share of the estate as an individual. On the other hand, the nephews and nieces inherit per stirpes, meaning they collectively receive the share that their deceased parent (the sibling who died earlier) would have inherited, to be divided equally among them. So the estate is divided into as many shares as there are living siblings plus the number of deceased siblings who left children, with each living sibling taking one share, and each group of nephews/nieces taking their parent's share divided equally.

Can you explain what Article 476 of the Philippine Civil Code is about?

Article 476 of the Philippine Civil Code allows a property owner to file a legal action to remove a 'cloud' on their title to real property. Additionally, the article allows for a preventive action to stop a cloud from being cast upon the title before it actually happens.

Can you explain Article 1207 of the Philippine Civil Code? I don't understand the difference between joint and solidary obligations.

Article 1207 states that when there are two or more creditors or two or more debtors in one obligation, it does not automatically mean that each creditor can demand the entire obligation or each debtor must pay the entire obligation. By default, such an obligation is considered joint, meaning each debtor is liable only for his proportionate share, and each creditor can demand only his respective share. Solidary liability (where one debtor can be compelled to pay the whole debt, or one creditor can collect the whole amount) only exists if it is expressly stated in the obligation, or if the law or the nature of the obligation requires solidarity. So unless there is a clear indication of solidarity, the obligation is joint.

Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag sa akin ang Artikulo 1190 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas?

Ang Artikulo 1190 ay tungkol sa mga obligasyon na may kondisyon na kapag natupad ay nagpapawalang-bisa sa obligasyon (resolutory condition). Kapag natupad ang kondisyon, dapat ibalik ng bawat panig sa isa't isa ang anumang natanggap nila. Halimbawa, kung nagbenta ka ng isang bagay sa ilalim ng kasunduan na mawawalan ng bisa ang bentahan kapag nangyari ang isang pangyayari, at nangyari nga ito, kailangan mong ibalik ang iyong natanggap, at ang kabilang panig ay dapat ding ibalik ang kanilang natanggap.

Kung ang bagay na dapat ibalik ay nawala, nasira, o napabuti, ang mga tuntunin sa Artikulo 1189 (na karaniwang ginagamit sa isang may utang sa suspensive condition) ay ilalapat sa panig na obligadong magbalik. Ibig sabihin, kung ang bagay ay nawala nang walang kasalanan ng panig na iyon, maaaring hindi siya managot; kung nawala dahil sa kanyang kasalanan, maaaring managot siya sa danyos; kung nasira, may mga pagpipilian ang nagpautang; at kung napabuti, ang pagpapabuti ay maaaring makinabang sa nagpautang.

STATUTORY TEXT: Gross inadequacy of price does not affect a contract of sale, except as it may indicate a defect in the consent, or that the parties really intended a donation or some other act or contract.

I bought a parcel of land from my uncle for only P100,000 even though its market value is around P2 million. He signed the deed of sale freely, but now he wants to cancel, claiming the sale is void because the price is grossly inadequate. Is the sale valid? Can he back out just because of the very low price?

Absent such proof, the sale is valid and enforceable.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1470 of the Civil Code, gross inadequacy of price does not by itself affect the validity of a contract of sale. The sale remains valid and binding if the parties freely consented and truly intended a sale. The fact that the price is extremely low compared to the market value is not, on its own, a ground to annul or cancel the contract. However, if the gross inadequacy of price indicates a defect in consent—such as fraud, mistake, intimidation, or undue influence—or shows that the parties really intended a donation or some other contract, then the transaction may be challenged on those specific grounds. [Art. 1470].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, if your uncle knowingly and voluntarily agreed to sell the land for P100,000 without any vitiated consent, and the deed of sale reflects a true sale, then the contract stands and he cannot back out merely because the price is low. He would need to prove that his consent was defective or that the true intention was not a sale.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1470, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

This means that they will go to the legal heirs of your father, which typically include the surviving spouse (if any) and the children (you and your siblings), in accordance with the proportions set by law. The will controls only the properties explicitly covered, while everything else passes through intestacy.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1498 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas? Ano ang ibig sabihin kapag ang pagbebenta ay ginawa sa pamamagitan ng public instrument, at paano ang delivery ng movable property gamit ang mga susi?

Ang Artikulo 1498 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay tungkol sa delivery ng bagay na ipinagbili sa isang kontrata ng pagbebenta. Sinasabi nito na kapag ang pagbebenta ay ginawa sa pamamagitan ng isang public instrument (isang notarized na dokumento), ang pag-execute o pagpirma ng instrumentong iyon ay katumbas na ng delivery ng bagay na ipinagbili. Ito ay isang constructive delivery, ibig sabihin ang mamimili ay itinuturing na natanggap na ang bagay kahit walang pisikal na paglipat, maliban kung ang kasulatan mismo ay nagsasaad ng iba o malinaw na mahihinuha na hindi nilayon ng mga partido ang agarang delivery. Para naman sa movable property, maaari ring gawin ang delivery sa pamamagitan ng pagbibigay ng mga susi ng lugar o depository kung saan nakaimbak o nakalagay ang bagay. Ito ay isang symbolic delivery. Kaya, kung bumili ka ng kotse at pumirma ng notarized deed of sale, ang kotse ay itinuturing na delivered na sa pagpirma, maliban kung iba ang nakasaad sa kasulatan. Kung ang mga kalakal ay nasa bodega, ang pagbibigay ng susi ng bodega sa mamimili ay sapat nang delivery.

Can you explain Article 1412 of the Philippine Civil Code about void contracts with an unlawful cause that is not a criminal offense?

Article 1412 of the Philippine Civil Code applies when a contract has an unlawful or forbidden cause, but that cause does not constitute a criminal offense. In such cases, the law provides two rules: (1) If both parties are at fault, neither can recover what they gave under the contract, nor can they demand the other to perform their obligation. (2) If only one party is at fault, the guilty party cannot recover what he gave or demand performance, but the innocent party may demand the return of what he gave without having to comply with his own promise. This means the law prevents wrongdoers from benefiting from an illegal contract, while protecting the party who acted in good faith.

Can you explain Article 1144 of the Philippine Civil Code? What actions must be filed within ten years?

Article 1144 of the Philippine Civil Code provides a ten-year prescriptive period for filing certain court actions. Specifically, the following actions must be brought within ten years from the time the right of action accrues: (1) actions based on a written contract; (2) actions based on an obligation created by law; and (3) actions based on a judgment. The right of action accrues when the cause of action arises, typically when the obligation becomes due or when a breach occurs. After the ten-year period lapses, the creditor or claimant can no longer file a lawsuit to enforce that right because the action is barred by prescription.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 867(1) of the Philippine Civil Code, a fideicommissary substitution that is not made expressly is void. A fideicommissary substitution exists when a testator institutes a first heir and then a second heir to whom the first heir must deliver the property upon a certain event, usually the first heir's death. For such a substitution to be valid, it must be made expressly—either by naming it a 'fideicommissary substitution' or by imposing upon the first heir (the fiduciary) an absolute obligation to deliver the property to the second heir. SUBSECTION 1.—Partition

My father passed away and left a house and some land to his four children. However, before he died, he gave a valuable car to one of my brothers as a gift. Now during partition, some of us believe that the car should be brought back into the estate (collation) so that it can be divided equally. My brother disagrees. We are stuck and the partition is delayed. Can we proceed with dividing the other properties while we resolve this issue about the car? What do we need to do?

Therefore, you may proceed with the division of the other assets, provided that the heirs demanding collation post adequate security.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1077 of the Civil Code, the distribution of the estate should not be interrupted merely because there is a question among co-heirs about the obligation to bring property to collation or about which properties are subject to collation. [Art. 1077].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, you and your siblings disagree on whether the car given to your brother should be collated. This dispute should not prevent you from proceeding with the partition of the other properties (the house and land). However, to continue with the partition, the party who is claiming that the car should be collated (i.e., those who want it included in the estate) must provide adequate security. Adequate security typically means a bond or other guarantee sufficient to cover the value of the car in case the collation is ultimately determined to be required but the property cannot be returned. This security protects the rights of all heirs pending the resolution of the collation dispute.

This means that reasonable medical expenses for your daughter are also part of your support obligation, provided they are commensurate with your family's social standing. [Art. 290].

STATUTORY TEXT: No marriage license shall be necessary when a man and a woman who have attained the age of majority and who, being unmarried, have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years, desire to marry each other. The contracting parties shall state the foregoing facts in an affidavit before any person authorized by law to administer oaths. The official, priest or minister who solemnized the marriage shall also state in an affidavit that he took steps to ascertain the ages and other qualifications of the contracting parties and that he found no legal impediment to the marriage.

My partner and I have been living together for six years. We are both 27 years old and have never been married. We want to get married but we heard that getting a marriage license takes time and money. Is there a way for us to get married without a license? What do we need to do?

Ensure that all conditions are met to avoid any legal issues.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Based on Article 76 of the Civil Code, you and your partner may get married without a marriage license. [Art. 76].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This provision applies to you because you are both of legal age (27 years old, which is above the age of majority of 18), both unmarried, and have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years—in your case, six years. To avail of this exception, you must state these facts in an affidavit sworn before any person authorized by law to administer oaths, such as a notary public or a judge. The affidavit should affirm that you have attained the age of majority, are both unmarried, and have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years. Additionally, the priest, minister, or official who will solemnize your marriage must also execute an affidavit stating that he or she took steps to ascertain your ages and other qualifications and found no legal impediment to the marriage. Therefore, you do not need to secure a marriage license, but you must prepare these affidavits and present them to the solemnizing officer.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 76, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.

I am a father of two young children. My company recently implemented a mandatory overtime policy requiring employees to work 12-hour shifts, six days a week. This leaves me with almost no time to spend with my family. I read that the Civil Code says the family is cherished and protected by public policy. Thus, while Article 216 is not a self-executing right, it reinforces the importance of family and can be a persuasive argument for family-friendly workplace policies.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Article 216 of the Civil Code declares that the family is a basic social institution which public policy cherishes and protects. This provision is a statement of State policy and a guiding principle in interpreting laws. It does not, by itself, create a specific right to a particular work schedule. However, it can be invoked to argue that any law, regulation, or contract provision that unreasonably interferes with family life should be interpreted or applied in a manner consistent with the protection of the family as an institution. [Art. 216].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, your right to reasonable working hours is primarily governed by labor laws, such as the Labor Code provisions on hours of work and overtime. Article 216 can support arguments that excessively long working hours that deprive you of family time may be contrary to public policy. You may raise this principle in negotiations with your employer or in any legal complaint regarding unfair labor practices, but the direct legal basis for demanding a specific schedule will come from labor regulations, not Article 216 alone. Moreover, government agencies and courts may consider the family protection principle when interpreting ambiguous labor provisions or when balancing employer interests and employee welfare.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

Failure to replace may be considered a violation of your obligations as a usufructuary.

Under Article 575 of the Civil Code, as a usufructuary of fruit-bearing trees, you are allowed to make use of the dead trunks and even those that were cut off or uprooted by accident, such as due to a typhoon. This means you may use the wood from the fallen or dead mango trees, but you must plant new mango trees (or similar fruit-bearing plants) to replace them. [Art. 575].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The replacement should be done to maintain the usufruct property's character and productivity.

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you broke into your neighbor's house to rescue his dog during a fire, which is a clear case of acting to save property from imminent danger. STATUTORY TEXT: The legatee or devisee of two legacies or devises, one of which is onerous, cannot renounce the onerous one and accept the other. If both are onerous or gratuitous, he shall be free to accept or renounce both, or to renounce either. My uncle passed away and in his will, he left me two properties: a commercial building on the condition that I pay his outstanding bank loan of ₱2,000,000, and a residential lot with no conditions. I am his compulsory heir. I want to accept the residential lot but reject the commercial building to avoid the loan. Is this allowed? What are my options?

You cannot accept the residential lot alone while rejecting the commercial building.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 955 of the Civil Code, if a legatee or devisee is given two legacies/devises, one onerous (with a burden, such as paying a loan) and the other gratuitous (without burden), they cannot accept the gratuitous one and renounce the onerous one. [Art. 955].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the commercial building is onerous because you must pay the ₱2,000,000 loan, while the residential lot is gratuitous. Therefore, you cannot accept the lot and reject the building; you must either accept both or renounce both, unless the testator (your uncle) intended them to be inseparable, which is not indicated. However, because you are a compulsory heir, you have additional options under the second paragraph of Art. 955: you may (a) waive your inheritance as compulsory heir and accept both legacies (building and lot, including the loan obligation), (b) renounce both legacies and accept only your inheritance as compulsory heir, (c) accept both the inheritance and the legacies (subject to the onerous condition), or (d) waive both.

STATUTORY TEXT: The testator may devise and bequeath the free portion as he may deem fit.

My father recently passed away. In his will, he left a large sum of money to his favorite charity, and only a small amount to me and my siblings. We are his only children. ### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Philippine law, compulsory heirs (like children) are entitled to their legitimes, which are fixed by law. The testator cannot deprive them of those shares. However, after the legitimes are satisfied, the remainder is called the free portion. Article 914 allows the testator to dispose of that free portion to anyone, including a charity, as he deems fit. Therefore, your father can give to charity from the free portion, but he cannot reduce your legitimes below what the law requires. You and your siblings are entitled to your respective legitimes; any excess beyond the legitimes is the free portion that he could validly give to charity. [Art. 914].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the amount given to charity encroaches on your legitimes, that disposition may be reduced to protect your legitimes.

The creditor's acceptance does not affect your right to seek reimbursement from your friend, because your friend was unjustly enriched at your expense.

STATUTORY TEXT: In every inheritance, the relative nearest in degree excludes the more distant ones, saving the right of representation when it properly takes place.
Relatives in the same degree shall inherit in equal shares, subject to the provisions of article 1006 with respect to relatives of the full and half blood, and of article 987, paragraph 2, concerning division between the paternal and maternal lines. (921a)
SUBSECTION 1.—Relationship
My father died without a will. He has three living children (including me) and two grandchildren from a deceased child. Who are the legal heirs and how should the estate be divided?

This result is consistent with Article 962's rule that relatives of the same degree inherit equally, with representation creating an exception for the deceased child's line.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 962 of the Civil Code, the nearest relatives exclude more distant ones, but the right of representation is preserved when it properly takes place. [Art. 962].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, your father's children are first-degree relatives, while the grandchildren from the deceased child are second-degree. Normally, the living children would exclude the grandchildren. However, because one child predeceased your father, the right of representation under Articles 970 to 977 allows that child's own children (the grandchildren) to step into their parent's place and inherit by representation. Thus, the estate is divided into four equal shares: one share for each of the three living children, and one share for the branch of the predeceased child. That fourth share is then divided equally between the two grandchildren, so each grandchild receives one-eighth of the estate, while each living child receives one-fourth.

STATUTORY TEXT: Novation, compensation, confusion or remission of the debt, made by any of the solidary creditors or with any of the solidary debtors, shall extinguish the obligation, without prejudice to the provisions of article 1219.

I am one of three solidary creditors for a loan of PHP 300,000. Without consulting the other two, one of my co-creditors agreed with the debtor to reduce the debt to PHP 200,000 (novation) or even forgave the entire debt. What is the effect of his act? Can we still collect our shares from the debtor? What are our rights as the other creditors?

If he only reduced it to PHP 200,000, the extinguished portion is PHP 100,000, and you can claim your share of that extinguished portion from him.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1215, the act of novation or remission made by any solidary creditor extinguishes the entire obligation. This means that if your co-creditor agreed to reduce the debt or forgave it entirely, that act is valid and binding on all creditors, and the debtor is released from the obligation to the extent of the novation or remission. You cannot collect from the debtor anymore because the obligation has been extinguished. However, the second paragraph of the article provides that the creditor who executed the act (your co-creditor) is liable to the others for their share in the obligation. Therefore, you and the other co-creditor can demand from the acting co-creditor the amount corresponding to your respective shares in the original debt. [Art. 1215].

### 💡 Application to Facts
For example, if the original debt was PHP 300,000 and each of you is entitled to PHP 100,000, and one co-creditor forgave the whole debt, you can each claim PHP 100,000 from that co-creditor.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1215 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Please explain Article 731 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding donation subject to a resolutory condition of the donor's survival.

Article 731 provides that when a person donates something subject to the resolutory condition of the donor's survival, the donation is considered a donation inter vivos (between living persons), not a donation mortis causa (upon death). This means the transfer of ownership occurs immediately during the donor's lifetime, but it is subject to revocation if the donor survives. In other words, the donee receives the property now, but if the donor remains alive, the donation is extinguished and the property returns to the donor. This classification is important because donations inter vivos have different formalities and effects compared to mortis causa donations, which take effect only upon death and require the formalities of a will.

STATUTORY TEXT: When the testator charges one of the heirs with a legacy or devise, he alone shall be bound.
Should he not charge anyone in particular, all shall be liable in the same proportion in which they may inherit.

Ang aking tiyuhin ay pumanaw at nag-iwan ng testamento. Sa kanyang testamento, may iniwan siyang halagang ₱100,000 bilang legacy sa kanyang matalik na kaibigan, pero hindi niya binanggit kung sino sa mga tagapagmana ang dapat magbigay nito. Nagtatalo ang mga tagapagmana kung sino ang magbabayad. Sino po ba ang dapat managot?

Kung sakaling may isang tagapagmana na tanging tinukoy sa testamento bilang sasagot, siya lamang ang mananagot, ngunit sa kasong ito ay wala, kaya lahat ay mag-aambag ayon sa proporsyon.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa ilalim ng Article 926 ng Civil Code, kapag hindi tinukoy ng testator kung sino sa mga tagapagmana ang dapat magbigay ng legacy o devise, lahat ng tagapagmana ay mananagot sa parehong proporsyon ng kanilang mamanahin mula sa mana. [Art. 926].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Sa iyong sitwasyon, dahil hindi binanggit ng iyong tiyuhin kung sino ang sasagot sa ₱100,000 na legacy, ang bawat tagapagmana ay dapat mag-ambag ayon sa kani-kanilang bahagi sa mana. Halimbawa, kung ang isang tagapagmana ay may 50% share sa mana, siya ay sasagot ng 50% ng ₱100,000 o ₱50,000; kung may 25% share, sasagot siya ng ₱25,000, at iba pa.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) kung ang monetary claim ay hindi hihigit sa ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court kung hindi hihigit sa ₱1,000,000 alinsunod sa SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) kung ang claim ay hihigit sa ₱2,000,000 o kung incapable of pecuniary estimation alinsunod sa RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay alinsunod sa RA 7160) bago maghain ng kaso sa korte, maliban na lamang kung magkaiba ng lungsod/munisipalidad ang mga partido o kung nangangailangan ng agarang provisional remedy (injunction/TRO).

PROVISION: Article 1332 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 2 - ESSENTIAL REQUISITES OF CONTRACTS > SEC 1.—Consent > Art. 1332
STATUTORY TEXT: When one of the parties is unable to read, or if the contract is in a language not understood by him, and mistake or fraud is alleged, the person enforcing the contract must show that the terms thereof have been fully explained to the former.

I am an elderly person who cannot read well. I signed a loan agreement in English which I don't fully understand. Now the lender is demanding payment based on terms I was not aware of, like high interest and penalty charges. I believe I was misled. What does the law say about this situation?

You should gather evidence of your inability to read or understand English, and insist that the lender demonstrate how they explained the terms to you.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1332 of the Civil Code, since you cannot read well and the loan agreement is in English which you do not fully understand, and you are alleging mistake or fraud, the burden of proof shifts to the lender as the party enforcing the contract. The lender must prove that the terms of the loan agreement, including the high interest and penalty charges, were fully explained to you before you signed. If the lender cannot show that they clearly explained all the terms in a manner you could understand, the contract may not be enforceable against you based on those terms. [Art. 1332].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This provision protects you because the law recognizes that consent must be informed, and when there is a language or literacy barrier, the enforcing party must ensure the other party truly understood the contract's contents.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1332, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1332 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

LOCATION: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE IV.—SOME SPECIAL PROPERTIES > CH 1 - WATERS > SEC 1.—Ownership of Waters > Art. 501
STATUTORY TEXT: Every co-owner shall, after partition, be liable for defects of title and quality of the portion assigned to each of the other co-owners.

My siblings and I inherited a piece of agricultural land from our parents. We agreed to partition it into three equal parts, and we each got our respective lots. Later, it turned out that the lot assigned to me is smaller than what was stated in the partition plan because the neighbor's fence has encroached several meters into my lot, and also there is a pending court case from a distant relative claiming ownership of a portion of the land that falls within my lot. Can I require my siblings to compensate me or share in the loss?

However, if it can be shown that you knew of these defects and accepted the portion anyway, or if the defects arose after partition due to your own neglect, then the liability of your siblings may be reduced or extinguished.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 501 of the Civil Code, every co-owner shall, after partition, be liable for defects of title and quality of the portion assigned to each of the other co-owners. This provision establishes a mutual warranty among former co-owners after partition. [Art. 501].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the portion assigned to you has a defect in quality (the reduction in actual area due to the neighbor's encroachment) and a defect in title (the adverse claim by a distant relative). These defects existed before or at the time of partition, and there is no indication that you were aware of them or that they were caused by your own fault. Therefore, your siblings, as your former co-owners, are liable to you for these defects. They may be required to compensate you for the loss in value, or they may themselves share proportionately in the burden, such as by adjusting the partition to equalize the shares. You can demand that they either reimburse you for the deficiency or contribute to any legal costs to defend against the adverse claim.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 501, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 501 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

I own a small farm where I plant and harvest rice, and I also have a goat that recently gave birth to a kid. Additionally, I lease out a portion of my land to a tenant who pays me monthly rent. Under Article 442 of the Civil Code, how should these items be classified as fruits?

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 442 of the Civil Code, the rice you harvest from your farm is classified as an industrial fruit because it is produced by land through cultivation or labor—you actively planted and tended the rice. ### 💡 Application to Facts
The monthly rent you receive from leasing your land is a civil fruit because it is income derived from property by virtue of a juridical relation, specifically a lease contract.

Can you explain Article 152 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 152 provides that if one spouse owns a credit that is payable over a number of years, or if one spouse is entitled to a life pension, the rules in Articles 156 and 157 must be followed to determine what portion is the separate property of that spouse (paraphernal if the wife, capital if the husband) and what portion belongs to the conjugal partnership. Under Article 156, for a credit payable over time, the principal amount collected during marriage is the separate property of the owning spouse, while the interest portion is conjugal. Under Article 157, for a life pension, the right to receive the pension is separate property of the spouse to whom it belongs, but the pension payments received during marriage are conjugal partnership property because they are considered fruits of the separate property. In simple terms, the article tells us how to classify periodic payments from certain assets: the underlying asset or principal is separate, but the income or fruits are conjugal.

Under Article 723 of the Civil Code, you are the owner of the physical letter because it was addressed and delivered to you. In your case, exposing personal matters on social media is unlikely to meet that standard; you would need to seek court authorization if you believe it is justified, but generally, personal grievances do not qualify.

In the collateral line, representation is only allowed for children of brothers and sisters (nieces and nephews), whether they are of full or half blood. This means that if a sibling dies before the decedent, that sibling's children can inherit their parent's share, but other collateral relatives like cousins cannot represent.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1225 ng Civil Code tungkol sa mga obligasyong divisible at indivisible.

Ipinapaliwanag ng Artikulo 1225 ng Civil Code kung paano malalaman kung ang isang obligasyon ay divisible (maaaring gawin nang baha-bahagi) o indivisible (dapat gawin nang buo). Sinasabi nito na ang mga obligasyong magbigay ng tiyak o partikular na bagay ay indivisible, gayundin ang mga obligasyong hindi maaaring bahagyang tuparin nang hindi nababago ang kalikasan nito. Ngunit kahit pisikal na divisible ang isang obligasyon, ituturing itong indivisible kung itinatakda ng batas o kung malinaw na intensyon ng mga partido na maging indivisible ito. Can you explain what Article 542 of the Philippine Civil Code means regarding possession of real property and movable property inside it?

Article 542 establishes a legal presumption: if a person has possession of real property (like land or a building), it is presumed that they also possess the movable properties (like furniture, appliances, etc.) located inside that real property. STATUTORY TEXT: For the purposes of the preceding articles, obligations to give definite things and those which are not susceptible of partial performance shall be deemed to be indivisible.
When the obligation has for its object the execution of a certain number of days of work, the accomplishment of work by metrical units, or analogous things which by their nature are susceptible of partial performance, it shall be divisible.
However, even though the object or service may be physically divisible, an obligation is indivisible if so provided by law or intended by the parties.
In obligations not to do, divisibility or indivisibility shall be determined by the character of the prestation in each particular case.

Good day. I have a contract with a supplier to deliver 1,000 sacks of rice to my store. The contract includes a penalty of ₱50,000 if the delivery is late. The supplier delivered 700 sacks on time, but the remaining 300 sacks were delivered two weeks late. I want to claim the full penalty because the contract says penalty for late delivery. But the supplier says that since the obligation is divisible, I can only claim a proportional part of the penalty for the 300 sacks that were late. Who is correct under Article 1225 of the Civil Code?

Thus, the supplier's argument is generally correct, but you should check the exact terms of your contract for any provision stating that any delay will incur the full penalty or that the delivery must be made in full as an indivisible obligation.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1225 of the Civil Code, an obligation is divisible when it is susceptible of partial performance. The delivery of 1,000 sacks of rice is an obligation to give generic things, which by its nature can be performed in parts. Therefore, the obligation is divisible. Since the supplier delivered 700 sacks on time and only 300 sacks were delayed, the breach is only partial. [Art. 1225].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Consequently, the penalty should generally be proportionally reduced to correspond only to the delayed portion, unless the parties clearly intended the obligation to be indivisible or the penal clause itself is stipulated to be indivisible.

Since you never signed an agreement assigning your rights, there is no contract that would transfer ownership. [Art. 712].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, you remain the owner of the song under the first paragraph of Article 712.

Article 452 provides an exception to the general rule that a person who builds, plants, or sows on another's land in bad faith loses all rights to the improvements. Can you explain what Article 1050 of the Philippine Civil Code means? When is an inheritance considered accepted?

Article 1050 of the Civil Code provides specific situations where an inheritance is deemed accepted by the heir. First, if the heir sells, donates, or assigns his inheritance rights to a stranger or to any of his co-heirs, that act implies acceptance. Second, if the heir renounces the inheritance, even without receiving anything in return, in favor of one or more of his co-heirs, it is considered acceptance. Third, if the heir renounces for a price in favor of all his co-heirs indiscriminately, that is also acceptance. However, there is an exception: if the renunciation is gratuitous (without price) and the co-heirs in whose favor it is made are those who would receive the renounced portion by accretion (i.e., by operation of law because they are the other heirs), then the inheritance is not deemed accepted. In other words, certain acts of disposition or specific types of renunciation indicate that the heir has chosen to accept the inheritance.

Can you explain Article 1530 of the Philippine Civil Code about the right of stoppage in transitu?

Article 1530 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with the right of stoppage in transitu. It provides that when the buyer of goods is or becomes insolvent, the unpaid seller who has already parted with possession of the goods (e.g., by delivering them to a carrier for transmission to the buyer) may stop the goods while they are in transit and resume possession. Once the seller exercises this right, he becomes entitled to the same rights over the goods as if he had never parted with possession. This right is available only when the buyer is insolvent and the goods are still in transit.

Can you explain Article 1343 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1343 states that if a person makes a misrepresentation (a false statement) but does so in good faith, meaning they honestly believe it to be true and have no intention to deceive, then that misrepresentation is not considered fraudulent (dolo). However, it may still constitute an error (mistake) on the part of the party who relied on it. If that error is substantial and affects consent, it could make the contract voidable. So good faith misrepresentation does not give rise to liability for fraud, but it may be a ground to annul the contract based on error.

Can you explain Article 1113 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean regarding prescription of property?

Article 1113 states that all things which are within the commerce of men are susceptible of prescription, unless otherwise provided. This means that any property that can be privately owned or transferred may be acquired or lost through prescription (i.e., through the lapse of time under conditions set by law). However, property of the State or any of its subdivisions that is not patrimonial in character—such as public roads, plazas, rivers, and other properties intended for public use or public service—cannot be acquired by prescription. Only patrimonial property of the State (property not devoted to public use or public service and which the State owns in its private capacity) may be subject to prescription.

What does Article 41 of the Philippine Civil Code say about when a foetus is considered born for civil purposes?

Article 41 provides that for civil purposes, a foetus is considered born if it is alive at the time it is completely delivered from the mother's womb. However, if the foetus had an intra-uterine life of less than seven months, it is not deemed born if it dies within twenty-four hours after its complete delivery from the maternal womb. This means that a premature foetus (less than 7 months gestation) must survive at least 24 hours after complete delivery to be considered born; otherwise, it is treated as if it never had civil personality.

Can you explain Article 716 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 716 covers the rights of owners of swarms of bees and domesticated animals that end up on another person's property or are caught by someone else. For a swarm of bees, the owner may follow the bees onto another person's land, but must pay for any damage caused to the landowner or possessor of that land. If that period expires without a claim, the animal belongs to the person who caught and kept it.

Can you explain Article 608 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding usufruct and insurance?

Article 608 deals with the rights of a usufructuary (the person who has the right to use and enjoy a property owned by another) when the property is insured and then lost. If the usufructuary agrees to share the insurance premium with the owner, then if the property is lost, the usufructuary either continues to enjoy the new building if the owner rebuilds, or receives the interest on the insurance money if the owner does not rebuild. If the usufructuary refuses to contribute to the insurance and only the owner pays for it, then the owner gets the full insurance proceeds, but the usufructuary still has the right to receive the interest on that money (as provided in Article 607).

Can you explain what Article 1344 of the Philippine Civil Code says about fraud in contracts?

Article 1344 states that for fraud to make a contract voidable, the fraud must be serious, meaning it was the main reason the party agreed to the contract. Also, the fraud must not have been committed by both parties; if both sides used fraud, neither can ask to void the contract. If the fraud is only incidental—meaning it did not really influence the party's decision to enter the contract—then the contract remains valid, but the party who committed the fraud must pay damages to the other.

A married woman, twenty-one years of age or over, is qualified for all acts of civil life, except in cases specified by law.

I am 23 years old and married. I want to start my own business and sign a lease for a commercial space, but my husband says I cannot do that without his permission because I am a married woman. Is that correct? Please explain my legal capacity under Philippine law.

You may proceed, but it is advisable to check if the specific transaction falls under any exception requiring spousal participation.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 39 of the Civil Code, a married woman who is at least 21 years old is qualified for all acts of civil life, except in cases specified by law. This means that generally, being a married woman does not automatically limit your capacity to enter contracts, including a lease for a business. Your age (23) meets the threshold, so you are presumed capable. However, note that if the lease or business involves conjugal property or affects the family's interests, other laws like the Family Code may require spousal consent or authority. But as a general rule, you have the capacity to act on your own. [Art. 39].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, your husband's claim that you need his permission solely because you are a married woman is not supported by Article 39.

Can you explain Article 500 of the Philippine Civil Code about co-ownership partition?

Article 500 states that when co-owners partition their property, they must settle accounts among themselves. This means each co-owner must share any benefits they received from the property (like rental income) with the others, and they can be reimbursed for necessary expenses they incurred for the property (like repairs or taxes). Additionally, if a co-owner caused damage to the property through their negligence or fraud, they are personally liable to pay for that damage to the other co-owners. The goal is to ensure fairness and equity when ending the co-ownership.

Mayroon akong pinautang na pera sa isang tao, at ang tanging ari-arian niya na alam ko ay isang negotiable warehouse receipt para sa mga kalakal na nakaimbak. Ayaw niyang magbayad, at hindi ko alam kung paano ko makukuha ang halaga mula sa dokumentong iyon. Ano ang maaari kong gawin ayon sa batas?

Sa praktika, maaari kang mag-file ng aksyon sa korte upang ipa-attach ang dokumento at pagkatapos ay ipagbili ang mga kalakal na kinakatawan nito upang mabayaran ang utang, alinsunod sa mga patakaran ng korte.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 1520 ng Civil Code, bilang isang pinagkakautangan na ang may-utang ay nagmamay-ari ng negotiable document of title (tulad ng warehouse receipt), ikaw ay may karapatang humingi ng tulong mula sa mga hukuman. Dahil ang negotiable document of title ay kumakatawan sa mga kalakal, ito ay itinuturing na ari-arian na hindi madaling ma-attach o ma-levy sa pamamagitan ng ordinaryong proseso, kaya pinapayagan ng batas ang mga espesyal na remedyo sa korte.

STATUTORY TEXT: The legitime of each of the acknowledged natural children and each of the natural children by legal fiction shall consist of one-half of the legitime of each of the legitimate children or descendants.
The legitime of an illegitimate child who is neither an acknowledged natural, nor a natural child by legal fiction, shall be equal in every case to four-fifths of the legitime of an acknowledged natural child.
The legitime of the illegitimate children shall be taken from the portion of the estate at the free disposal of the testator, provided that in no case shall the total legitime of such illegitimate children exceed that free portion, and that the legitime of the surviving spouse must first be fully satisfied.

My father died leaving a will that gave his entire estate of PHP 1,000,000 to a friend. He is survived by his wife, two legitimate children, one acknowledged natural child, and one illegitimate child who is not acknowledged natural nor by legal fiction. How should the legitimes be computed, especially for the illegitimate children, under Article 895?

The remaining PHP 25,000 is the true free portion that the testator could dispose of by will, so the friend named in the will gets only PHP 25,000, not the entire estate.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 895, legitimes of compulsory heirs cannot be defeated by a will. The estate is divided as follows: First, the legitime of legitimate children is one-half of the estate: PHP 500,000, shared equally by the two legitimate children at PHP 250,000 each. Second, the surviving spouse's legitime is equal to that of each legitimate child, so she receives PHP 250,000 from the remaining half of the estate. After these, the free portion available for the testator and for illegitimate children's legitime is PHP 250,000. The acknowledged natural child's legitime is one-half of a legitimate child's legitime: PHP 125,000 (half of 250,000). The other illegitimate child, being neither acknowledged natural nor natural by legal fiction, gets four-fifths of the acknowledged natural child's legitime: PHP 100,000 (4/5 of 125,000). [Art. 895].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The total legitime of the two illegitimate children is PHP 225,000, which does not exceed the free portion of PHP 250,000, so they receive these amounts.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1298 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa novation at mga walang bisang obligasyon.

Ayon sa Artikulo 1298, ang novation ay walang bisa kung ang orihinal na obligasyon ay walang bisa (void). Sa madaling salita, hindi maaaring gawing balido ang isang talagang void na obligasyon sa pamamagitan ng novation, ngunit kung ito ay voidable lamang at may karapatan ang may utang na ipawalang-bisa, ang novation ay maaaring magsilbing pagpapatibay.

I am a married woman but separated from my husband. I now need financial support. I have three children and my parents are still alive and capable. According to the law, from whom should I first demand support?

Therefore, you should first demand support from your husband.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 294 of the Civil Code, when support is proper and several persons are obliged to give it, the claim must be made in a specific order. [Art. 294].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the first person from whom you should demand support is your spouse, even if you are separated, as long as the marriage is still valid and no legal separation or other order has changed the obligation. If they are also unable, you may claim from your ascendants of the nearest degree, which would be your parents. Only if none of these are available can you demand from your brothers and sisters. Among descendants and ascendants, the order follows the rules of intestate succession, so if you have children of different degrees, those of the nearest degree are first.

Can you explain Article 4 of the Civil Code of the Philippines about retroactive effect of laws?

Article 4 of the Civil Code states that laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided. This means that a new law generally applies only to situations or acts that occur after it takes effect, not to those that happened before. In short, laws are prospective by default, and retroactive application is the exception that must be expressly stated in the law.

What is the meaning of partition under Article 1079 of the Civil Code of the Philippines?

Article 1079 defines partition as the separation, division, and assignment of a thing held in common among those who have rights to it. This means that if multiple people co-own a property, partition is the process of dividing that property among them. The division can be done in two ways: either by physically dividing the thing itself (if possible) or by dividing its value. For example, if co-owners cannot physically divide a piece of land because it is too small, they may sell it and divide the proceeds, or one may take the property and pay the others their share.

STATUTORY TEXT: Legitimate children shall have the right:
(1) To bear the surnames of the father and of the mother;
(2) To receive support from them, from their ascendants, and in a proper case, from their brothers and sisters, in conformity with article 291;

I am a legitimate child of my parents. My father refuses to give me financial support and also does not allow me to use my mother's surname. He claims that as the father, he has the sole right to decide on these matters. What are my rights under Philippine law? Please explain based on the Civil Code.

You may also have successional rights, but the immediate issues are your right to use the surname and your right to support.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 264 of the Philippine Civil Code, as a legitimate child, you have the right to bear the surnames of both your father and your mother. Therefore, your father cannot prevent you from using your mother's surname. Additionally, you have the right to receive support from your parents. Your father is legally obligated to provide financial support for your needs, such as food, shelter, education, and healthcare. If he refuses, you may seek legal remedies to compel him to fulfill this obligation. [Art. 264].

### 💡 Application to Facts

Can you explain Article 896 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the share of illegitimate children when there are legitimate parents or ascendants?

Article 896 provides that if the deceased is survived by illegitimate children together with legitimate parents or ascendants, the illegitimate children are entitled to one-fourth of the hereditary estate. The efficacy of such a sale is subject to the condition that the thing will come into existence. When a contract of sale is ineffective due to the non-happening of the condition, both parties are bound to return what they have received. Therefore, the farmer must return the payment you made. ### 💡 Application to Facts
The sale is not void from the beginning because the hope of a harvest was not vain—there was a reasonable expectation that the crop would grow.

Your friend's insistence on returning the identical bills is unnecessary, though not illegal; his obligation is satisfied by paying the equivalent amount.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 418 of the Civil Code, money is classified as consumable movable property because it cannot be used according to its nature without being consumed—meaning it is spent or transferred in normal use. In a loan of consumable goods (mutuum), the borrower is not required to return the exact same thing but only an equal amount of the same kind and quality. Therefore, your friend is not obligated to return the exact same banknotes; he may repay with any legal tender amounting to P10,000. [Art. 418].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The article distinguishes between consumable and nonconsumable movables: nonconsumables like a car are returned in the same form, while consumables are returned by equivalent quantity and quality.

Because you acted in bad faith, you are also liable for damages. Your neighbor has the right to remove the materials; because of your bad faith, he may do so even if it damages the shed, and he can also claim damages. [Art. 447].

However, if he chooses to remove the materials, the obligation to pay their value is generally considered satisfied since the materials are returned, but he may still seek indemnity for any damages caused.

(1) That which is acquired by onerous title during the marriage at the expense of the common fund, whether the acquisition be for the partnership, or for only one of the spouses;
