### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, under Article 29 of the Philippine Civil Code, even after your acquittal in the criminal case based on reasonable doubt, the complainant may still file a civil action for damages arising from the same act or omission. In this civil case, the complainant only needs to prove his claim by preponderance of evidence, which means it is more likely than not that you are liable for the damages. This is a lower standard of proof compared to the criminal case's requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt. [Art. 29].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Regarding the bond, you as the defendant may file a motion asking the court to require the complainant to post a bond to answer for damages in case the civil complaint is found to be malicious. The court has discretion to grant this request if it deems it appropriate. Additionally, the criminal court's judgment of acquittal should have stated that the acquittal was based on reasonable doubt; if it did not, you can still establish that ground by examining the text of the decision.

Can you explain Article 347 of the Philippine Civil Code? It talks about rescission of adoption by a minor.

Article 347 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that a minor or other incapacitated person who has been adopted may ask for the rescission (cancellation) of the adoption through a guardian ad litem. This means that the adopted child, if a minor or otherwise legally incapacitated, cannot file the petition personally but must be represented by a guardian ad litem appointed by the court to protect the child's interests. The grounds for seeking rescission are the same as those that cause the loss of parental authority, such as cruelty, neglect, abandonment, or other acts that would justify depriving a parent of parental authority. Therefore, if the adoptive parent has committed acts that would normally result in losing parental authority over a biological child, the adopted child may seek to have the adoption set aside.

My father left a holographic will. After he passed, we noticed that some parts were crossed out and new words were written on top, but there is no signature near those changes. Are the changes valid? Can the original crossed-out words still be considered?

It is important to present the will to the probate court to resolve these issues.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 814 of the Civil Code, any insertion, cancellation, erasure, or alteration in a holographic will must be authenticated by the full signature of the testator. [Art. 814].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the crossed-out words and the new words written are alterations. Since there is no full signature near those changes, the alterations are not valid. The effect is that the original crossed-out words may still be given effect if they remain legible. If they are completely illegible, the court may have to determine the testator's true intention from the rest of the will or other evidence. But the changes themselves cannot be given effect because they were not authenticated as required by law.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

I have been occupying a parcel of land for 7 years without the owner's permission. Last month, the registered owner filed a court case against me to recover possession of the land. Therefore, the 7 years you have occupied the land will not be credited for purposes of acquiring ownership by prescription.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1120 of the Philippine Civil Code, possession is interrupted for the purposes of prescription either naturally or civilly. Civil interruption occurs by a judicial summons, which includes the filing of a court case against the possessor. [Art. 1120].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the registered owner's filing of a case to recover possession constitutes a civil interruption of your possession. As a result, the period of your possession that has already elapsed (the 7 years) is not counted. Under the rules on prescription, once possession is interrupted, the time that has passed is lost, and if you later resume possession, a new period of prescription would begin from the time the interruption ceases.

Can you explain Article 1514 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when a document of title has been transferred but not negotiated?

Article 1514 says that if someone receives a document of title (like a warehouse receipt or bill of lading) through a simple transfer but not through proper negotiation, that person still gets the title to the goods as against the person who transferred it, but subject to any agreement they had. Once notified, the bailee must hold the goods for the transferee according to the document's terms. However, before that notification is made, the transferee's rights can be defeated if a creditor of the transferor levies an attachment on the goods, or if the transferor or a later buyer notifies the bailee of a subsequent sale.

Can you explain Article 1248 of the Philippine Civil Code about partial payments?

Article 1248 states that, as a general rule, a creditor cannot be forced to accept partial payment or performance of an obligation, and a debtor cannot be required to make partial payments, unless there is an express agreement allowing it. If that person is unable or unwilling to fix the price, the contract is inefficacious unless the parties later agree on a price. However, the same article provides that if the third person is prevented from fixing the price by the fault of one party, the party not at fault may have remedies against the party at fault. These remedies could include filing a case for damages or seeking specific performance of the contract, where the court may fix the price based on evidence presented by both parties. The buyer cannot rely on the absence of a fixed price to escape liability because he caused that absence through his own wrongful act.

I received a laptop from a store on a 7-day trial basis. I didn't like it but I kept it for 10 days before trying to return it. The store says I now own it and must pay. Is that correct under Philippine law?

You are now obligated to pay the price.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

What does Article 781 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Can you explain Article 1533 of the Philippine Civil Code about an unpaid seller's right to resell goods?

Article 1533 provides that an unpaid seller who has a right of lien or has stopped the goods in transit may resell the goods if they are perishable, if the seller expressly reserved the right of resale upon the buyer's default, or if the buyer has been in default in paying the price for an unreasonable time. After such resale, the seller is no longer liable to the original buyer on the contract of sale or for any profit made from the resale, but may recover damages for any loss caused by the buyer's breach. The new buyer acquires a good title against the original buyer. Notice of intention to resell is not required for validity, but if the right to resell is based solely on unreasonable delay (not on perishable nature or express agreement), the presence or absence of notice may be relevant in determining whether the buyer's default was unreasonable. Notice of the time and place of resale is also not required. The seller must exercise reasonable care and judgment in making the resale, and may choose between a public or private sale, but cannot directly or indirectly buy the goods.

Can you explain Article 490 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding co-ownership of different stories of a house?

Article 490 provides rules for sharing expenses when different stories of a house are owned by different persons and the titles or agreements do not specify how to divide necessary expenses. The main and party walls, roof, and other common elements must be maintained by all owners in proportion to the value of each one's story. Can you explain Article 535 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 535 states that minors and incapacitated persons can acquire possession of things, but they need the assistance of their legal representatives to exercise the rights that arise from that possession. Possession is the fact of having control or custody over a thing. Acquiring possession is different from exercising the rights that come with possession, such as selling, leasing, or using the property as collateral. Because minors and incapacitated persons lack full legal capacity, they cannot exercise these rights on their own; a parent, guardian, or other legal representative must act on their behalf.

Can you explain Article 1251 of the Philippine Civil Code? I want to understand the rules about where payment should be made.

Article 1251 of the Philippine Civil Code provides rules on the place of payment. First, payment must be made in the place designated in the obligation. If no place is stipulated and the obligation is to deliver a specific (determinate) thing, payment shall be made wherever the thing was located at the time the obligation was constituted. In all other cases (such as monetary debts), payment shall be made at the domicile of the debtor. If the debtor changes his domicile in bad faith or after he has incurred in delay, any additional expenses caused by the change shall be borne by him. These rules do not affect rules on venue under the Rules of Court.

Article 444 of the Philippine Civil Code states that natural and industrial fruits are only considered as such when they are manifest (for plants) or born (for animals). STATUTORY TEXT: The husband is the administrator of the conjugal partnership.

My husband and I are married under the conjugal partnership of gains. He has been making decisions about our conjugal properties without consulting me, like selling a piece of land we own together. Is he allowed to do that under Article 165 of the Civil Code?

Therefore, the husband cannot validly sell the conjugal land solely by invoking his role as administrator under Article 165, and the wife may have legal grounds to challenge the sale.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 165 of the Civil Code, the husband is the administrator of the conjugal partnership. As administrator, he generally has the authority to manage, preserve, and control the conjugal partnership properties. However, this power of administration does not automatically include the power to dispose of or alienate conjugal real property without the wife's consent. Acts of administration typically involve acts of management and preservation, not acts of ownership such as selling, mortgaging, or encumbering real property. [Art. 165].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In the scenario described, the husband's act of selling a piece of conjugal land without the wife's consent may exceed his authority as administrator under Article 165 because such disposition is not a mere act of administration but an act of ownership that usually requires the joint consent of both spouses.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 165, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.

The substitution takes effect only upon the default of the original heir, meaning your brother must be unable or unwilling to inherit for the substitution to operate.

What does Article 1067 of the Philippine Civil Code state about expenses that are not subject to collation?

Article 1067 states that certain expenses are not subject to collation. Collation is the process of adding back to the estate any property or gifts that an heir received from the decedent during the decedent's lifetime, so that all heirs share equally. This article exempts expenses for support, education, medical attendance (even in extraordinary illness), apprenticeship, ordinary equipment, and customary gifts. These are considered as part of the decedent's obligation to support and educate his heirs, not as advances on their inheritance, and therefore they are not deducted from the heir's share.

Under Article 456, your good faith in believing the land was yours does not automatically excuse you from liability for negligence. Even if you were in good faith, if you failed to take reasonable steps to verify boundaries or supervise construction, and that failure caused damage to your neighbor's fence and pipes, you may be liable for damages under Article 2176. Article 2176 requires that there be fault or negligence causing damage to another, and the damage must be proven. [Art. 456].

In your case, if your lack of care in checking boundaries or managing construction directly caused the damage, you can be held liable despite your good faith.

Can you explain what Article 271 of the Philippine Civil Code says about legitimated children?

Article 271 says that a natural child (born out of wedlock) can be legitimated by the subsequent marriage of their parents only if the child was recognized by the parents either before or after the marriage, or if the child was declared a natural child by a final court judgment. Additionally, if one natural child is recognized or judicially declared, that recognition automatically extends to his or her full-blood brothers and sisters. These siblings are considered to have given their implied consent to the recognition if they do not challenge it within four years from the time of recognition, or if they are minors, within four years after they reach the age of majority (18 years old).

Can you explain Article 209 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 209 states that when a husband and wife separate in fact (i.e., they live apart) without obtaining judicial approval (no court decree of separation), the rules of Article 178 apply. Article 178 says that such separation does not affect the conjugal partnership (the property regime remains in force), but the spouse who leaves the conjugal home without just cause loses the right to be supported by the other. However, if the wife leaves the conjugal home and she has a just cause for leaving, the husband is still obligated to support her. So an informal separation does not change property relations, but it can affect the right to support depending on who left and why.

A customary gift is one that is given according to family tradition or practice, not an extraordinary or excessive gift relative to the estate. [Art. 1067].

Can you explain Article 1226 of the Philippine Civil Code about obligations with a penal clause?

Article 1226 states that if an obligation has a penal clause (a stipulated amount to be paid in case of breach), that penalty generally substitutes for damages and interest for noncompliance, unless the parties agreed otherwise. Can you explain what Article 191 of the Philippine Civil Code says about separation of property between spouses?

Article 191 of the Civil Code provides the grounds for separation of property between spouses. Either spouse may petition the court for separation of property if: (1) the other spouse has been sentenced to a penalty carrying civil interdiction; (2) the other spouse has been declared absent; or (3) legal separation has been granted. Additionally, if the husband abuses his administration of the conjugal partnership property or abandons the family, the court may also order separation of property. In all these cases, presenting the final judgment against the guilty or absent spouse is sufficient. The article further permits spouses to voluntarily dissolve the conjugal partnership during marriage, subject to judicial approval, with notice to creditors and measures to protect their interests. After dissolution, Articles 214 and 215 on liquidation and Articles 498 to 501 on partition apply.

Can you explain Article 572 of the Philippine Civil Code about the rights of a usufructuary to lease or alienate the property?

Article 572 states that a usufructuary, or the person who has the right to use and enjoy someone else's property, may do any of the following: personally enjoy the property, lease it to another person, or transfer (alienate) his right of usufruct to someone else, even without receiving anything in return (gratuitous title). However, any contract he enters into as usufructuary will automatically terminate when the usufruct itself ends. There is one exception: leases of rural lands are considered to continue until the end of the agricultural year, even if the usufruct ends earlier.

STATUTORY TEXT: Things subject to a resolutory condition may be the object of the contract of sale.

I bought a second-hand car from a seller who said he was still paying installments to a financing company. The contract he showed me had a clause that if he fails to pay the remaining balance, the car will be repossessed by the financing company. Now, he missed payments and the financing company is threatening to take the car from me. Is the sale valid? Do I have any rights? Please explain based on the law.

You should review the sale contract for any warranties or representations by the seller and consider seeking legal recourse against the seller for any losses you incur.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1465 of the Philippine Civil Code, things subject to a resolutory condition may be the object of a contract of sale. [Art. 1465].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the car was subject to a resolutory condition: if the seller fails to pay the remaining installments, the ownership or possession reverts to the financing company. The sale between you and the seller is still valid even though the car is under this condition. However, you as the buyer acquired the car subject to that same condition. This means that if the seller defaults and the financing company repossesses the car, you may lose possession and any rights to the car because the condition resolves the seller's title and consequently your derivative title. You may have a claim against the seller for breach of warranty against eviction or for damages, but you cannot prevent the financing company from enforcing its rights under the condition. The law allows such sales to protect commerce, but the buyer takes the risk of the condition being fulfilled.

Can you explain Article 1151 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about when prescription starts for obligations involving principal with interest or annuity?

Article 1151 provides that for obligations to pay principal plus interest or an annuity, the prescriptive period for filing an action to enforce the obligation begins to run from the last payment of the interest or annuity, not from the date the principal became due. This means that as long as interest or annuity payments are being made, the creditor's right to sue for the entire obligation (including the principal) does not start to prescribe until the last such payment is made. Once the debtor stops paying the interest or annuity, the clock starts for the creditor to file a case within the applicable prescriptive period.

Can you explain Article 763 of the Philippine Civil Code about revocation or reduction of donations?

Please explain Article 418 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the classification of movable property as consumable or nonconsumable.

Article 418 of the Philippine Civil Code classifies movable property (personal property) into two types: consumable and nonconsumable. Consumable movables are those that cannot be used according to their nature without being consumed or used up, such as food, fuel, or money. Nonconsumable movables are all other movable properties that can be used repeatedly without being destroyed or consumed, like furniture, books, or tools. This distinction matters in legal transactions like loans, usufruct, or leases because consumable goods may need to be returned in equal quantity and quality, while nonconsumable goods are returned in the same form.

STATUTORY TEXT: The nullity of the penal clause does not carry with it that of the principal obligation.
The nullity of the principal obligation carries with it that of the penal clause. (1155)
General Provisions

I entered into a contract for the sale of a parcel of land. The contract includes a penalty clause stating that if I fail to pay the remaining balance on time, I will pay a penalty of 50% of the total price. Later, I was told that the penalty clause might be void because it is excessive. Does that mean my obligation to pay the balance is also void? Also, what happens to the penalty clause if the sale itself is found to be void?

The accessory follows the principal; hence, when the principal obligation is void, the penal clause cannot stand independently.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1230 of the Civil Code, the nullity of the penal clause does not carry with it that of the principal obligation. Thus, if the penal clause is void (for example, because the penalty is excessive or unconscionable), your obligation to pay the remaining balance under the contract of sale remains valid and enforceable. You are still required to pay the balance, but the invalid penalty cannot be enforced against you. [Art. 1230].

### 💡 Application to Facts
On the other hand, if the principal obligation (the sale) is void—for instance, because it lacks an essential requisite or is contrary to law—then the penal clause is likewise void, because the penal clause is only an accessory to the principal obligation.

This provision balances your property rights with the need to protect neighboring landowners from water damage.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Based on Article 515 of the Civil Code, as the owner of the land where the defensive work (the old dike) is located, you are legally obliged to either make the necessary repairs yourself or permit the owners of lands that are suffering or clearly exposed to suffer injury (your neighbor) to do the repairs on your land, provided it is done without damage to you. Since your neighbor's land is being flooded due to the defective dike and the change in the river's course, he is clearly suffering injury. Therefore, you must choose one of the two options. ### 💡 Application to Facts
If you refuse both, you may be compelled by law to allow him to do the repairs, and you cannot unreasonably prevent it as long as no damage is caused to your property.

The buyer does not receive a specific physical portion of the land; instead, they acquire a proportional undivided interest in the whole property. This means you can continue to use the land for farming as before, but now you share ownership with the buyer. [Art. 1463].

### 💡 Application to Facts

Can you explain Article 1222 of the Philippine Civil Code? What defenses can a solidary debtor raise against the creditor?

Article 1222 states that a solidary debtor, when sued by the creditor, may use two types of defenses: (1) defenses derived from the nature of the obligation itself (like payment, prescription, or nullity of the whole obligation) and (2) defenses that are personal to him or pertain to his own share (like his own minority or his own condonation). However, if a defense is personal to another solidary debtor, he can only use that defense to reduce the debt by that other debtor's share, not to escape the entire obligation. In short, you cannot borrow another debtor's personal defense to avoid your own solidary liability, but you can use it to lower the amount you are asked to pay.

Can you explain Article 1538 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1538 states that if the thing sold is lost, deteriorates, or improves before delivery, the rules in Article 1189 apply, with the seller considered as the debtor. This means: (1) If the thing is lost without the seller's fault, the obligation to deliver is extinguished; (2) If lost through the seller's fault, the seller must pay damages; (3) If it deteriorates without the seller's fault, the buyer bears the impairment and must still accept the thing and pay the price; (4) If it deteriorates through the seller's fault, the buyer may choose to cancel the sale or demand delivery, plus damages; (5) If the thing improves naturally or by time, the improvement benefits the buyer; (6) If the seller spends for improvements, the seller only has rights of a usufructuary. In short, before delivery, the seller is treated as debtor and the buyer as creditor for risks and benefits concerning the specific thing sold.

Under Article 1399 of the Civil Code, since the contract is voidable due to your incapacity as a minor, you are not obliged to make full restitution. You are only required to return the laptop or its value to the extent that you were benefited. This means you may return the laptop in its current condition or pay the equivalent of the benefit you received from its use, such as a reasonable rental value. You are also entitled to recover any installments you have already paid, because you should not bear the loss from a contract that is annulled due to your incapacity. [Art. 1399].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The store cannot demand full restitution of the original price or the laptop in its original condition because you were not capacitated to contract.

Can you explain Article 453 of the Philippine Civil Code about bad faith in building on another's land?

Article 453 states that if both the person who built, planted, or sowed on another's land and the landowner acted in bad faith, their rights are the same as if both had acted in good faith. In other words, mutual bad faith cancels out the penalties that would normally apply to a bad-faith builder. The landowner is considered in bad faith if he knew about the act and did not oppose it. As a result, the landowner cannot use the builder's bad faith to avoid paying for improvements if he chooses to keep them; the normal rules for good faith improvements apply.

Can you explain Article 80 of the Philippine Civil Code? What marriages are considered void from the beginning?

Article 80 of the Philippine Civil Code lists the marriages that are void from the very beginning, meaning they have no legal effect from the start, as if they never happened. These include: (1) marriages where the male is under 16 or the female is under 14, even if the parents consented; (2) marriages solemnized by someone not legally authorized to perform marriages; (3) marriages without a valid marriage license, except for those allowed by law as exceptional (like marriages in articulo mortis or in remote areas); (4) bigamous or polygamous marriages that do not fall under the exceptions in Article 83, number 2; (5) incestuous marriages as defined in Article 81; (6) marriages where one or both parties have been convicted of killing the spouse of either party; and (7) marriages between stepbrothers and stepsisters and others specified in Article 82. These marriages are void ab initio, so they produce no legal rights or obligations between the parties.

What does Article 1178 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 1178 states that all rights acquired by virtue of an obligation are generally transmissible or transferable to another person, including heirs or assignees. This means that if you have a right to demand something from another person under an obligation (like a right to collect a debt), you can usually transfer that right to someone else. However, this rule is subject to two exceptions: first, if there is a law that prohibits the transmission of that particular right (for example, rights that are purely personal, like the right to receive support, are not transmissible); and second, if the parties have stipulated or agreed in their contract that the right cannot be transferred. Unless one of these exceptions applies, the right can be transmitted.

What does Article 1443 of the Philippine Civil Code mean regarding express trusts over immovable property?

Article 1443 states that an express trust concerning an immovable (real property) or any interest in it cannot be proven by oral testimony alone. In other words, if someone claims that an express trust was created over land, they must present a written document evidencing that trust. Parol (oral) evidence is not admissible to establish the existence of such an express trust. This rule aims to prevent fraud and ensure certainty in transactions involving real property. It applies only to express trusts, not to implied trusts, which may still be proven by oral evidence under certain circumstances.

Can you explain Article 842 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the disposal of property by will?

STATUTORY TEXT: Every donation between the spouses during the marriage shall be void. This prohibition does not apply when the donation takes effect after the death of the donor.
Neither does this prohibition apply to moderate gifts which the spouses may give each other on the occasion of any family rejoicing.

I am a married woman. I want to give my husband a parcel of land as a gift while we are both still alive. However, a friend told me that donations between spouses are void under Philippine law. Is that correct? Are there any exceptions, such as giving it as an anniversary gift or through my last will?

The donation as planned would be void and unenforceable.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 133 of the Civil Code, any donation between spouses made during the marriage is void. This means that transferring a parcel of land to your husband as a gift while you are both still alive would not be legally effective. The prohibition applies to all donations inter vivos, regardless of value, unless it falls under the two exceptions. First, donations that take effect after the death of the donor are allowed, such as those made through a will. Second, moderate gifts given on occasions of family rejoicing, like anniversaries, are permitted. However, a parcel of land is not considered a moderate gift; it is a substantial property transfer and would not qualify for the exception. [Art. 133].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, to give the land to your husband, you should consider making a will that bequeaths the property to him upon your death, or you may explore other legal means such as selling it to him or transferring it after the marriage is dissolved.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 133, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.

Can you explain Article 891 of the Philippine Civil Code about reserva troncal?

Article 891 of the Philippine Civil Code establishes the rule of 'reserva troncal' or 'reserva lineal'. It states that when an ascendant (parent, grandparent, etc.) inherits property from a descendant (child, grandchild, etc.), and that property was originally acquired by the descendant through gratuitous title (like donation or inheritance) from another ascendant or from a brother or sister, the inheriting ascendant is obliged to reserve the property for the benefit of relatives who are within the third degree of consanguinity and who belong to the line from which the property originally came. This means the property must be kept and eventually passed on to the relatives from the side of the family that originally owned it, preventing it from leaving that family line.

STATUTORY TEXT: The father and mother jointly exercise parental authority over their legitimate children who are not emancipated. In case of disagreement, the father's decision shall prevail, unless there is a judicial order to the contrary.
Children are obliged to obey their parents so long as they are under parental power, and to observe respect and reverence toward them always.
Recognized natural and adopted children who are under the age of majority are under the parental authority of the father or mother recognizing or adopting them, and are under the same obligation stated in the preceding paragraph.
Natural children by legal fiction are under the joint authority of the father and mother, as provided in the first paragraph of this article.

My husband and I disagree about our 15-year-old son's education. He wants our son to stop schooling and work in the family business, but I strongly oppose because I want him to finish high school. My husband insists that as the father, his decision should prevail. Is he correct under Philippine law?

It is advisable to settle the disagreement through proper legal channels if you cannot agree.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 311 of the Philippine Civil Code, both the father and mother jointly exercise parental authority over their legitimate children who are not emancipated. In case of disagreement between the parents, the father's decision shall prevail, unless there is a judicial order to the contrary. [Art. 311].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, in your situation, if your husband insists that your son stop schooling, his decision would generally prevail over your objection, absent any court intervention. However, you may seek a judicial order from the court to override your husband's decision if you believe it is not in the best interest of your child. The court has the authority to issue an order contrary to the father's decision. Additionally, your son, being under parental authority, is obliged to obey his parents, but the law also requires parents to act in the best interest of the child.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 311, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 311 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Therefore, the party claiming that you were in bad faith (the person alleging the car was stolen and that you knew or should have known the seller was not the real owner) must present evidence to overcome the presumption of good faith. ### 💡 Application to Facts
You do not need to prove your good faith; it is presumed by law.

LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE I.—OBLIGATIONS > CH 4 - EXTINGUISHMENT OF OBLIGATIONS > SEC 4.—Confusion or Merger of Rights > Art. 1275
STATUTORY TEXT: The obligation is extinguished from the time the characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person.

I lent money to my friend last year. He still owes me P100,000. Recently, his aunt died and left him a substantial inheritance. But here's the twist: I also owed his aunt P100,000 for some business transaction. Now, the aunt's estate is asking me to pay, but I told them that since I am both creditor and debtor now? I'm confused. Can you explain what happens to the debt my friend owes me and the debt I owe to his aunt under the law?

You could potentially set off or compensate if both debts are due and demandable, but that is a different legal concept (compensation), not confusion.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
In your situation, Article 1275 of the Civil Code on confusion or merger of rights may apply. [Art. 1275].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Under this provision, an obligation is extinguished when the characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person. Here, your friend owes you P100,000. You also owe his aunt P100,000. If the aunt has died and left an inheritance to your friend, he may inherit her rights as creditor against you. However, this does not directly merge the obligations between you and your friend, because the debts are between different parties: one is your friend's debt to you, and the other is your debt to the aunt. Confusion would occur if the same person becomes both creditor and debtor in the same obligation. For your friend's debt to you, you are the creditor and he is the debtor; that obligation would only be extinguished if you and your friend became the same person, which is not the case. For your debt to the aunt, you are the debtor and the aunt (or her estate) is the creditor; if your friend inherits that credit, he becomes your creditor for that debt. That does not extinguish your obligation; rather, he can collect from you. So no confusion arises from these facts because the two obligations are separate and do not merge in one person. You still owe the estate (or your friend as heir) P100,000, and your friend still owes you P100,000.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1275, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1275 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

STATUTORY TEXT: Mining claims and rights and other matters concerning minerals and mineral lands are governed by special laws.

I inherited a piece of land that appears to contain gold deposits. My neighbor claims that under the Civil Code, he has a right to a portion of the minerals because he has been using the land for farming. I want to know if the Civil Code applies to mineral rights or if there is a different law I should follow.

You should also check with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) or the Mines and Geosciences Bureau for the specific legal requirements and procedures regarding mineral deposits on your property.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 519 of the Philippine Civil Code, matters concerning minerals and mineral lands are not governed by the Civil Code but by special laws. In the Philippines, the primary special law is the Philippine Mining Act of 1995 (Republic Act No. 7942). This law provides that all mineral resources in public or private lands are owned by the State, and the exploration, development, and utilization of these resources require permits or agreements from the government. Therefore, your neighbor's claim based on the Civil Code—such as rights arising from possession or accession—does not automatically grant him any right to the minerals. [Art. 519].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The Civil Code does not apply to the mineral aspect of your land; instead, you must refer to the Mining Act and its implementing rules to determine any existing mining rights, permits, or claims.

STATUTORY TEXT: Ownership and other real rights over immovable property are acquired by ordinary prescription through possession of ten years.

I have been occupying and using a parcel of agricultural land in the province for more than 10 years now. I have been paying the real property taxes and have a deed of sale from the previous owner, but the title is still in the previous owner's name. I believe I have a right to the land because I have been in possession for over 10 years. Can I now claim ownership under Article 1134 of the Civil Code?

Therefore, you need to verify whether your possession meets the strict requirements of ordinary prescription to claim ownership under Article 1134.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1134, ownership and other real rights over immovable property are acquired by ordinary prescription through possession of ten years. However, to invoke ordinary prescription, the possession must be in good faith and with just title. Just title means a title that is valid and sufficient to transfer ownership, such as a deed of sale, even if the seller was not the true owner, provided the buyer believed in good faith that the seller had the right to sell. Good faith means that the possessor was not aware of any flaw or defect in his title. If you have a deed of sale and you honestly believed the seller was the legitimate owner, and you have possessed the land openly, continuously, and peacefully for ten years, then you may have acquired ownership through ordinary prescription. [Art. 1134].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If your possession does not meet these requirements (e.g., you knew the seller was not the owner, or you lack a just title), then you may still acquire ownership through extraordinary prescription, which requires thirty years of possession under Article 1137, regardless of good faith or title.

The law does not prohibit one party from proposing a price; it only prohibits a situation where the price is determined solely by one party without the other's consent. Since the buyer has indicated he will accept whatever price you set, once you actually fix the price and he accepts, there is mutual agreement and the sale is perfected. But note that before you fix the price and he accepts, there is no perfected sale yet because the price is still uncertain.

Can you explain Article 1102 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1102 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that if an heir has sold or otherwise alienated the whole or a considerable part of the real property that was adjudicated to him in the partition of the estate, he cannot later file an action for rescission of the partition on the ground of lesion (i.e., that the property was overvalued or undervalued causing damage to him). This is because the property is no longer in his possession to return if the partition were to be rescinded. Instead, his remedy is limited to claiming indemnification in cash for any loss he suffered due to the lesion.

Article 1587 states that when goods are delivered to a buyer and the buyer refuses to accept them, and the buyer has a valid right to refuse, the buyer is not required to return the goods to the seller. Can you explain Article 83 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about marriages contracted while a previous marriage still exists?

Article 83 provides that if a person contracts a subsequent marriage while the first spouse is still alive and the subsequent marriage is with a person other than the first spouse, that subsequent marriage is illegal and void from its performance. However, there are exceptions: (1) if the first marriage was annulled or dissolved, meaning it is no longer valid; or (2) if the first spouse had been absent for seven consecutive years at the time of the second marriage without the spouse present having news of the absentee being alive, or if the absentee, though absent for less than seven years, is generally considered as dead and believed to be so by the spouse present, or if the absentee is presumed dead under Articles 390 and 391. In these three exceptional situations, the subsequent marriage is valid, but only until a competent court declares it null and void. Thus, such marriages are not automatically void; they are voidable and remain valid unless and until annulled by a court.

Article 884 provides that when a testator imposes conditions on heirs in a will, those conditions are governed by the general rules on conditional obligations under the Civil Code, except for matters specifically covered by Section 4 on Conditional Testamentary Dispositions. Ayon sa Artikulo 1470, ang labis na kababaan ng presyo ay hindi mismo nagpapawalang-bisa sa isang kontrata ng pagbebenta. Kahit na napakababa ng presyo kumpara sa tunay na halaga ng bagay na ipinagbili, mananatiling valid at may bisa ang bilihan. Ngunit may dalawang pagbubukod: una, kung ang labis na kababaan ng presyo ay nagpapahiwatig ng depekto sa pagsang-ayon ng isang partido (tulad ng pandaraya, pagkakamali, pananakot, o undue influence), maaaring ipawalang-bisa ang kontrata batay doon; pangalawa, kung ang presyo ay napakababa na nagpapakita na ang tunay na layunin ng mga partido ay hindi pagbebenta kundi donasyon o ibang uri ng kontrata, ang transaksyon ay ituturing ayon sa kanilang tunay na layunin. Sa madaling salita, ang labis na kababaan ng presyo lamang ay hindi sapat na dahilan para ipawalang-bisa ang bilihan, ngunit maaari itong maging babala na may problema sa pagsang-ayon o hindi talaga pagbebenta ang pinagkasunduan.

Article 1481 of the Civil Code of the Philippines provides that in a contract of sale of goods by description or by sample, the buyer may have the contract rescinded (cancelled) if the bulk of the goods delivered does not correspond with the description or the sample. Can you explain Article 1531 of the Philippine Civil Code about when goods are considered in transit?

Article 1531 clarifies the meaning of "goods in transit" for the purpose of stoppage in transitu, which is the right of an unpaid seller to stop goods while they are being transported to the buyer. Goods are considered in transit from the time they are delivered to a carrier or bailee for transmission to the buyer until the buyer or his agent takes delivery. If the buyer rejects the goods and the carrier remains in possession, the goods are still in transit even if the seller refuses to take them back. Goods are no longer in transit if: (1) the buyer obtains delivery before arrival at the destination; (2) after arrival, the carrier acknowledges to the buyer that he holds the goods on the buyer's behalf; or (3) the carrier wrongfully refuses to deliver. If the carrier is chartered by the buyer, it depends on whether the carrier is acting as an independent carrier or as the buyer's agent. A partial delivery does not prevent the seller from stopping the remainder unless the circumstances show an agreement to give up possession of the whole.

Article 1237 says that if a person pays someone else's debt without that debtor's knowledge or against the debtor's will, the person who paid cannot force the creditor to transfer to them the creditor's rights, such as a mortgage, guaranty, or penalty clause. I have a contract where two friends borrowed my specific vintage car and are both obligated to return the same car. The contract does not say they are solidarily liable. Can I demand the car from just one of them?

Therefore, you cannot legally require only one of them to turn over the car unless solidarity is established.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1210 of the Civil Code, the indivisibility of an obligation does not necessarily give rise to solidarity. [Art. 1210].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the obligation to return the specific vintage car is indivisible because the car cannot be divided. However, since the contract does not state that your friends are solidarily liable, they are only jointly liable—each is liable only for his respective share. Because the object is indivisible, you cannot demand partial performance; you must demand performance from both debtors collectively. You cannot compel one debtor alone to deliver the entire car unless solidarity exists or that debtor voluntarily agrees to perform the whole obligation. If one of them voluntarily returns the car, that extinguishes the obligation, and that debtor may seek reimbursement from the other for the latter's share.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1210, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1210 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

May lease contract po ako bilang tenant. Nakalagay: 'the lessee may renew the lease for another term upon written notice to the lessor at least 30 days before expiration.' Therefore, applying Article 1373, the clause should be construed to allow the tenant to renew the lease by simply sending a written notice at least 30 days before expiration, without needing the landlord's further consent, provided the other terms of the lease are met.

Under Article 1373, when a contractual stipulation admits of several meanings, it must be interpreted in the way that renders it effectual. The renewal clause in question is ambiguous: it could mean the tenant has an absolute right to renew by giving timely written notice, or it could mean the tenant merely has an option that still requires the landlord's acceptance. To give the clause effect and purpose, the interpretation favoring the tenant's right to renew upon proper notice should be adopted. [Art. 1373].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the landlord's consent were required, the notice provision would be largely illusory because the tenant's act would have no binding consequence.

STATUTORY TEXT: The wife may, by express authority of the husband embodied in a public instrument, administer the conjugal partnership property.

My husband and I own a small grocery store that is part of our conjugal partnership. He has always verbally told me I can manage the store and sign contracts for it. But now a supplier refuses to accept my signature, saying I need a notarized authority from my husband. Is that correct under the law? What should we do?

Once notarized, you can present this to the supplier and any other third parties to validate your acts.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 168 of the Philippine Civil Code, the wife may administer the conjugal partnership property only if the husband gives his express authority embodied in a public instrument. A mere verbal permission from your husband is not sufficient. Since the grocery store is conjugal property, your authority to manage it and sign contracts on behalf of the partnership must be formalized in a notarized document (public instrument) signed by your husband. The supplier is correct in requiring such proof. [Art. 168].

### 💡 Application to Facts
To resolve this, you and your husband should execute a public instrument (e.g., a special power of attorney) granting you express authority to administer the conjugal partnership property.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 168, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.

Sinasabi nito na kung sa isang kontrata sa pagitan ng ibang tao, ang isa sa kanila ay nalinlang ng isang tao tungkol sa pagmamay-ari o tunay na karapatan sa lupa, ang taong nanlinlang ay hindi na maaaring igiit ang kanyang sariling titulo o interes sa ari-arian, basta't natutugunan ang apat na kundisyon: (1) may mapanlinlang na pagsasabi o maling pagtatago ng mga katotohanang alam ng partido; (2) layunin ng partidong iyon na umasa ang kabilang partido sa maling impormasyon; (3) ang nalinlang na partido ay walang kaalaman sa tunay na katotohanan; at (4) ang nalinlang na partido ay kumilos ayon sa maling impormasyon. Sa madaling salita, kung manloloko ka tungkol sa pagmamay-ari ng lupa, hindi ka makakapag-claim ng sarili mong karapatan laban sa taong naniwala sa iyong panloloko.

[Statutory Article 1]
SOURCE TYPE: PHILIPPINE CIVIL CODE ARTICLE
PROVISION: Article 1435 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE IV.—ESTOPPEL (n) > Art. 1435
STATUTORY TEXT: If a person in representation of another sells or alienates a thing, the former cannot subsequently set up his own title as against the buyer or grantee.

I sold a parcel of land as the authorized representative of my brother. The buyer paid me and took possession. Later, I discovered that my brother had actually transferred the title to me before the sale, so I am now the registered owner. Can I claim the land back from the buyer on the ground that my brother was not the owner when I sold it?

Your remedy, if any, may lie against your brother for any misrepresentation, but as against the buyer, the sale is valid and you cannot recover the property.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1435 of the Civil Code, you are estopped from claiming the land back from the buyer. The article provides that if a person sells or alienates a thing in representation of another, the former cannot subsequently set up his own title as against the buyer or grantee. [Art. 1435].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you sold the land as the authorized representative of your brother. By doing so, you represented that your brother was the owner and that you were acting on his behalf. The buyer relied on this representation and purchased the property in good faith. Even though you later discovered that the title had been transferred to you before the sale, you cannot now assert your own ownership to defeat the buyer's rights. The law prevents you from contradicting the representation you made at the time of the sale.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1435, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1435 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

STATUTORY TEXT: When the conditions have for their purpose the extinguishment of an obligation to give, the parties, upon the fulfillment of said conditions, shall return to each other what they have received.
In case of the loss, deterioration or improvement of the thing, the provisions which, with respect to the debtor, are laid down in the preceding article shall be applied to the party who is bound to return.
As for obligations to do and not to do, the provisions of the second paragraph of article 1187 shall be observed as regards the effect of the extinguishment of the obligation.

I bought a piece of land from Mr. Santos with a condition that if he repays the loan within one year, the sale will be cancelled. He repaid within the year, so now we need to return the property and the money. However, while I was in possession, a storm damaged the property. What does Article 1190 say about my obligation to return the damaged property?

If the land had been lost entirely due to the storm without your fault, your obligation to return it would be extinguished.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1190, when a resolutory condition is fulfilled, the obligation to give is extinguished, and the parties must return what they received. [Art. 1190].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you must return the land to Mr. Santos, and he must return the purchase price to you. Since the land was damaged by a storm while in your possession, the second paragraph of Article 1190 directs us to apply Article 1189 regarding the debtor's responsibilities to you as the party bound to return the land. Under Article 1189, if the thing deteriorates without the fault of the debtor (you), the impairment is borne by the creditor (Mr. Santos). Therefore, you are only obliged to return the land in its damaged condition, and you are not liable for the damage caused by the storm. Mr. Santos, on the other hand, must still return the full purchase price to you.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 201 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas. Anong mga ari-arian ang hindi kasama sa community property?

Nililista ng Artikulo 201 ang mga ari-arian na hindi kabilang sa community property ng mag-asawa sa ilalim ng sistema ng absolute community of property. Ang mga hindi kasama ay: (1) Ari-arian na nakuha ng alinmang asawa sa pamamagitan ng gratuitous title (tulad ng donasyon o mana), kung itinakda ng donor o testador na hindi ito magiging bahagi ng community; (2) Ari-arian na minana ng alinmang asawa mula sa pagkamatay ng isang anak sa naunang kasal, kung may mga kapatid sa buong dugo ang namatay na anak; (3) Bahagi ng ari-arian ng alinmang asawa na katumbas ng presumptive legitime (ang bahaging nakalaan sa batas para sa mga compulsory heirs) ng mga anak sa naunang kasal; (4) Mga personal na gamit ng bawat asawa. Gayunpaman, ang lahat ng bunga at kita mula sa mga nabanggit na ari-arian ay kabilang pa rin sa community property.

STATUTORY TEXT: The choice shall produce no effect except from the time it has been communicated.

I have an alternative obligation to my creditor: I can either give him my motorcycle or pay him PHP 50,000. I already decided in my mind to give the motorcycle, but I haven't told him yet. Now he is demanding the money. Is my silent choice binding? Can I still change my mind and pay instead?

Once you communicate your choice, it becomes binding and you must comply with the chosen alternative.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1201 of the Civil Code, the choice in an alternative obligation produces no effect until it has been communicated. Your internal decision to give the motorcycle is not yet effective because you have not informed the creditor. Therefore, you are not yet bound by that choice and may still change it. [Art. 1201].

### 💡 Application to Facts
You may still choose to pay the PHP 50,000 instead, but you must communicate that choice to your creditor for it to take effect.

Article 1396 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that ratification cleanses a voidable contract from all its defects from the moment it was constituted. Can you explain Article 164 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding gambling losses and the conjugal partnership?

Article 164 states that any money or property lost by a spouse through gambling, betting, or games of chance during the marriage is the personal responsibility of the losing spouse. STATUTORY TEXT: Contracts are perfected by mere consent, and from that moment the parties are bound not only to the fulfillment of what has been expressly stipulated but also to all the consequences which, according to their nature, may be in keeping with good faith, usage and law.

I agreed to buy a second-hand laptop from an online seller. We settled on the price and that I would pay cash upon delivery. The next day, the seller told me he changed his mind because I haven't paid anything yet and there is no written contract. Is he allowed to just cancel our agreement? What does the law say about this?

If the seller refuses to proceed, he may be liable for breach of contract, and you can demand fulfillment of the obligation or claim damages.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1315 of the Civil Code, contracts are perfected by mere consent. Once you and the seller agreed on the object (the laptop) and the price (the cause), the contract was perfected at that moment, even without payment or a written document. The sale of a movable property does not require any special form for validity, so the absence of writing and payment does not prevent the contract from existing. From that moment, the seller is bound to deliver the laptop and you are bound to pay the agreed price. The seller cannot unilaterally cancel just because you haven't paid yet or there is no written contract; those are not requirements for perfection. [Art. 1315].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Moreover, the seller is bound not only to fulfill what was expressly agreed (delivering the laptop for the price) but also to all consequences in keeping with good faith, usage, and law, such as delivering the item in the condition agreed upon and acting fairly.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1315, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1315 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Article 736 of the Philippine Civil Code states that guardians and trustees cannot donate the property entrusted to them. This is because they are not the owners of the property; they only hold and manage it for the benefit of another person (the ward, minor, or beneficiary). Article 1206 defines a facultative obligation. In this type of obligation, only one prestation (thing or service) is due, but the obligor (debtor) is allowed to substitute another prestation in its place. If the substitute is lost or deteriorates due to the obligor's negligence before the substitution is made, the obligor is not liable because the original prestation still remains due. However, once the substitution has been made, the substitute becomes the object of the obligation, and if it is lost due to the obligor's delay, negligence, or fraud, the obligor is liable for that loss.

Under Article 1392 of the Civil Code, ratification extinguishes the action to annul a voidable contract. By impliedly ratifying the contract through your conduct, you have lost the right to annul it.

Can you explain what Article 1256 of the Philippine Civil Code says about consignation?

Article 1256 provides that if a debtor makes a valid tender of payment to the creditor, but the creditor refuses to accept it without just cause, the debtor can be released from his obligation by consigning (depositing) the thing or money due with the proper court or judicial authority. This is called consignation. The article also lists cases where consignation alone, even without a prior tender of payment, is enough to produce the same effect: (1) when the creditor is absent, unknown, or fails to appear at the place of payment; (2) when the creditor is incapacitated to receive payment at the time it is due; (3) when the creditor refuses without just cause to issue a receipt; (4) when two or more persons claim the same right to collect; and (5) when the title of the obligation has been lost.

In your case, if your brother's need for support is due to his own laziness or refusal to work, then you may stop providing support as long as that condition continues. You do not need to continue supporting him if he is able to work but chooses not to.

What does Article 1585 of the Civil Code say about when a buyer is considered to have accepted the goods?

The measure of damages is the estimated loss directly and naturally resulting in the ordinary course of events, from the buyer's breach of contract.
Where there is an available market for the goods in question, the measure of damages is, in the absence of special circumstances showing proximate damage of a different amount, the difference between the contract price and the market or current price at the time or times when the goods ought to have been accepted, or, if no time was fixed for acceptance, then at the time of the refusal to accept.

I entered into a contract to sell 100 sacks of rice to a buyer at ₱2,000 per sack, with delivery on March 15. Before the delivery date, the buyer informed me that he no longer wants the rice and will not accept it. I had already spent ₱5,000 on transportation and storage to prepare the rice for delivery. Therefore, you can sue for the price difference plus the expenses incurred before the repudiation and your lost profit.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1596, since the buyer wrongfully refused to accept and pay for the rice, you may maintain an action for damages for non-acceptance. The measure of damages is the difference between the contract price (₱2,000 per sack) and the market price at the time when the goods ought to have been accepted, which is March 15 (₱1,800 per sack). The difference is ₱200 per sack, so for 100 sacks, the total damages for non-acceptance would be ₱20,000. Additionally, because you incurred labor and expenses (₱5,000 for transportation and storage) to enable you to fulfill the contract before the buyer repudiated, you can also recover those expenses. [Art. 1596].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The profit you would have made if the contract had been fully performed should also be considered in awarding damages.

Please explain Article 959 of the Philippine Civil Code. What does it mean when a will says 'I leave my property to my relatives'?

Article 959 provides a rule of interpretation for wills. If a testator makes a disposition in general terms in favor of his or her relatives, without specifying which particular relatives or degrees, the law presumes that the testator intended to benefit those relatives who are nearest in degree of relationship. In other words, the closest blood relatives will be the ones entitled to inherit under that provision, to the exclusion of more distant relatives. For example, if a will says 'I give P100,000 to my relatives,' and the testator has a brother, a nephew, and a second cousin, the brother, being nearest in degree, will be considered the intended beneficiary.

Can you explain Article 1205 of the Philippine Civil Code about alternative obligations when the choice is given to the creditor?

Article 1205 states that when the choice among alternative prestations is expressly given to the creditor, the obligation remains alternative until the creditor communicates his selection to the debtor. Once communicated, the obligation becomes a simple one. Before that communication, the debtor's responsibility is governed by these rules: (1) If one thing is lost due to a fortuitous event, the debtor must deliver whichever the creditor chooses from the remaining things, or the only one left if only one subsists; (2) If one thing is lost through the debtor's fault, the creditor may claim any of the remaining things or the price of the lost thing plus damages; (3) If all things are lost through the debtor's fault, the creditor may choose the price of any one of them plus damages. The same rules apply to obligations to do or not to do if any of the prestations become impossible.

Can you explain Article 1595 of the Philippine Civil Code about the seller's right to sue for the price?

Article 1595 of the Philippine Civil Code allows a seller to sue the buyer for the price of goods in three situations. First, if ownership of the goods has already passed to the buyer and the buyer wrongfully refuses or neglects to pay, the seller can file an action for the price. Second, if the contract states that the price is payable on a specific date regardless of delivery or transfer of ownership, and the buyer fails to pay, the seller can sue for the price even if ownership has not yet transferred. However, the buyer can defend by proving that the seller has shown an inability or unwillingness to perform the contract before judgment. Third, even if ownership has not passed, if the goods cannot be easily resold at a reasonable price and Article 1596(4) does not apply, the seller can offer to deliver the goods to the buyer. If the buyer refuses delivery, the seller may notify the buyer that the goods will be held as bailee for the buyer. After that, the seller may treat the goods as belonging to the buyer and sue for the price.

Can you explain Article 621 of the Philippine Civil Code? I want to understand how the prescriptive period for acquiring easements is computed.

Article 621 of the Philippine Civil Code provides the rules for computing the period of possession required to acquire an easement by prescription. It distinguishes between positive and negative easements. For positive easements (where the owner of the dominant estate actively uses the servient estate, like a right of way or water drawing), the prescriptive period starts from the day the dominant estate owner or any person who made use of the easement began exercising it on the servient estate. For negative easements (where the owner of the dominant estate prohibits the servient owner from doing an act that would otherwise be lawful, like building above a certain height or blocking light), the prescriptive period starts from the day the dominant estate owner formally forbade the servient owner from doing that act, using an instrument acknowledged before a notary public. In short, for positive easements, the clock starts with actual use; for negative easements, it starts with a formal notarized prohibition.

Article 1263 states that if you are obligated to deliver a generic thing (like a certain quantity of rice, or a car of a particular make and model), and the thing you intended to deliver is lost or destroyed, your obligation is not extinguished. You can still fulfill it by delivering another thing of the same kind and quality. The principle is that a generic thing never perishes because you can always find a replacement. The obligation is only extinguished if the entire class or genus of the thing is destroyed, which is practically impossible.

Article 176 of the Philippine Civil Code states that in case of legal separation, the spouse who is at fault (the guilty spouse) will lose his or her share of the profits from the conjugal partnership. In your case, since only 10 years have passed, the prescriptive period for claiming inheritance (which is generally 30 years for immovable property under the Civil Code) has not yet expired, so he or his children can still claim his share. Therefore, when registering the land in the names of the co-heirs, the Register of Deeds must annotate on the title that the property is subject to the provisions of Article 395. This annotation serves as notice to third parties that the absentee may still come forward to claim his share.

STATUTORY TEXT: Marriages between the following are incestuous and void from their performance, whether the relationship between the parties be legitimate or illegitimate:
(1) Between ascendants and descendants of any degree;
(2) Between brothers and sisters, whether of the full or half blood;
(3) Between collateral relatives by blood within the fourth civil degree.

I am in a relationship with my first cousin, and we want to get married. Our families are objecting, saying our marriage would be incestuous and void under Philippine law. Is that true? What does Article 81 say about marriages between first cousins?

Thus, you and your first cousin cannot legally marry under Philippine law.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 81 of the Philippine Civil Code, marriages between collateral relatives by blood within the fourth civil degree are incestuous and void from their performance. First cousins are collateral relatives by blood within the fourth civil degree because they share the same grandparents, and the degree of relationship is computed as four steps: from one cousin up to their parent (1), up to the common grandparent (2), down to the other parent (3), and down to the other cousin (4). Therefore, a marriage between first cousins falls squarely within the prohibition. [Art. 81].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Such a marriage is void from the beginning, regardless of whether the relationship is legitimate or illegitimate, and cannot be ratified or validated by consent or subsequent events.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 81, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.

In your situation, the trust is likely an implied trust, not an express trust. [Art. 1441].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Article 1441 of the Civil Code says that an express trust is created by the intention of the trustor or parties, while an implied trust comes into being by operation of law. Since there was no explicit written or verbal agreement to create a trust, but your uncle provided the purchase money and caused the title to be placed in your name without intending a donation, the law may impose a resulting trust under Article 1448 (which is a type of implied trust) to prevent unjust enrichment. Can you explain Article 1480 of the Philippine Civil Code? I want to understand who bears the risk of loss or damage to the thing sold between the time the contract is perfected and the time of delivery.

Article 1480 states that after a contract of sale is perfected but before delivery, any loss, damage, or improvement to the thing sold is governed by Articles 1163 to 1165 and 1262 of the Civil Code. This means the buyer is entitled to the fruits or benefits of the thing from the moment of perfection, but also bears the risk of loss if the thing is destroyed without the seller's fault. In other words, if a specific item (like a particular car or a parcel of land) is sold, and it is destroyed by an accident before delivery, the seller is excused from delivering it, but the buyer may still be obligated to pay the price, unless the seller was at fault or in delay. However, if the sale involves fungible goods (like rice or sugar) sold by weight, number, or measure, the risk does not pass to the buyer until they have been weighed, counted, or measured and delivered, unless the buyer is in delay. This article ensures that the parties know their rights and obligations during the gap between agreement and delivery.

As instituted heirs, you are called to succeed to his property (such as the house and lot) and also to his transmissible rights and obligations. This means that, in principle, you also inherit his unpaid debts, because obligations that are transmissible form part of the inheritance. However, you are not automatically forced to accept the inheritance with its obligations; you may accept it, accept it with the benefit of inventory, or repudiate it as provided by law. [Art. 840].

The institution of heir simply identifies who is called to inherit; the full extent and conditions of liability are governed by other provisions on acceptance and partition of inheritance.

Can you explain Article 470 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding bad faith in the incorporation of movable property?

Article 470 of the Civil Code deals with situations where two movable things owned by different persons are incorporated or joined together. If the owner of the accessory thing (the lesser or attached item) makes the incorporation in bad faith, he loses that accessory thing and must indemnify the owner of the principal thing for damages. If the owner of the principal thing acts in bad faith, the owner of the accessory thing has the right to choose between being paid the value of the accessory or having the accessory separated, even if it requires destroying the principal; in either case, the bad faith actor must also pay damages. If either owner made the incorporation with the knowledge of the other and without objection, their rights are determined as if both acted in good faith.

Ipinapaliwanag ng Artikulo 966 kung paano binibilang ang mga degree ng pagkakamag-anak. Ang isang 'degree' ay ang distansya sa pagitan ng dalawang kamag-anak, na sinusukat sa pamamagitan ng mga henerasyon. Ang tuntunin: bilangin ang bilang ng mga henerasyon, hindi kasama ang pinagmulan (progenitor). Kaya ang magkakapatid ay dalawang degree ang pagitan (akyat sa magulang, pagkatapos baba sa kapatid); ang tiyuhin at pamangkin ay tatlong degree ang pagitan (akyat sa lolo, pagkatapos baba sa tiyuhin); ang magpinsang buo ay apat na degree ang pagitan (akyat sa lolo, pagkatapos baba sa pinsan).

Can you explain Article 1078 of the Philippine Civil Code to me?

Article 1078 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that when a person dies leaving more than one heir, the entire estate of the deceased is owned in common by all the heirs before it is partitioned. This means that until the estate is actually divided among the heirs, they collectively own the whole property as co-owners. Each heir has an undivided interest in the whole estate, but no one owns a specific portion yet. However, this co-ownership is subject to the payment of the debts of the deceased, meaning that the estate must first be used to settle any outstanding obligations before the heirs can enjoy their respective shares.

Can you explain Article 1022 of the Philippine Civil Code about what happens to vacant shares in testamentary succession?

Article 1022 provides that in testamentary succession, if a share of an instituted heir becomes vacant because the right of accretion cannot take place (for example, there are no co-heirs to whom the share can accrue, or accretion is not applicable) and the testator did not designate a substitute heir, then that vacant share shall be given to the testator's legal heirs. These legal heirs will receive the share subject to the same charges and obligations that were imposed on the original instituted heir.
