Can you explain Article 327 of the Civil Code of the Philippines? What are the grounds for termination of parental authority?

Article 327 of the Civil Code provides that parental authority terminates upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) death of the parents or of the child; (2) emancipation of the child, such as reaching the age of majority or other legal means; (3) adoption of the child by another person, which transfers parental authority to the adopter; and (4) appointment of a general guardian, usually when the parents are incapacitated or absent. When any of these events happens, the rights and duties of the parents over the child cease by operation of law.

Can you explain Article 26 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 26 of the Philippine Civil Code states that every person must respect the dignity, personality, privacy, and peace of mind of his neighbors and other persons. It provides that certain acts, even if they are not criminal offenses, can give rise to a civil case for damages, prevention, and other relief. These acts include: (1) prying into the privacy of another's residence; (2) meddling with or disturbing the private life or family relations of another; (3) intriguing to cause another to be alienated from his friends; and (4) vexing or humiliating another on account of his religious beliefs, lowly station in life, place of birth, physical defect, or other personal condition. The phrase 'and similar acts' means that other analogous acts that violate a person's dignity, privacy, or peace of mind may also be actionable. So, even if the act is not a crime, the victim can sue in civil court to stop the behavior, claim damages, or obtain other relief.

Can you explain Article 1302 of the Philippine Civil Code about legal subrogation?

Article 1302 of the Civil Code provides situations where legal subrogation is presumed. Legal subrogation means the law automatically transfers the rights of the original creditor to another person who paid the debt. The three situations are: (1) When a creditor pays another creditor who has a preferred claim, even if the debtor does not know about it; (2) When a third person who is not obligated to pay does so with the debtor's express or tacit consent; (3) When a person who has an interest in the obligation pays, even without the debtor's knowledge, but subject to rules on confusion for their own share. In these cases, the payer steps into the shoes of the original creditor and can exercise the same rights.

Tandaan na kapag napili at naigawad na ang isang remedyo, hindi na kayo maaaring lumipat sa iba.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa sitwasyon ninyo, kung ang dealer ay nagbigay ng warranty (hayag man o ipinahiwatig) na walang sira ang makina, at nasira agad ang transmission nang hindi dahil sa inyong paggamit, may breach of warranty. Ayon sa Artikulo 1599 ng Civil Code, may mga pagpipilian kayo: (1) itago ang kotse at bawasan o alisin ang presyo; (2) itago ang kotse at magsampa ng kaso para sa danyos; (3) tanggihan ang kotse kung hindi pa ninyo tinanggap at magsampa ng kaso para sa danyos; o (4) ipawalang-bisa ang kontrata at ibalik ang kotse o mag-alok na ibalik ito upang mabawi ang bayad. Dahil tinanggap na ninyo ang kotse, maaari lamang kayong mag-rescind kung: (a) hindi ninyo alam ang depekto noong tinanggap ninyo; (b) nag-abiso kayo sa dealer sa loob ng makatwirang panahon ng inyong balak na ipawalang-bisa; at (c) maibabalik ninyo ang kotse sa halos parehong kondisyon, maliban kung ang pagkasira ay dulot mismo ng breach (tulad ng transmission defect). Kung valid ang pag-rescind, hindi na kayo mananagot sa presyo at dapat ibalik ng dealer ang anumang bayad kapag naibalik o inalok ninyong ibalik ang kotse. Kung tumanggi ang dealer na tanggapin ang pagbabalik, kayo ay magiging bailee na may lien para sa bayad na presyo. [Art. 1599].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Kung pipiliin ninyong humingi ng danyos sa halip na mag-rescind, ang danyos para sa breach ng warranty sa kalidad ay karaniwang ang pagkakaiba ng halaga ng kotse sa oras ng delivery at ang halaga sana kung walang depekto.

Can you explain Article 1218 of the Philippine Civil Code about reimbursement for solidary debtors?

Under Article 1218 of the Philippine Civil Code, if a solidary debtor pays the obligation after it has already prescribed (i.e., the creditor can no longer demand payment because the prescriptive period has lapsed) or after the obligation has become illegal, that debtor cannot seek reimbursement from his co-debtors. Can you explain Article 790 of the Philippine Civil Code about interpreting words in a will?

Article 790 provides rules for interpreting the language of a will. Generally, words are given their ordinary and grammatical meaning. STATUTORY TEXT: If by the will of only one owner, but in good faith, two things of the same or different kinds are mixed or confused, the rights of the owners shall be determined by the provisions of the preceding article.

I own a small rice mill. I accidentally poured my low-grade rice into a container that already contained my neighbor's high-grade rice because I thought the container was empty. My neighbor accuses me of doing it on purpose to mix my poor rice with his good rice so I could sell the mixture at a higher price. He now demands that I forfeit my rice and pay him damages. What does the law say under Article 473 of the Civil Code?

Since you claim it was an accident, the good faith provision applies, and you retain ownership of your proportional share.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 473 of the Civil Code, if two movable things are mixed or confused by the will of only one owner, the legal consequences depend on whether that owner acted in good faith or bad faith. If the mixing was done in good faith—meaning you had no intention to defraud and it was a genuine accident—then the rights of the owners are determined by Article 472. Article 472 provides that when things are mixed by accident, each owner acquires a right proportional to the value of his respective thing. Therefore, if your pouring of low-grade rice into the container with high-grade rice was truly accidental, you and your neighbor would each own a share of the mixed rice in proportion to the market value of the rice each contributed. You would not lose your rice. [Art. 473].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, if it is proven that you acted in bad faith—that is, you intentionally mixed your low-grade rice with his high-grade rice to gain an advantage—then under the second paragraph of Article 473, you would lose your own rice (it would become the property of your neighbor) and you would also be liable to pay damages for any loss he suffered as a result of the mixing.

Can you explain Article 888 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 888 states that legitimate children and descendants are entitled to a legitime consisting of one-half of the hereditary estate of their father and mother. This means that when a parent dies, one-half of the property they leave behind is automatically reserved for their legitimate children. The parent can freely dispose of the other half through a will, but that free half is subject to the rights of illegitimate children and the surviving spouse, who may also have legal claims to portions of the estate. So in practice, if there are illegitimate children or a spouse, the free portion may be reduced to satisfy their legitimes.

STATUTORY TEXT: Should the vendee be disturbed in the possession or ownership of the thing acquired, or should he have reasonable grounds to fear such disturbance, by a vindicatory action or a foreclosure of mortgage, he may suspend the payment of the price until the vendor has caused the disturbance or danger to cease, unless the latter gives security for the return of the price in a proper case, or it has been stipulated that, notwithstanding any such contingency, the vendee shall be bound to make the payment. A mere act of trespass shall not authorize the suspension of the payment of the price.

I bought a residential lot from a seller and paid 50% of the purchase price. We agreed that I would pay the remaining balance in monthly installments. A month after moving in, I received a notice from a bank that they are foreclosing the mortgage on the property, and I also learned that a distant relative of the seller has filed a court case claiming ownership of the same lot. I am afraid I might lose the property. The seller is still demanding that I continue paying the installments. Can I legally stop paying until the seller resolves these problems? What are my rights under Article 1590 of the Civil Code?

If the seller fails to resolve them, you may have further remedies under the law, such as rescission or damages, depending on the circumstances.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1590 of the Civil Code, you may suspend payment of the remaining installments because you are being disturbed in your possession and ownership by a foreclosure of mortgage and a vindicatory action (the court case claiming ownership). [Art. 1590].

### 💡 Application to Facts
These are specifically recognized grounds for suspension. The law allows the buyer to withhold payment until the seller causes the disturbance or danger to cease, unless the seller gives security for the return of the price in a proper case, or you had agreed to pay despite such contingencies. Since you did not mention any stipulation requiring you to continue paying despite these threats, you can suspend payment. The suspension is not a cancellation of the sale; it is a temporary remedy to protect you. You should notify the seller in writing of your decision to suspend and the reasons, and demand that the seller clear the title or provide adequate security. If the seller resolves the issues, you must resume payment.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

May karapatan akong usufruct sa isang lupa at bahay. Kinuha ng gobyerno ang property para sa road widening at binayaran ang may-ari ng pera. Maaari mong hilingin na sumunod ang may-ari sa mga obligasyong ito.

Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 609 ng Civil Code, kapag ang property na nasa ilalim ng usufruct ay na-expropriate para sa pampublikong gamit, ang may-ari ay may dalawang obligasyon: (1) palitan ang na-expropriate na property ng ibang property na may parehong halaga at katulad na kondisyon, o (2) bayaran ka (ang usufructuary) ng legal na interes sa halaga ng indemnity para sa buong natitirang panahon ng usufruct. My uncle died last month without a will. He was not married and had no children, but he has a brother (my father) and a sister. He also has an illegitimate son. How will his property be divided? Does Article 961 apply?

You should consult the specific articles to compute the exact shares.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, Article 961 applies to your uncle's situation because he died without a will (in default of testamentary heirs). Under this article, the law will vest the inheritance in the legitimate and illegitimate relatives, the surviving spouse, and the State, according to the rules set forth in the subsequent articles. Since your uncle had no spouse and no legitimate children, his estate will be distributed among his relatives: his illegitimate son is a relative recognized by law, and his siblings (your father and his sister) are also relatives. The specific shares and order of priority will be determined by the detailed rules in Articles 962 onwards, but Article 961 confirms that the law, not a will, will govern the succession. [Art. 961].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Generally, the illegitimate child and the siblings may inherit, but the exact proportions depend on the relevant provisions.

Can you explain Article 613 of the Philippine Civil Code about easements?

Article 613 defines an easement (or servitude) as a burden or encumbrance placed on a piece of real property (immovable) for the benefit of another piece of real property owned by a different person. The property that receives the benefit is called the dominant estate, while the property that carries the burden is called the servient estate. For example, if your neighbor has a right of way across your land to access their property, your land is the servient estate and your neighbor's land is the dominant estate.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1496 of the Civil Code, ownership of the thing sold is acquired by the buyer only upon delivery. Delivery may be actual, constructive, or in any other manner that signifies an agreement to transfer possession (as provided in Articles 1497 to 1501). [Art. 1496].

In your situation, despite full payment and a signed deed of sale, the car has not been delivered to you. There is no indication that possession has been transferred—you do not have the keys, and the seller has not allowed you to take the car. The deed of sale creates an obligation for the seller to deliver, but without delivery, ownership does not transfer.

Can you explain Article 1157 of the Philippine Civil Code? What are the sources of obligations under this article?

Article 1157 of the Philippine Civil Code states that obligations arise from five sources: (1) Law, which imposes obligations independently of the will of the parties; (2) Contracts, which arise from the agreement of the parties and have the force of law between them; (3) Quasi-contracts, which are lawful, voluntary, and unilateral acts that create obligations to prevent unjust enrichment; (4) Acts or omissions punished by law (also called delicts or crimes), which give rise to civil liability for damages; and (5) Quasi-delicts (also called torts or culpa aquiliana), which arise from damage caused to another through fault or negligence without a pre-existing contractual relation.

Can you explain Article 1190 of the Philippine Civil Code to me?

Article 1190 deals with obligations that are subject to a condition which, when fulfilled, extinguishes the obligation (a resolutory condition). When such a condition is fulfilled, the parties must return to each other what they received. For example, if you sold something under an agreement that the sale would be cancelled if a certain event happened, and that event happens, you must give back what you got, and the other party must give back what they got.

If the thing that has to be returned is lost, damaged, or improved, the rules in Article 1189 (which normally apply to a debtor in a suspensive condition) apply to the party who is required to return it. This means that if the thing was lost without that party's fault, they may not have to pay; if lost due to their fault, they may be liable for damages; if it deteriorated, the creditor may have options; and if it improved, the improvement may benefit the creditor.

For obligations to do or not to do, Article 1187 second paragraph applies: the courts will determine, in each case, the retroactive effect of the condition that has been fulfilled.

Can you explain Article 1345 of the Philippine Civil Code about simulation of contracts?

Article 1345 distinguishes between two kinds of simulation of contracts. Absolute simulation occurs when the parties do not intend to be bound at all; the contract is void because there is no real consent to be legally bound. Relative simulation occurs when the parties conceal their true agreement; the apparent contract is void, but the hidden or true agreement may be valid and binding between the parties if it has all the essential requisites of a contract.

My marriage was annulled six months ago. Last week, I found out I am pregnant, and I am sure the father is my former husband. I am worried about the legal implications. What does Philippine law require me to do in this situation?

Therefore, you should promptly inform your former husband or his heirs of your pregnancy; failure to do so may affect the legal recognition of your child's status and the rights that flow from it.

The law imposes this duty to protect inheritance rights and prevent fraudulent claims regarding paternity. [Art. 260].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The same rule applies to a widow who believes she was left pregnant by her deceased husband, or to a wife who believes she is pregnant by her husband from whom she is legally separated.

STATUTORY TEXT: The payment of debts in money shall be made in the currency stipulated, and if it is not possible to deliver such currency, then in the currency which is legal tender in the Philippines.
The delivery of promissory notes payable to order, or bills of exchange or other mercantile documents shall produce the effect of payment only when they have been cashed, or when through the fault of the creditor they have been impaired.

I borrowed $1,000 from my friend, and we agreed that I would pay him back in US dollars. However, I couldn't get US dollars, so I gave him a check for the equivalent amount in Philippine pesos. He hasn't deposited the check for over two months, and now he's demanding payment again. I thought giving him the check already settled my debt. Am I still obligated to pay?

Once the check is honored, your obligation will be extinguished.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1249, if the stipulated currency (US dollars) cannot be delivered, payment may be made in Philippine legal tender (pesos). However, the delivery of a check is not considered payment until it has been cashed or if the check has been impaired due to the fault of the creditor. [Art. 1249].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, since your friend has not cashed the check and there is no fault on his part (unless he deliberately delayed or caused the check to become worthless), the check does not extinguish your debt. The original obligation remains, but its enforcement is held in abeyance while the check is outstanding. To fully settle the debt, you should either provide cash in pesos (legal tender) or ensure that the check is cashed.

Under Article 106 of the Philippine Civil Code, since you are the offending spouse, the following effects apply: (1) You and your wife are entitled to live separately, but your marriage bonds are not severed. (2) Your conjugal partnership will be dissolved and liquidated, but you will have no right to any share of the profits earned by the partnership, without prejudice to Article 176. (3) Custody of your two minor children will be awarded to your wife, the innocent spouse, unless the court directs otherwise in the best interests of the children, and the court may appoint a guardian for them. (4) You are disqualified from inheriting from your wife by intestate succession, and any provisions in her will that favor you are revoked by operation of law.

Can you explain Article 1465 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean that things subject to a resolutory condition may be the object of the contract of sale?

Article 1465 of the Philippine Civil Code states that things subject to a resolutory condition may be the object of a contract of sale. A resolutory condition is a future and uncertain event upon which the obligation or right is extinguished. This means that even if the thing being sold is subject to a condition that could later terminate the seller's right or the thing's existence, the sale can still be valid. The buyer acquires the thing subject to that same condition. If the condition occurs, the sale may be resolved or the buyer's right may be affected. For example, if a person sells a property that is subject to a condition that ownership will revert to the original owner if a certain event happens, the buyer takes the property with that risk.

Can you explain Article 1021 of the Philippine Civil Code about accretion among compulsory heirs?

Article 1021 states that among compulsory heirs, the right of accretion only applies to the free portion of the estate, not to the legitime. If the free portion is left to two or more compulsory heirs, or to one compulsory heir and a stranger, and one of them repudiates their share, the other co-heirs or the stranger can add that share to their own by accretion. However, if a compulsory heir repudiates their legitime (the portion reserved by law), the other co-heirs will inherit that legitime in their own right as compulsory heirs, not by accretion. This means the legitime is distributed according to the rules on legitime, not as a testamentary accretion.

Under Article 1549 of the Philippine Civil Code, your failure to appeal the court's decision does not bar you from holding the seller liable for eviction. The seller's liability arises from the fact that the eviction resulted from a defect in the seller's title or a prior right of a third party. [Art. 1549].

### 💡 Application to Facts
As long as you notified the seller of the lawsuit and gave the seller an opportunity to defend, and you are not at fault, you can still demand the return of the price, damages, and other expenses as provided by law.

Mayroon akong warehouse receipt na negotiable para sa 100 sako ng bigas na naka-imbak sa isang bodega. May isang pinagkakautangan ko na gustong kunin ang bigas bilang bayad sa utang ko sa pamamagitan ng pag-levy ng sheriff. Pwede ba nilang kunin ang bigas kahit hawak ko pa ang warehouse receipt?

Possession of the negotiable document gives you control over the goods, and the law protects that right.

Under Article 1519 of the Civil Code, if goods are delivered to a bailee and a negotiable document of title is issued for them, the goods cannot be attached, garnished, or levied while in the bailee's possession unless the document is first surrendered to the bailee or its negotiation is enjoined by a court. In your situation, since you hold a negotiable warehouse receipt for the rice stored in the warehouse, the sheriff cannot levy or take the rice without first requiring the surrender of that receipt. Therefore, your creditor cannot simply seize the goods through execution; they must either obtain the receipt from you or seek a court order stopping its negotiation.

If the child is born before 180 days after the second marriage is solemnized, it is presumed to have been conceived during the first marriage, provided the child is born within 300 days after the death of the first husband. This presumption is disputable. If the child is born after 180 days following the second marriage, it is presumed to have been conceived during the second marriage, even if born within 300 days after the death of the first husband. This presumption is prima facie. Both presumptions can be rebutted with evidence.

STATUTORY TEXT: In testamentary succession, when the right of accretion does not take place, the vacant portion of the instituted heirs, if no substitute has been designated, shall pass to the legal heirs of the testator, who shall receive it with the same charges and obligations.

My uncle wrote a will leaving his property to his two friends, but one friend died before him. The will did not name any substitute, and the other friend cannot take the entire property because the will says they only get half. What happens to the share of the friend who died? I am my uncle's nephew and his only living relative. Do I get that share?

You should verify your status as a legal heir under the law on intestate succession.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1022 of the Civil Code, in testamentary succession, if the right of accretion does not take place (here, because the will gave each friend a distinct share and there is no co-heir to whom the vacant share can accrete, since the other friend's share is limited to half), and no substitute heir was designated by the testator, the vacant portion shall pass to the legal heirs of the testator. As the nephew and the only living relative, you may be one of the testator's legal heirs (depending on the rules of intestate succession), and you would receive the vacant share subject to the same charges and obligations imposed on the original instituted heir. [Art. 1022].

### 💡 Application to Facts
You should verify your status as a legal heir under the law on intestate succession.

STATUTORY TEXT: Whenever in an obligation a period is designated, it is presumed to have been established for the benefit of both the creditor and the debtor, unless from the tenor of the same or other circumstances it should appear that the period has been established in favor of one or of the other.

I borrowed money from a friend with an agreement to pay after one year. After six months, I already have the money and want to pay early to stop the interest, but my friend refuses to accept the payment and insists that I wait until the due date. Can I legally pay early without my friend's consent?

If your friend voluntarily agrees to accept early payment, then it is allowed, but you cannot force it.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1196 of the Civil Code, when a period is designated in an obligation, it is presumed to have been established for the benefit of both the creditor and the debtor. This means that the creditor cannot demand payment before the due date, and the debtor cannot compel the creditor to accept payment before the due date, unless the presumption is rebutted. The presumption can be overturned if it appears from the tenor of the obligation or other circumstances that the period was intended for the benefit of only one party. [Art. 1196].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, absent any indication that the one-year period was solely for your benefit as the debtor, the presumption stands that the period benefits both you and your friend. Therefore, you cannot legally pay early without your friend's consent.

Can you explain Article 1535 of the Civil Code about the unpaid seller's lien and stoppage in transitu?

Article 1535 says that if a buyer has not paid for goods, the seller's right to a lien or to stop the goods in transit is not affected by any sale or disposition that the buyer makes, unless the seller agreed to that sale. However, if a negotiable document of title (like a bill of lading) has been issued for the goods, then the seller's lien or stoppage right cannot defeat the rights of a good faith purchaser for value to whom that document has been negotiated. This is true whether the negotiation happened before or after the seller notified the carrier or bailee of his claim. So, the seller's rights are generally preserved against the buyer's resale, but a good faith purchaser of a negotiable document of title gets priority.

LOCATION: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE I.—OBLIGATIONS > CH 3 - DIFFERENT KINDS OF OBLIGATIONS > SEC 5.—Divisible and Indivisible Obligations > Art. 1222
STATUTORY TEXT: A solidary debtor may, in actions filed by the creditor, avail himself of all defenses which are derived from the nature of the obligation and of those which are personal to him, or pertain to his own share. With respect to those which personally belong to the others, he may avail himself thereof only as regards that part of the debt for which the latter are responsible.

I signed a loan agreement together with two friends as solidary debtors. The creditor is now suing me for the entire amount. One of my friends, who is a co-debtor, was only 17 years old when he signed, so the contract is voidable as to him. He has raised that defense. Can I also raise his minority as a defense to avoid paying the full debt? I am of legal age and the loan itself is valid.

In practice, if there are three solidary debtors and one is a minor, the creditor can still demand the full amount from you, but you may later seek reimbursement from the other solvent co-debtor for his share and you may be able to reduce the judgment against you by the minor's share if the minor successfully avoids liability.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1222 of the Civil Code, you, as a solidary debtor, may raise defenses that are derived from the nature of the obligation (e.g., the loan was already paid, or the contract is void for all) and defenses personal to you (e.g., if you were also a minor or if the creditor condoned your share). However, your friend's minority is a defense personal to him; it is not a defense derived from the nature of the obligation because the loan itself is valid for the other debtors. Therefore, you cannot use your friend's minority to avoid the entire debt. But you can invoke that personal defense 'only as regards that part of the debt for which the latter [your friend] are responsible.' This means you can argue that you should not be held liable for your friend's share of the debt, because as to him the obligation is voidable and he may be released. [Art. 1222].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, you remain solidarily liable for the shares of all other debtors, including your own and the other co-debtor who has no defense.

What does Article 351 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 351 states that a general guardian or a guardian over the person has the same authority over the ward's person as parents do. This means the guardian can make decisions about the ward's care, custody, education, and other personal matters, just like a parent would. However, when it comes to the ward's property, the guardian's authority is not the same as that of parents. Instead, the Rules of Court on guardianship apply, which means the guardian must follow court procedures and may need a separate appointment to manage the ward's property.

Can you explain Article 539 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 539 protects a person's right to possession. Every possessor has the right to be respected in their possession. If someone disturbs that possession, the possessor can be protected or restored to possession through legal means. The court must decide this motion within thirty days.

Can you explain what Article 880 of the Philippine Civil Code means about inheritance subject to a condition or term?

Article 880 provides that if a will names an heir but subject to a suspensive condition (something that must happen before the heir can inherit) or a term (a specific date or period), the estate will not be immediately turned over to that heir. Instead, the estate must be placed under administration, meaning a person (like an executor or administrator) will manage the property. This administration continues until the condition is fulfilled, or it becomes certain that the condition cannot be fulfilled, or until the term arrives. Additionally, if the heir fails to give the security required by the preceding article (Article 879), the same rule applies: the estate is placed under administration until the security is provided.

STATUTORY TEXT: The owner of a swarm of bees shall have a right to pursue them to another's land, indemnifying the possessor of the latter for the damage. Under Article 716 of the Civil Code, the owner of a swarm of bees has the right to pursue them onto another's land, but must indemnify the land possessor for any damage. However, if the owner ceases to pursue the swarm for two consecutive days, the possessor of the land may occupy or retain the swarm. [Art. 716].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Here, your neighbor chased the bees for only one day and then stopped completely for a week. Since he ceased pursuing for more than two consecutive days, you as possessor of the land are allowed to keep the swarm, subject to your right to claim compensation for the plant damage caused. As for the goat, Article 716 provides that the owner of domesticated animals may claim them within twenty days from their occupation by another person. The original owner came after 22 days, which is beyond the 20-day period.

Para sa pagkabaliw ng isang partido, ang matinong asawa na walang kaalaman sa pagkabaliw, o sinumang kamag-anak o tagapag-alaga ng baliw na partido, ay maaaring magsampa anumang oras bago mamatay ang alinman sa partido. Para sa pandaraya, ang naagrabyadong partido ay dapat magsampa sa loob ng apat na taon pagkatapos matuklasan. Para sa puwersa o pananakot, sa loob ng apat na taon mula nang tumigil ito. Para sa dahilan sa bilang 6 ng Artikulo 85, ang naagrabyadong partido ay may walong taon pagkatapos ng kasal upang magsampa.

STATUTORY TEXT: All things and rights which are within the commerce of man may be bequeathed or devised.

I am a market vendor and I have been occupying a stall in the public market for 20 years. The stall was assigned to me by the local government, but I do not own it; I only have a permit to use it. I am now preparing my last will and testament. Can I include in my will my right to use that market stall and pass it on to my son? I heard about Article 924 of the Civil Code, but I am not sure what it means for my situation.

Only assets that you actually own and that are legally alienable, such as private property, money, or assignable contractual rights, may be included in your will.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 924 of the Philippine Civil Code, only things and rights that are within the commerce of man may be bequeathed or devised. 'Within the commerce of man' refers to property or rights that can be legally owned, transferred, or disposed of by a person. Your right to occupy a stall in a public market is not a property right that you own; it is a mere privilege or permit granted by the local government, which is generally personal to you and non-transferable. [Art. 924].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Since it is not within the commerce of man, it cannot be bequeathed or devised in your will. Therefore, you cannot pass on the right to use the market stall to your son through your last will and testament.

I am one of three guarantors for a loan taken by a friend. The creditor is now demanding the entire amount from me personally, even though the other two guarantors are also solvent and have not been asked to pay. Is this allowed? What does the law say about my liability?

Under Article 2065 of the Philippine Civil Code, when there are several guarantors for only one debtor and for the same debt, the obligation to answer for the debt is divided among all the guarantors. At the time of the birth, my remaining assets (excluding the donated land) were only 2 million pesos. So my total estate including the donated land would be 10 million. I want to know if I can revoke or reduce the donation, and by how much.

You may recover 3 million from the donee, leaving the donee with 5 million, which corresponds to the disposable free portion.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 760 of the Civil Code, a donation made by a person without children may be revoked or reduced if a child is later born. Article 761 limits the revocation or reduction to the excess over the portion that could be freely disposed of by will, considering the whole estate at the time of the child's birth. [Art. 761].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the whole estate at birth includes the 2 million remaining assets plus the 8 million donated land, totaling 10 million pesos. For one legitimate child, the legitime is one-half of the estate, which is 5 million pesos. The free portion is the other half, also 5 million pesos. Since the donation of 8 million exceeds the free portion of 5 million by 3 million, the donation can be reduced by 3 million pesos.

STATUTORY TEXT: The written consent of the following to the adoption shall be necessary:
(1) The person to be adopted, if fourteen years of age or over;
(2) The parents, guardian or person in charge of the person to be adopted.
I want to adopt my 15-year-old nephew. His father is still alive but has not been in contact for years. His mother (my sister) passed away. Do I need the father's consent under Article 340?

You should consult with a lawyer to explore if the father's consent can be dispensed with based on other legal provisions.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 340 of the Philippine Civil Code, the written consent of the following is necessary for adoption: (1) the person to be adopted, if fourteen years of age or over; and (2) the parents, guardian or person in charge of the person to be adopted. [Art. 340].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In this scenario, your nephew is 15 years old, so his own written consent is required. Since his father is still alive, he is considered a parent, and his written consent is also required, even if he has not been in contact for years. Unless there is a legal basis to terminate or waive parental consent (such as abandonment under other laws), the father's consent remains necessary under Article 340.

- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 340, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.

Can you explain Article 195 of the Civil Code? When does the separation of property between spouses cease?

Article 195 provides that the separation of property between spouses ends in five situations: (1) upon reconciliation after legal separation; (2) when civil interdiction terminates; (3) when the absent spouse appears; (4) when the court authorizes the husband to resume administering the conjugal partnership upon being satisfied he will not abuse his powers; and (5) when the husband who abandoned the wife rejoins her. Once separation ceases, the property relations revert to the same rules as before the separation, but acts and contracts legally executed during the separation remain valid. The spouses must execute a public document listing all property they return to the marriage, which becomes the separate property of each, and record it in the Registry of Property. All property brought in is considered newly contributed.

Can you explain Article 876 of the Philippine Civil Code about conditions imposed on heirs?

Article 876 of the Civil Code deals with purely potestative conditions in a will. A purely potestative condition is one whose fulfillment depends solely on the heir's own will. If a testator imposes such a condition on an heir, the heir must fulfill it as soon as he learns of the testator's death. However, if the condition has already been complied with before the heir learns of the death and it cannot be fulfilled again (because it is a one-time act), then this rule does not apply. In that case, the condition is considered satisfied and the heir may inherit without further action.

Can you explain Article 30 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 30 provides that if a person files a separate civil case to claim damages or other civil liability arising from a criminal act, and no criminal case is filed while that civil case is ongoing, then the plaintiff only needs to prove their claim by preponderance of evidence. This means they must show that it is more likely than not that the defendant committed the act complained of. The usual higher standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt used in criminal cases does not apply here because there is no criminal proceeding. This makes it easier for the victim to recover civil damages even without a criminal conviction.

Can you explain Article 1566 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1566 provides that the seller is liable to the buyer for any hidden defects in the thing sold, even if the seller was not aware of those defects. However, this liability can be excluded if the parties have stipulated otherwise and the seller was genuinely unaware of the hidden defects. In other words, the parties may agree that the seller will not be responsible for hidden defects, but only if the seller did not actually know about them. If the seller knew about the defects, any such stipulation is invalid and the seller remains liable.

STATUTORY TEXT: A partition legally made confers upon each heir the exclusive ownership of the property adjudicated to him.

My father passed away and left several properties to us, his three children. We executed an extrajudicial settlement of estate where each of us was assigned specific properties. Now, one of my brothers wants to sell a property that was assigned to me, claiming he still has a share because we are all heirs. Can he do that?

You have the exclusive right to possess, use, and dispose of that property as you see fit.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1091 of the Civil Code, a partition legally made confers upon each heir the exclusive ownership of the property adjudicated to him. [Art. 1091].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the extrajudicial settlement of estate you executed constitutes a legal partition. Once that partition was perfected and the properties were assigned to each heir, the property assigned to you became solely yours. Your brother, even though he is a co-heir, no longer has any right or interest over that specific property. His claim that he still has a share because you are all heirs is not valid. He cannot sell or interfere with the property that was adjudicated to you.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 1091, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 1091 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Article 635 states that easements established for public or communal use are primarily governed by special laws and regulations that specifically deal with them. Can you explain Article 863 of the Philippine Civil Code about fideicommissary substitution?

Article 863 allows a fideicommissary substitution, where a testator names a first heir (fiduciary) who is obligated to preserve the inheritance and later transmit it to a second heir. This substitution is valid only if: (1) it does not go beyond one degree from the heir originally instituted, meaning there can be only one substitution after the first heir, with no further chain of substitutions; and (2) both the first heir (fiduciary) and the second heir are living at the time of the testator's death. This restriction prevents property from being tied up across multiple generations. For example, a testator may leave property to A, with the obligation to preserve it and give it to B after A's death, provided both A and B are alive when the testator dies and there is no further substitution after B.

Can you explain Article 61 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 61 of the Philippine Civil Code lays down additional requirements for marriage licenses in two situations. First, if either party is widowed or divorced, they must submit the death certificate of the deceased spouse or the divorce decree instead of a baptismal or birth certificate. If the death certificate cannot be found, the party may submit an affidavit stating that fact, their actual civil status, and the name and date of death of the deceased spouse. Second, if either or both parties are not widowed or divorced but are below the required age (male under 20, female under 18), they must present to the local civil registrar the written consent of their father, mother, guardian, or person having legal charge, in that order. This consent must be under oath, either made personally before the local civil registrar or in an affidavit sworn before two witnesses and attested by an official authorized to administer oaths.

Can you explain Article 1540 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding excess area in a sale of immovable property?

Article 1540 applies when an immovable property is sold at a rate per unit (e.g., per square meter) and the actual area delivered is greater than what was stated in the contract. In this situation, the buyer (vendee) has two options: (1) accept only the area that was agreed upon in the contract and reject the excess portion; or (2) accept the entire area, including the excess, but then must pay for the excess portion at the same contract rate per unit. This article protects the buyer by giving them the choice not to be forced to buy more than what was originally agreed.

As a co-owner, you have an undivided interest in the property. Under the rules on co-ownership, unless there is proof of a different sharing, your shares are presumed equal. Therefore, you are entitled to your proportionate share, typically half, of the property. You may demand partition or ask the court to recognize your co-ownership and divide the property accordingly. Can you explain Article 201 of the Civil Code of the Philippines? What properties are excluded from the community property?

Article 201 lists the properties that are excluded from the community property of spouses under the absolute community of property regime. These exclusions are: (1) Property acquired by either spouse through gratuitous title (such as donation or inheritance), if the donor or testator explicitly states that it should not become part of the community; (2) Property inherited by either spouse from the death of a child from a former marriage, provided the deceased child has brothers or sisters of full blood; (3) A portion of the property of either spouse equal to the presumptive legitime (the share reserved by law for compulsory heirs) of children from a former marriage; (4) Personal belongings of either spouse. However, all fruits and income derived from these excluded properties are still considered part of the community property.

Can you explain Article 1176 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1176 establishes two legal presumptions regarding payment. First, if a creditor gives a receipt for the principal amount without making any reservation regarding interest, it is presumed that the interest has been paid. Second, if a creditor gives a receipt for a later installment of a debt without reserving rights as to earlier installments, it is presumed that those earlier installments have been paid. These presumptions are not conclusive; they can be rebutted by evidence showing the contrary.

Can you explain Article 546 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 546 of the Philippine Civil Code distinguishes between necessary and useful expenses incurred by a possessor of property. Necessary expenses are those required for the preservation of the thing or to prevent its loss or deterioration. These must be refunded to every possessor, whether in good faith or bad faith. However, only a possessor in good faith has the right to retain the property until he is reimbursed for necessary expenses. Useful expenses are those that enhance the value or improve the property but are not strictly necessary. These are refunded only to a possessor in good faith, and he also has the right of retention. The person who defeats the possessor in a court case has the option to either reimburse the amount spent on useful improvements or pay the increase in value that the property acquired because of those improvements.

I bought a specific second-hand car from a seller. The car was at a mechanic's garage in Quezon City when we made the deal. The seller has a business address in Manila. Our contract didn't say where delivery would happen. The seller told me to just pick up the car from his office, but the car is still at the mechanic's garage. The mechanic hasn't told me anything about holding the car for me. Also, the car needs some minor repairs to be roadworthy. Who pays for those repairs? And can I demand the car at midnight?

Because the car is a specific good that both parties knew was located at the mechanic's garage in Quezon City at the time of sale, that garage is the place of delivery, not the seller's office in Manila. Therefore, the seller's instruction for you to pick up the car from his office is not correct. You are entitled to take delivery at the garage. Additionally, since the car is currently in the possession of a third person (the mechanic), the seller has not fulfilled his obligation to deliver until the mechanic acknowledges to you that he holds the car on your behalf. This means the mechanic must expressly recognize that he is now holding the car for you. [Art. 1521].

### 💡 Application to Facts

Since the repairs are necessary to make the car deliverable, the seller should pay for them unless your contract says otherwise. Finally, a demand for delivery must be made at a reasonable hour. Demanding the car at midnight is likely not reasonable. What constitutes a reasonable hour is a question of fact, but generally, it should be during normal business hours.

Can you explain Article 119 of the Philippine Civil Code about the property relations between husband and wife?

Article 119 allows future spouses to choose their property regime before marriage through a marriage settlement. They can agree on absolute community of property, relative community (conjugal partnership of gains), complete separation of property, or any other regime allowed by law. If they do not execute a marriage settlement, or if the settlement is void, the default regime is the conjugal partnership of gains, where each spouse retains ownership of property acquired before marriage, but they share in the fruits and income during marriage, and property acquired during marriage is generally considered conjugal.

Can you explain Article 1000 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding inheritance when there are legitimate ascendants, a surviving spouse, and illegitimate children?

Article 1000 provides that when a person dies without a will and is survived by legitimate ascendants (such as parents or grandparents), a surviving spouse, and illegitimate children, the estate is divided as follows: the legitimate ascendants inherit one-half (1/2) of the estate. The remaining one-half is shared between the surviving spouse and the illegitimate children: the spouse receives one-fourth (1/4) of the total estate, and the illegitimate children collectively receive the other one-fourth (1/4). This means the estate is split into proportions of 1/2 for ascendants, 1/4 for the spouse, and 1/4 for illegitimate children.

I sold a piece of land to Maria. During the sale, I assured her that the land was free from any liens or encumbrances. Maria relied on my statement and completed the purchase. Your obligation or estoppel is limited to Maria and those who derive rights from her.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1439 of the Civil Code, estoppel is effective only as between the parties thereto or their successors in interest. [Art. 1439].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the estoppel arising from your assurance to Maria that the land was free from liens operates only between you and Maria (and her successors, if any). Jose, being a third party who is not a party to the sale and is not a successor in interest of Maria, cannot invoke that estoppel against you. The representation you made to Maria does not create an estoppel that benefits Jose. Therefore, Jose cannot use your statement to Maria as a basis to estop you from denying something in relation to the land.

Can you explain what Article 1358 of the Philippine Civil Code is about? What transactions must appear in a public document?

Article 1358 of the Civil Code lists acts and contracts that must appear in a public document, which means a notarized document. These include: (1) acts and contracts that create, transfer, modify, or extinguish real rights over immovable property, such as sales of land (but sales of real property are also governed by Articles 1403 and 1405 on the Statute of Frauds); (2) cession, repudiation, or renunciation of hereditary rights or rights in the conjugal partnership of gains; (3) powers of attorney to administer property or to perform acts that must appear in a public document or affect third persons; and (4) assignment of actions or rights arising from an act in a public document. All other contracts involving more than five hundred pesos must at least be in writing, even if only a private document. However, the requirement of a public document generally does not determine the validity of the contract itself; it is mainly for registration, evidentiary weight, and binding effect against third parties. Failure to notarize does not necessarily make the contract void unless a specific law requires notarization for validity.

Can you explain Article 72 of the Philippine Civil Code about marriage without a license in exceptional cases?

Article 72 allows marriage without a marriage license if either of the contracting parties is at the point of death, or if the female's habitual residence is more than fifteen kilometers from the municipal building and there is no communication by railroad or by provincial or local highways between the residence and the municipal building. In such cases, the official, priest, or minister who solemnizes the marriage must make an affidavit before the local civil registrar or any person authorized to administer oaths. The affidavit must state that the marriage was performed in articulo mortis (at the point of death) or at a place more than fifteen kilometers from the municipal building, and if the latter, the name of the barrio where the marriage was solemnized must be given. The person who solemnized the marriage must also state that he took the necessary steps to ascertain the ages and relationship of the contracting parties and that in his opinion there was no legal impediment to the marriage at the time it was solemnized.

I owe a contractor money for a construction project. Part of the bill is fixed for materials (P100,000) but the labor cost is still being computed because there were change orders. The contractor is demanding payment of the fixed P100,000 now, but I want to wait until the total bill is finalized and pay everything at once. Can I refuse to pay the P100,000 now and insist on paying the full amount later? What does the law say?

The law permits the creditor to collect the certain portion without waiting for the uncertain portion to be settled.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1248 of the Civil Code, the general rule is that a debtor cannot be compelled to make partial payments, and a creditor cannot be forced to accept partial performance, unless there is an express stipulation. However, this article provides an important exception: when a debt is in part liquidated and in part unliquidated, the creditor may demand and the debtor may effect payment of the liquidated part without waiting for the liquidation of the unliquidated part. [Art. 1248].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the P100,000 for materials is a liquidated amount—it is certain and fixed. The labor cost is still unliquidated because it depends on change orders that are not yet finalized. Therefore, the contractor, as creditor, has the right to demand payment of the liquidated P100,000 now, and you, as debtor, are allowed to pay that amount immediately. You cannot refuse to pay the P100,000 solely because the labor portion is still being computed.

The personal letter, if it is an ordinary private letter without notarization or other form of authentication, does not qualify as an 'authentic writing' and thus is not a valid mode of recognition under this article. To be an authentic writing, the document must be notarized or executed before a competent officer. [Art. 278].

A mere verbal acknowledgment before relatives, even if witnessed by many, is insufficient because it does not fall under any of the required formalities.

STATUTORY TEXT: Acceptance may be express or tacit.
An express acceptance must be made in a public or private document.
A tacit acceptance is one resulting from acts by which the intention to accept is necessarily implied, or which one would have no right to do except in the capacity of an heir.
Acts of mere preservation or provisional administration do not imply an acceptance of the inheritance if, through such acts, the title or capacity of an heir has not been assumed.

My father died recently and left a house. I have been paying the real property taxes and making necessary repairs to prevent further deterioration. I am worried that by doing these things, I might have automatically accepted the inheritance, and then I will be liable for his debts. Is that correct?

Since you are only preserving the property, you likely have not accepted the inheritance yet, and you may still choose to repudiate it if you wish.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Based on Article 1049 of the Civil Code, your actions of paying real property taxes and making necessary repairs to prevent deterioration are considered acts of mere preservation or provisional administration. These acts do not imply acceptance of the inheritance if, through such acts, you have not assumed the title or capacity of an heir. This means that as long as you are only preserving the property and not exercising ownership rights—such as renting it out for your own benefit, selling it, or declaring yourself as the owner in public documents—you are not deemed to have accepted the inheritance. Therefore, you would not automatically become liable for your father's debts merely by performing these preservation acts. [Art. 1049].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, if you take actions that go beyond preservation and clearly indicate an intention to accept the inheritance, such as using the property as your own, distributing assets, or executing documents as the heir, then tacit acceptance may be inferred.

Can you explain Article 1395 of the Philippine Civil Code about ratification of voidable contracts?

Article 1395 states that when a contract is voidable, ratification does not require the conformity of the contracting party who has no right to bring the action for annulment. Their consent is not necessary because they have no standing to object to the ratification.

Can you explain Article 987 of the Philippine Civil Code? What happens when someone dies without a will and their parents are already dead?

Article 987 provides that if a person dies without a will (intestate) and both parents are already dead, the inheritance goes to the nearest ascendants (grandparents, great-grandparents, etc.). If there are ascendants of the same degree in the same line (e.g., both paternal grandparents), they share equally per capita. If there are ascendants of equal degree but from different lines (paternal vs maternal), the estate is divided equally: half to the paternal ascendants and half to the maternal ascendants. Within each line, the share is divided per capita among those of equal degree.

Can you explain Article 1209 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding joint obligations when division is impossible?

Article 1209 states that if an obligation is indivisible (meaning the object cannot be divided), and there are multiple creditors or multiple debtors who are jointly bound, the following rules apply: (1) The creditors can only be prejudiced by their collective acts, meaning no single creditor can act alone to the detriment of the others. (2) The debt can be enforced only by proceeding against all the debtors together; the creditor cannot sue just one debtor for the whole obligation. (3) If one of the debtors becomes insolvent, the other debtors are not liable for his share. This is because the obligation is joint, not solidary, so each debtor is only responsible for his proportionate part, even though the object is indivisible and must be performed as a whole by all of them collectively.

You may use the water while it is on your land, but you cannot divert or consume all of it to the extent that it prevents the natural flow onto public domain.

Can you explain Article 1049 of the Philippine Civil Code about acceptance of inheritance?

Article 1049 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that acceptance of an inheritance may be express or tacit. Express acceptance must be made in a public or private document. Tacit acceptance is one resulting from acts by which the intention to accept is necessarily implied, or which one would have no right to do except in the capacity of an heir. I have a plain gold ring, and my friend gave me a small diamond as a gift. I had the diamond set into the ring. Is he correct under the law?

Thus, your friend cannot claim ownership of the entire ring simply because the diamond is more valuable.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 467 of the Civil Code, when two movable things are incorporated, the principal thing is determined not by value but by the purpose of the union. The article states that the principal thing is that to which the other has been united as an ornament, or for its use or perfection. [Art. 467].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the diamond was set into the ring, making it an ornament for the ring or perfecting the ring (enhancing its appearance). The ring is the thing that received the diamond for its beautification or perfection. Therefore, the ring is the principal thing, and the diamond is the accessory. Your friend's claim based on higher value is not supported by this rule. The owner of the principal thing (the ring) generally becomes the owner of the whole, subject to the obligation to indemnify the owner of the accessory for its value if the accessory was incorporated in good faith.

Can you explain Article 1107 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1107 of the Philippine Civil Code states that anyone who has the legal capacity to acquire property or rights through other modes, such as purchase, donation, or inheritance, can also acquire them through prescription. Prescription is a mode of acquiring ownership by possessing a thing for a certain period of time as provided by law. The article further clarifies that minors and other incapacitated persons are not excluded; they may also acquire property or rights by prescription, either personally (if they have sufficient discernment) or through their parents, guardians, or legal representatives.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1179 of the Civil Code, an obligation that contains a resolutory condition is demandable at once, without prejudice to the effects of the happening of the event. You have the right to demand delivery of the land now, because the resolutory condition does not suspend the demandability of the obligation. However, if you fail to pay the balance within the one-year period, the condition will be fulfilled, and the sale will be automatically cancelled. [Art. 1179].

In that case, the seller would be entitled to recover the land, and the effects of the cancellation would apply retroactively as provided by law.

Can you explain Article 134 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding donations made by a spouse to certain persons during marriage?

Article 134 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that if a spouse, during the marriage, makes a donation to the children of the other spouse from a previous marriage, or to persons who are presumptive heirs of the other spouse at the time of the donation, such donation is voidable. This means the donation is valid until challenged, but it can be annulled. The right to challenge or void the donation belongs to the heirs of the donor spouse, and they may exercise this right only after the donor's death. The purpose is to protect the donor's own heirs from having their inheritance diminished by donations made possibly under undue influence of the other spouse.

Can you explain the order of payment of legacies and devises under Article 950 of the Civil Code of the Philippines when the estate is insufficient?

Article 950 provides the order of priority for paying legacies and devises if the estate's assets are not enough to satisfy all of them. The order is: 1) Remuneratory legacies or devises (those given in return for services); 2) Legacies or devises that the testator declared to be preferential; 3) Legacies for support; 4) Legacies for education; 5) Legacies or devises of a specific, determinate thing that is part of the estate; and 6) All other legacies or devises, which are paid proportionally (pro rata) from whatever remains.

Nagpautang ako kay Juan ng P500,000 noong 2010, na dapat bayaran noong 2015. Hindi ko siningil hanggang 2023. Ngayon, siningil ko si Juan. Sinabi ni Juan na hindi na niya gagamitin ang depensa ng reseta at babayaran na lang niya ako. Pero may guarantor si Juan na si Pedro na pumirma bilang guarantor. Ayaw ni Pedro na magbayad dahil sabi niya tapos na ang panahon para maningil. Maaari bang gamitin ni Pedro ang reseta kahit tinanggihan na ito ni Juan?

Samakatuwid, kahit na sinabi ni Juan na babayaran ka niya, maaari pa ring itaas ni Pedro ang reseta bilang depensa upang maiwasan ang pananagutan.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 1114 ng Kodigo Sibil, maaaring gamitin ni Pedro ang reseta kahit tinanggihan na ito ni Juan. Ang reseta ay isang depensa na maaaring ihabol ng sinumang may interes sa pagiging epektibo nito. Can you explain Article 1154 of the Civil Code of the Philippines? What does it mean regarding fortuitous events and prescription?

Article 1154 states that if a creditor (obligee) is prevented by a fortuitous event—meaning an unforeseen event beyond his control, like a natural disaster, war, or accident—from enforcing his right or filing a case within the period allowed by law (prescription period), that time of prevention is not counted against him. This protects the creditor from losing his right due to circumstances he could not avoid.

Can you explain Article 762 of the Philippine Civil Code about the revocation or reduction of donations due to the birth, appearance, or adoption of a child?

Article 762 provides that if a donation is revoked or reduced because a child is born, appears, or is adopted after the donation, the donated property must be returned to the donor. Can you explain Article 1539 of the Philippine Civil Code about the vendor's obligation to deliver real estate with a stated area?

Article 1539 states that when selling real estate with a specified area and a price per unit (like per square meter), the seller must deliver the entire area stated in the contract if the buyer demands it. If that is not possible, the buyer may choose either a proportional reduction of the price (paying only for the actual area received) or cancel the sale (rescission). However, cancellation is only allowed if the shortage in area is at least one-tenth of the stated area. The same rules apply if part of the property is not of the quality promised. For quality issues, the buyer may cancel only if the inferior value exceeds one-tenth of the agreed price. Nevertheless, even if the shortage or quality defect is less than one-tenth, the buyer may still cancel the sale if he proves that he would not have bought the property had he known of the smaller area or inferior quality.

My father died and left a will. During his lifetime, he gave a piece of land to my brother as a gift. Now we are three siblings, all compulsory heirs. Do we need to include that land in the computation of our inheritance? How does that affect our shares?

This collation ensures equality among all compulsory heirs in the partition of the estate.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, under Article 1061 of the Civil Code, your brother must bring the donated land into the mass of the estate for collation. This means the value of the land at the time of donation will be added to the total value of your father's remaining estate to determine the entire hereditary estate. If the value of the donated land is less than his legitime or share in the estate, he will still be entitled to receive additional property from the estate to complete his share. [Art. 1061].

If the value exceeds his share, he may have to return the excess to the estate so that the other compulsory heirs receive their proper legitimes.

Can you explain what Article 198 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 198 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that if the future spouses, in their marriage settlements (also called a prenuptial agreement), agree that the system of absolute community shall govern their property relations during marriage, then the provisions of the Civil Code on absolute community will apply in a supplementary manner. This means that the detailed rules on absolute community (such as what constitutes community property, how it is administered, and how it is liquidated) will automatically apply to the spouses, unless they have expressly stipulated otherwise in their marriage settlements. In other words, the law fills in the gaps to ensure that the absolute community regime operates fully if the spouses have chosen it but have not provided for every detail.

Can you explain Article 335 of the Philippine Civil Code? Who are not allowed to adopt?

Article 335 of the Philippine Civil Code lists the people who cannot adopt. They are: (1) Those who already have legitimate, legitimated, acknowledged natural children, or natural children by legal fiction; (2) A guardian, with respect to the ward, before the final approval of his accounts; (3) A married person, without the consent of the other spouse; (4) Non-resident aliens; (5) Resident aliens whose government has broken diplomatic relations with the Philippines; (6) Any person convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude, if the penalty imposed was six months' imprisonment or more. These disqualifications apply to the adoption process under the Civil Code.

On the other hand, if you validly renounce the inheritance, the second paragraph of Article 533 applies: you will be deemed never to have possessed the property. Thus, a valid renunciation removes any legal effect of possession from the time of death, as if you never had possession. Therefore, until you make a decision, there is no automatic possession; acceptance and renunciation have different retroactive effects.

Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 936 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa mga legasiya sa may utang?

Sinasabi ng Artikulo 936 na kung ang isang testador ay nagbigay ng legasiya ng kredito o pagpapatawad ng utang pabor sa kanyang may utang, ngunit pagkatapos ay nagsampa ng kaso laban sa may utang upang singilin ang utang, ang legasiya ay mawawalan ng bisa o maglalaho. Ito ay kahit na hindi pa nababayaran ang utang sa oras ng kamatayan ng testador. Ang pagkilos ng testador na magsampa ng kaso ay nagpapakita ng kanyang intensyon na bawiin ang pagpapatawad. Bukod dito, kung ang legasiya ay tungkol sa bagay na isinanla ng may utang bilang garantiya, ang legasiya ay magpapawalang-bisa lamang sa karapatan ng pagsanla (pledge), hindi sa mismong utang. Nananatiling obligado ang may utang na bayaran ang utang.

Can you explain Article 1116 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding prescription?

Article 1116 is a transitional rule for prescription periods. It states that if a period of prescription (the time needed to acquire a right through possession or lose it through inaction) began before the new Civil Code took effect, the old law generally governs. However, if the entire period required by the new Civil Code has already elapsed since it took effect, then the new Civil Code applies, even if the old law required a longer period. In short, the shorter period under the new Code can be used to complete a prescription that started earlier.

Can you explain Article 912 of the Philippine Civil Code about reduction of devises when the property cannot be divided?

Article 912 of the Philippine Civil Code addresses the situation where a devise (a gift of real property in a will) is subject to reduction because it impairs the legitime of compulsory heirs, and the property cannot be conveniently divided. It provides: If the reduction needed is less than one-half of the value of the property, the property goes to the devisee, but the devisee must reimburse the compulsory heirs in cash for their share. If the reduction is one-half or more of the value, the property goes to the compulsory heirs, and they must reimburse the devisee in cash for his share. Additionally, if the devisee is himself a compulsory heir entitled to a legitime, he may retain the entire property if its value does not exceed the disposable portion plus his own legitime.

A possessor deprived of his possession through forcible entry may within ten days from the filing of the complaint present a motion to secure from the competent court, in the action for forcible entry, a writ of preliminary mandatory injunction to restore him in his possession. I have been peacefully occupying and using a small plot of land for several years as a tenant. Last week, my neighbor came with armed men, forcibly removed my belongings, and took over the land. I want to get my possession back immediately. What can I do under Philippine law?

You should act promptly and consult a lawyer to prepare the necessary pleadings.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 539 of the Civil Code, every possessor has the right to be respected in his possession. Even if you are not the owner, as a possessor (tenant), you are entitled to protection against forcible deprivation. The act of your neighbor forcibly taking over the land constitutes forcible entry, which is a criminal offense and a civil wrong. To recover possession immediately, you should file a complaint for forcible entry (accion interdictal) in the proper court. Within ten (10) days from filing the complaint, you may file a motion for the issuance of a writ of preliminary mandatory injunction. This writ, if granted, orders the defendant (your neighbor) to restore you to possession pending the resolution of the main case. The court is required to decide on this motion within thirty (30) days from filing. [Art. 539].

### 💡 Application to Facts
This is a summary remedy designed to quickly restore possession without delving into ownership.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 539, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

Can you explain what Article 502 of the Philippine Civil Code is about?

Article 502 of the Philippine Civil Code lists the different bodies of water that are considered part of the public dominion. This means they are owned by the State and intended for public use, and cannot be privately owned. The list includes rivers and their natural beds; continuous or intermittent waters of springs and brooks in their natural beds; waters rising continuously or intermittently on lands of public dominion; lakes and lagoons formed by nature on public lands; rainwater running through ravines or sand beds; subterranean waters on public lands; waters found within the zone of operation of public works; waters rising on private lands from the moment they leave such lands; and waste waters from fountains, sewers, and public establishments.

Can you explain Article 229 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 229 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with the judicial constitution of a family home. It specifies the required contents of the petition that a person must file in court to have a property declared as a family home. The petition must include: (1) a description of the property; (2) an estimate of its actual value; (3) a statement that the petitioner is actually residing in the premises; (4) any encumbrances on the property; (5) the names and addresses of all creditors, mortgagees, and other persons who have an interest in the property; and (6) the names of the beneficiaries as stated in Article 226 of the Civil Code.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 890 ng Civil Code tungkol sa legitime ng mga magulang at ninuno.

Ang Artikulo 890 ay nagtatakda ng mga patakaran sa paghahati ng legitime (sapilitang bahagi) na nakalaan para sa mga lehitimong magulang at ninuno. Kung parehong buhay ang mga lehitimong magulang ng testator, ang legitime ay hahatiin nang pantay sa kanilang dalawa. Kung isa sa mga magulang ay namatay na, ang buong legitime ay mapupunta sa nabubuhay na magulang. Kung parehong patay na ang mga magulang, ang legitime ay mapupunta sa mga ninuno: kung ang mga nabubuhay na ninuno ay magkapareho ng antas sa linya ng ama at ina, hahatiin nang pantay ang legitime sa dalawang linya. Kung magkaiba ang antas ng mga ninuno, ang buong legitime ay mapupunta sa pinakamalapit na ninuno sa antas, anuman ang linya.

Can you explain Article 1435 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1435 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that if a person sells or alienates a thing in representation of another, that person cannot later assert his own title against the buyer or grantee. In simpler terms, when someone acts as an agent or representative of the owner and sells property to a third party, that agent is barred from later claiming that he, not the principal, was the true owner of the property at the time of the sale. This rule is based on estoppel: the agent, by representing the principal as the owner, cannot be allowed to contradict that representation to the prejudice of the buyer who relied on it. The law thus protects the buyer or grantee who acquired the property in good faith from the agent's subsequent claim of ownership.

This means that all properties you each owned before the marriage will remain your respective exclusive properties. However, the fruits, income, and any property acquired during the marriage will generally be considered conjugal and will be owned jointly by both spouses.
