Can you explain Article 113 of the Philippine Civil Code about when a husband must be joined in suits with his wife?

Article 113 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that, as a general rule, the husband must be joined in all lawsuits filed by or against his wife. However, there are exceptions where the wife may sue or be sued alone. These exceptions are: (1) judicial separation; (2) actual separation for at least one year; (3) separation of property agreed upon in the marriage settlements; (4) administration of all property transferred to the wife under Articles 196 and 197; (5) litigation between husband and wife; (6) suits concerning the wife's paraphernal property; (7) actions upon civil liability arising from a criminal offense; (8) litigation incidental to the wife's profession, occupation, or business; (9) any civil action referred to in Articles 25 to 35; and (10) actions upon a quasi-delict. In cases listed in items 7 to 10, the husband must still be joined as a defendant if the third paragraph of Article 163 applies, which generally involves situations where the husband may be liable for the wife's obligations under certain conditions.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Can you explain Article 624 of the Philippine Civil Code about easements and apparent signs?

Article 624 provides that if the owner of two adjacent estates establishes or maintains a visible sign of an easement between them, such as a pathway or drain, and then one estate is sold or the ownership is divided, that visible sign is considered a title for the easement to continue. The same rule applies when co-owners divide property they own in common.

(1) The Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court;
(2) The Presiding Justice and the Justices of the Court of Appeals;
(3) Judges of the Courts of First Instance;

I am a barangay captain in our place. My neighbor asked me to officiate their wedding because they cannot afford to go to the city hall. They believe that as a public official, I am authorized to solemnize marriage. Am I allowed to do so under Philippine law?

You should advise your neighbor to have the marriage solemnized by one of the authorized persons, such as the city or municipal mayor, a judge, or a registered religious minister.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 56 of the Philippine Civil Code, the persons authorized to solemnize marriage are specifically enumerated. These include the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court, the Presiding Justice and Justices of the Court of Appeals, Judges of the Courts of First Instance (now Regional Trial Courts), Mayors of cities and municipalities, municipal judges and justices of the peace, duly registered priests/rabbis/ministers of any denomination, and ship captains, airplane chiefs, military commanders, and consuls/vice-consuls in special cases under Articles 74 and 75. A barangay captain is not included in this list. Therefore, you are not authorized to solemnize marriage under Philippine law. Even though mayors of cities and municipalities are authorized, a barangay captain is a lower-level official and does not have that power. [Art. 56].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If you solemnize a marriage without proper authority, the marriage may be considered void.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

Article 399 states that when a minor is emancipated—either by marriage or by voluntary concession from the parents—parental authority over the child's person ends. Paki-explain po ang Artikulo 1358 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas. Anong mga transaksiyon ang kailangang nasa pampublikong dokumento?

Ang Artikulo 1358 ng Kodigo Sibil ay naglilista ng mga akto at kontratang dapat nasa isang pampublikong dokumento, ibig sabihin, notaryado. Kabilang dito: (1) mga akto at kontratang lumilikha, naglilipat, nagbabago, o nagpapawalang-bisa ng mga tunay na karapatan sa hindi natitinag na ari-arian, tulad ng pagbebenta ng lupa (subalit ang pagbebenta ng lupa ay saklaw din ng Artikulo 1403 at 1405); (2) pagsesession, pagtatakwil, o pagtalikod sa mga karapatan sa mana o sa conjugal partnership of gains; (3) kapangyarihang mangasiwa ng ari-arian o anumang kapangyarihan para sa isang akto na dapat nasa pampublikong dokumento o makakaapekto sa ikatlong tao; at (4) paglilipat ng mga aksyon o karapatan mula sa isang akto na nasa pampublikong dokumento. Lahat ng iba pang kontrata na higit sa limandaang piso ang halaga ay dapat nasa sulat, kahit pribadong dokumento. Ngunit ang pangangailangang ito ay karaniwang hindi para sa bisa ng kontrata mismo; ito ay para sa rehistrasyon, ebidensya, at upang maging epektibo laban sa mga ikatlong tao. Ang hindi pagpapanotaryo ay hindi awtomatikong nagpapawalang-bisa ng kontrata, maliban kung may batas na nagsasabing kailangan.

Sa inyong sitwasyon, kung ang lupain ay talagang bahagi ng pampublikong dominion, hindi ito maaaring makuha sa pamamagitan ng prescription.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis

STATUTORY TEXT: All marriages performed outside the Philippines in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were performed, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country, except bigamous, polygamous, or incestuous marriages as determined by Philippine law.

I am a Filipino citizen who married my foreign partner in Canada. Our marriage is valid under Canadian law. However, I was previously married in the Philippines to a Filipina, and we never got an annulment or legal separation. I obtained a divorce in Canada from my first wife, but I know that Philippine law does not recognize divorce between two Filipinos. Then I married my current foreign partner. Will my second marriage be recognized in the Philippines under Article 71? I am worried because I heard that bigamous marriages are not recognized.

This means Philippine authorities will not recognize your second marriage for any legal purpose, and you may still be considered legally married to your first spouse.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 71 of the Civil Code, marriages performed outside the Philippines in accordance with the laws of the country where they were performed and valid there are also valid in the Philippines. However, this rule has an exception: bigamous, polygamous, or incestuous marriages as determined by Philippine law are not recognized. [Art. 71].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, your first marriage to a Filipina was performed in the Philippines and is governed by Philippine law. Since divorce is not recognized between two Filipino citizens, your divorce obtained in Canada does not dissolve your first marriage under Philippine law. Therefore, your first marriage is still subsisting. When you married your foreign partner in Canada, that second marriage was valid under Canadian law, but under Philippine law, it constitutes a bigamous marriage because you already had a valid and subsisting first marriage. Since Article 71 explicitly excludes bigamous marriages from recognition, your second marriage will not be considered valid in the Philippines.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 71, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Petition for Declaration of Absolute Nullity / Annulment of Marriage

Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 854 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa preterisyon ng mga sapilitang tagapagmana?

Ang Artikulo 854 ay tungkol sa preterisyon o pagtanggal sa testamento ng isa, ilan, o lahat ng sapilitang tagapagmana sa tuwirang linya (tulad ng mga anak, lehitimo man o hindi, o ampon) mula sa testamento, buhay man sa panahon ng paggawa ng testamento o ipinanganak pagkatapos mamatay ng testador. Kung ang mga tinanggal na sapilitang tagapagmana ay namatay bago ang testador, ang pagkakatatag ng tagapagmana ay magkakabisa, ngunit walang pinsala sa karapatan ng representasyon (ibig sabihin, ang kanilang mga tagapagmana ay maaaring pumalit sa kanila). Sa madaling salita, hindi maaaring basta balewalain ng testador ang mga sapilitang tagapagmana; kung gagawin niya, mawawalan ng bisa ang pangunahing pagtatalaga ng tagapagmana pero mananatili ang mga tiyak na pamana kung hindi ito lumalabag sa legitima, at kung namatay ang mga tinanggal na tagapagmana, mananatili ang pagkakatatag pero may representasyon.

Can you explain Article 893 of the Philippine Civil Code about the share of the surviving spouse when there are no descendants but there are ascendants?

Article 893 states that if a person dies without leaving legitimate descendants (children or grandchildren) but leaves legitimate ascendants (parents or grandparents), the surviving spouse is entitled to one-fourth of the hereditary estate. This share is taken from the free portion of the estate, meaning the portion not reserved by law for the ascendants' legitime. The ascendants still receive their legitime, which is half of the estate, and the spouse gets one-fourth, leaving one-fourth as disposable free portion.

Can you explain Article 866 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the right of the second heir?

Article 866 states that in a fideicommissary substitution, the second heir (fideicommissary) acquires a right to the succession from the moment of the testator's death. Therefore, even if the second heir dies before the fiduciary, his right does not lapse; instead, it passes to his own heirs. The article ensures that the second heir's interest is considered vested and transmissible.

Can you explain Article 257 of the Philippine Civil Code about a child being presumed illegitimate?

Article 257 states that if the wife committed adultery at or about the time of conception of the child, but there was no physical impossibility of access between her and her husband (meaning they could have had sexual relations), the child is prima facie presumed illegitimate if it appears highly improbable, for ethnic reasons, that the child is that of the husband. Can you explain Article 919 of the Philippine Civil Code about disinheritance?

Article 919 of the Philippine Civil Code lists the grounds that allow a testator (the person making a will) to disinherit his or her children and descendants, whether legitimate or illegitimate. The grounds are: (1) an attempt by the child or descendant against the life of the testator, the testator's spouse, descendants, or ascendants; (2) accusing the testator of a crime punishable by imprisonment of six years or more, if the accusation is found groundless; (3) conviction of adultery or concubinage with the testator's spouse; (4) causing the testator to make or change a will through fraud, violence, intimidation, or undue influence; (5) refusal without justifiable cause to support the parent or ascendant who disinherits; (6) maltreatment of the testator by word or deed; (7) leading a dishonorable or disgraceful life; and (8) conviction of a crime that carries the penalty of civil interdiction.

What does Article 1039 of the Philippine Civil Code mean regarding capacity to succeed?

Article 1039 states that the capacity to succeed (to be an heir or to inherit) is governed by the law of the nation of the decedent (the person who died). This means if the decedent is a foreign national, we look to that foreign country's laws to determine whether a person has the legal capacity to inherit, rather than applying Philippine law. For example, if a German citizen dies, German law will determine who has the capacity to succeed to the estate.

The husband and the wife may agree upon the dissolution of the conjugal partnership during the marriage, subject to judicial approval. Upon approval of the petition for dissolution of the conjugal partnership, the court shall take such measures as may protect the creditors and other third persons.

Please explain Article 1381 of the Philippine Civil Code. What are rescissible contracts?

Article 1381 lists the contracts that are considered rescissible. Rescissible contracts are those that are valid and enforceable, but they may be rescinded or set aside by the court because they cause damage or lesion to one of the parties or to a third person. The purpose is to ensure the integrity of the will and prevent unauthorized alterations.

Can you explain Article 214 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it say about the separate property of spouses?

Article 214 of the Philippine Civil Code states that each spouse has full ownership and control over their own separate property. This means each spouse can own, sell, possess, manage, and enjoy their separate property without needing the consent of the other spouse. Additionally, all earnings from a spouse's profession, business, or industry are considered their own separate property. So if a spouse earns income from working or from a business, that income belongs exclusively to that spouse and not to the marital partnership. This article applies when the marriage is governed by a system of complete separation of property, either by prenuptial agreement or court order. Under such a regime, spouses do not share property or earnings.

Can you explain Article 17 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the formalities of contracts, wills, and other public instruments?

Article 17 of the Philippine Civil Code states that the forms and solemnities of contracts, wills, and other public instruments are governed by the law of the country where they are executed. This means that if a contract or will is executed abroad, its formal validity is determined by the laws of that foreign country. However, if these acts are executed before Philippine diplomatic or consular officials in a foreign country, the solemnities required by Philippine law must be observed. Additionally, prohibitive laws concerning persons, their acts or property, and those aimed at public order, public policy, and good customs cannot be rendered ineffective by any foreign law, judgment, determination, or convention. In other words, Philippine laws that protect fundamental public interests will still apply even if a foreign law or agreement says otherwise.

Therefore, the mango trees are owned by you, the owner of the land, by right of accession. The fruits of the trees are also yours, as they are produced by the property (the trees, which are now part of the land). [Art. 440].

### 💡 Application to Facts

Under Article 1019 of the Civil Code, when an heir renounces their inheritance, their share is not left undistributed but accrues to the other heirs by the right of accretion. ### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you and your brother were originally given 50% and 30% respectively, which is a ratio of 5:3. Therefore, your sister's renounced 20% will be divided between you and your brother in that same 5:3 ratio. Specifically, you will receive 5/8 of the 20% (i.e., 12.5%) in addition to your original 50%, making your total share 62.5%. Your brother will receive 3/8 of the 20% (i.e., 7.5%) in addition to his original 30%, making his total share 37.5%.

STATUTORY TEXT: The rights to the succession are transmitted from the moment of the death of the decedent.

My father passed away last month. He left a house and some bank deposits. My siblings and I are wondering when exactly we become the owners of these properties. Is it only after we go through the court process or after we divide them among ourselves?

The transmission of rights does not mean you can automatically take full control without following legal processes, but your claim to the inheritance already exists from the time of death.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 777 of the Civil Code, the rights to the succession are transmitted from the moment of the death of the decedent. This means that upon your father's death, you and your siblings automatically acquired the right to inherit his estate, including the house and bank deposits. The succession opened at the time of his death, and your rights as heirs vested at that exact moment. [Art. 777].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, while the right to inherit is transmitted immediately, actual ownership and possession of specific properties may still require settlement of the estate—paying debts, taxes, and undergoing judicial or extrajudicial settlement procedures.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 777, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 777 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

In your situation, since your father is still living, any contract between you and your sibling regarding the division of his estate upon his death would be considered a contract upon future inheritance and is prohibited. Can you explain Article 1083 of the Philippine Civil Code about the right of co-heirs to demand partition of an estate?

Under Article 1083, every co-heir has the right to demand the division of the estate. However, the testator may expressly forbid partition in the will, but this prohibition cannot exceed twenty years from the time the co-ownership begins (as per Article 494). This power of the testator to prohibit division applies even to the legitime, meaning the testator can delay partition of the legitime, but only within the twenty-year limit. Even if partition is forbidden, the co-ownership automatically ends if any cause for dissolution of a partnership occurs, or if the court, upon petition of a co-heir, finds compelling reasons to order division earlier.

Your husband's half of those profits is his own, and he can freely give it to anyone in his will. This does not affect your own half, which remains yours. However, note that this only covers the profits, not the capital or other conjugal assets. [Art. 170].

### 💡 Application to Facts
You still retain your share of the profits and your rights as to the conjugal partnership properties.

What does Article 1112 of the Philippine Civil Code mean regarding renunciation of prescription?

Article 1112 provides that a person who has the capacity to transfer or dispose of property may renounce (waive) a prescription that has already been acquired. However, no one can renounce the right to prescribe in the future, because the law prohibits giving up a right before it even exists. Prescription can be renounced not only expressly but also tacitly, which means renunciation is considered to have occurred when a person performs acts that clearly show an intention to abandon the right already acquired through prescription.

However, if there were unpaid support amounts that accrued before his death, those may be claimed as a debt against his estate. [Art. 300].

Additionally, if his heirs have their own independent legal obligation to support your children (for example, if they are also ascendants like grandparents), that obligation would be separate.

Can you explain Article 832 of the Philippine Civil Code about revocation of wills?

Article 832 states that if a person makes a later will that revokes a previous will, that revocation is effective even if the later will itself cannot be carried out because the heirs, devisees, or legatees named in it are legally incapacitated to inherit, or they renounce the inheritance. Can you explain Article 1547 of the Philippine Civil Code? What are the implied warranties in a contract of sale?

Article 1547 provides that in a contract of sale, unless a contrary intention appears, there are two implied warranties: (1) the seller warrants that he has the right to sell the thing at the time ownership is to pass, and that the buyer shall have and enjoy legal and peaceful possession; and (2) the seller warrants that the thing is free from hidden faults or defects, and from any charge or encumbrance not declared or known to the buyer. However, the article exempts sheriffs, auctioneers, mortgagees, pledgees, or other persons selling by authority of law or fact from liability for selling a thing in which a third person has a legal or equitable interest.

Can you explain Article 936 of the Philippine Civil Code about legacies to debtors?

Article 936 provides that if a testator, after making a legacy of a credit or remission of a debt in favor of his debtor, later files a lawsuit against that debtor to collect the debt, the legacy is automatically revoked or lapses. This happens even if the debtor has not yet paid the debt at the time of the testator's death. The testator's act of suing shows an intention to no longer give the debt as a legacy. Additionally, if the testator gives a legacy of a thing that the debtor had pledged as security, that legacy only cancels the pledge (the right to hold the property as security) but does not cancel the underlying debt. The debtor remains obligated to pay the debt.

STATUTORY TEXT: The owner may construct any works and make any improvements of which the immovable in usufruct is susceptible, or make new plantings thereon if it be rural, provided that such acts do not cause a diminution in the value of the usufruct or prejudice the right of the usufructuary.

Ako ang may-ari ng isang rural na lupain na kasalukuyang nasa usufruct ng aking tiyahin. Gusto kong magtanim ng mga bagong puno ng prutas sa isang bahagi ng lupa, ngunit nagrereklamo siya na makakabawas ito sa kanyang paggamit. Pinapayagan ba ako ng batas na gawin ito?

Mahalagang timbangin ang epekto ng iyong gagawin sa karapatan ng usufructuary.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 595 ng Civil Code, maaari kang magtanim ng mga bagong pananim sa lupang rural na nasa usufruct, ngunit may kondisyon: hindi dapat ito magdulot ng pagbaba sa halaga ng usufruct o makapinsala sa karapatan ng usufructuary. Kung ang pagtatanim ay magbabawas sa lugar na magagamit ng iyong tiyahin o magpapababa sa mga benepisyong nakukuha niya mula sa lupa, ito ay labag sa batas. [Art. 595].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Ngunit kung hindi naman ito makakaapekto nang malaki sa kanyang paggamit at pakikinabang, maaari kang magpatuloy.

Can you explain Article 1436 of the Philippine Civil Code about estoppel for lessees or bailees?

Article 1436 of the Philippine Civil Code states that a lessee (one who leases property) or a bailee (one who receives property for safekeeping or other purpose) is estopped, or legally prevented, from claiming ownership of the thing leased or received, as against the lessor (the one who leases out) or bailor (the one who delivers the property). In simpler terms, if you rent a house or borrow an item, you cannot later claim that you own it in a dispute with the person who rented it to you or lent it to you. The law presumes that the lessor or bailor has better title, and the lessee or bailee cannot challenge that title while in possession under that relationship.

Paki-paliwanag po kung ano ang mga pananagutan ng conjugal partnership ayon sa Artikulo 161 ng Civil Code.

Ipinapaliwanag ng Artikulo 161 ang mga obligasyon na dapat bayaran ng conjugal partnership of gains. Pananagutan ng partnership: (1) mga utang na ginawa ng asawang lalaki o babae para sa kapakinabangan ng partnership, kung legal na maaaring italian ng babae ang partnership; (2) mga atraso o kita na dapat bayaran habang kasal mula sa mga obligasyong naka-sangla sa ari-arian ng alinmang asawa o ng partnership; (3) mga maliit na pagkukumpuni o pangangalaga sa sariling ari-arian ng bawat asawa, ngunit hindi ang malalaking pagkukumpuni; (4) lahat ng pagkukumpuni (malaki o maliit) sa ari-arian ng conjugal partnership; (5) pangangalaga sa pamilya at edukasyon ng mga anak ng mag-asawa, at ng mga lehitimong anak ng isa sa kanila; at (6) mga gastos para makapagtapos ang asawa ng propesyonal, bokasyonal, o iba pang kurso.

Can you explain Article 1312 of the Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 1312 states that when a contract creates real rights (such as ownership, mortgage, easement, or usufruct) over a property, any third person who later acquires possession of that property is bound by that contract. For example, if A grants B a right of way over A's land, and later C buys that land, C must respect B's right of way. However, this rule is subject to the Mortgage Law and the Land Registration Laws. These laws may require registration of the real right to bind third parties. If the right is not registered and a third person acquires the property in good faith and for value without knowledge of the right, that third person may not be bound. In essence, real rights generally follow the property, but registration laws can provide protection to innocent purchasers.

Can you explain Article 1421 of the Civil Code? What does it mean that the defense of illegality is not available to third persons whose interests are not directly affected?

Article 1421 means that only the parties to a contract or persons who have a direct interest in it can raise the defense that the contract is illegal or void. If a third person (someone not a party to the contract and whose interests are not directly affected) tries to challenge the contract's validity on the ground of illegality, the law does not allow it. This is because the defense of illegality is personal to those directly involved.

Should the co-ownership cease by reason of the division of the thing held in common, the usufruct of the part allotted to the co-owner shall belong to the usufructuary.

My father gave me a usufruct over his share in a commercial building that he co-owns with his two brothers. The building is being leased to tenants, and the rent is being collected by the co-owners. Now, the brothers want to divide the building among themselves by partition. I want to know: Can I continue collecting the rent from my father's share? And after partition, will I still have the right to use my father's allotted portion?

When the co-ownership is terminated by partition, your usufruct will automatically attach to the specific portion of the building allotted to your father, and you may continue to enjoy the fruits and use of that portion as usufructuary, subject to the obligations of a usufructuary under the law.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 582 of the Civil Code, as a usufructuary of your father's share in the co-owned building, you can exercise all the rights of your father as a co-owner regarding the administration of the property and the collection of fruits or income, such as rent. Therefore, you are entitled to collect the rent corresponding to your father's share. [Art. 582].

### 💡 Application to Facts
When the co-ownership is terminated by partition, your usufruct will automatically attach to the specific portion of the building allotted to your father, and you may continue to enjoy the fruits and use of that portion as usufructuary, subject to the obligations of a usufructuary under the law.

Can you explain Article 920 of the Philippine Civil Code about disinheriting parents or ascendants?

Article 920 lists the sufficient causes for a person to disinherit their parents or ascendants, whether legitimate or illegitimate. These causes include: (1) abandonment of children or inducing daughters to live a corrupt or immoral life or attempting against their virtue; (2) conviction for an attempt against the life of the testator, his or her spouse, descendants, or ascendants; (3) false accusation of a crime for which the law prescribes imprisonment for six years or more, if the accusation has been found false; (4) conviction for adultery or concubinage with the spouse of the testator; (5) causing the testator to make or change a will through fraud, violence, intimidation, or undue influence; (6) loss of parental authority for causes specified in the Civil Code; (7) refusal to support children or descendants without justifiable cause; and (8) attempt by one parent against the life of the other, unless there has been a reconciliation. If any of these grounds exists, the testator may disinherit the parent or ascendant in a will.

STATUTORY TEXT: Easements are also positive or negative.
A positive easement is one which imposes upon the owner of the servient estate the obligation of allowing something to be done or of doing it himself, and a negative easement, that which prohibits the owner of the servient estate from doing something which he could lawfully do if the easement did not exist.

My neighbor has been using a path across my lot for years to reach the main road. I want to build a fence along my property line that would block that path. However, I was told there is an easement. I read that easements can be positive or negative. Can you explain what kind of easement this is and whether I am allowed to block the path? The neighbor says I must let him pass, but I'm not sure what the law says under Article 616.

Here, because the easement is positive, it requires you to allow the neighbor's use.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 616, an easement of right of way is a positive easement. It imposes on you, as the owner of the servient estate, the obligation to allow something to be done — specifically, to allow your neighbor to pass through your property. This means you must refrain from blocking the path with a fence or any other obstruction, because doing so would violate the positive easement. The law requires the servient owner to either allow the act (passage) or to perform an act himself if that is the nature of the easement. Since the right of way has been established, you cannot unilaterally close it. If you believe the easement no longer exists or was never validly constituted, you would need to bring the matter to court, but under Article 616, while the easement exists, you are obligated to permit the passage. [Art. 616].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Note that a negative easement would be different: it would prohibit you from doing something you could otherwise lawfully do, such as building above a certain height.

This cloud may prejudice your title as it affects your ability to use the property as collateral. Therefore, you can bring an action in court to remove the cloud and have the deed declared null and void. The action to quiet title is a remedy to clear the title of any doubt or uncertainty regarding ownership. [Art. 476].

You must prove that the document is indeed invalid (e.g., by showing that the seller had no title to convey) and that it is prejudicial to your title.

Can you explain Article 287 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding illegitimate children?

Article 287 grants support and successional rights to illegitimate children who are neither natural children as defined in Article 269 nor natural children by legal fiction. These are children born outside wedlock whose parents had a legal impediment to marry at the time of conception (e.g., one was already married or they were too closely related). They are entitled to financial support from their parents and to inherit from them, but only to the extent provided by law, which historically gave them less than legitimate or natural children.

Can you explain Article 1298 of the Philippine Civil Code about novation and void obligations?

Article 1298 states that if the original obligation is void from the beginning, then any novation of that obligation is also void. However, there are two exceptions: first, if the obligation is voidable and the right to annul it belongs only to the debtor, then the debtor may novate the obligation, and that novation is valid because it implies a waiver of the right to annul; second, if the voidable obligation can be ratified (or confirmed), then the novation itself may serve as a ratification, making the novation valid. In short, novation cannot give life to an absolutely void obligation, but it may validate a voidable one if the conditions are met.

Here, if both you and the seller honestly believed the engine was in excellent condition solely because of the mechanic's false statement, then the mistake about the engine's condition—an essential aspect of the sale—was mutual and substantial. In that case, consent may be vitiated, and the contract could be voidable, giving you the right to seek annulment.

Ngunit hindi maaaring kunin ng may-ari ang bagong bagay kung ang halaga nito ay mas mataas nang malaki kaysa sa materyal dahil sa artistic o scientific na dahilan. Pwede po bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 1050 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas? Kailan po ba itinuturing na tinanggap ang isang mana?

Ang Artikulo 1050 ng Civil Code ay nagsasaad ng mga sitwasyon kung saan itinuturing na tinanggap ng tagapagmana ang mana. Una, kung ibinenta, ibinigay bilang donasyon, o inilipat ng tagapagmana ang kanyang karapatan sa mana sa isang estranghero o sa kanyang mga kapwa-tagapagmana, ito ay nangangahulugan ng pagtanggap. Pangalawa, kung tinalikuran ng tagapagmana ang mana, kahit walang kapalit, pabor sa isa o higit pa sa kanyang mga kapwa-tagapagmana, ito ay pagtanggap. Pangatlo, kung tinalikuran niya ito kapalit ng isang halaga pabor sa lahat ng kapwa-tagapagmana nang walang pinipili, iyon ay pagtanggap din. Ngunit may eksepsyon: kung ang pagtalikod ay walang bayad (gratuitous) at ang mga kapwa-tagapagmana na pinagpaboran ay yaong mga tatanggap sana ng bahagi sa pamamagitan ng accretion (ibig sabihin, sa bisa ng batas dahil sila ang iba pang tagapagmana), hindi ituturing na tinanggap ang mana. Sa madaling salita, may mga kilos na nagpapakita na pinili ng tagapagmana na tanggapin ang mana.

In your situation, the legacy of the commercial building comes with the onerous condition of paying the bank debt. Therefore, the original legatee (your uncle's beneficiary, now deceased) could not have accepted the building while rejecting the debt; the acceptance must be of the entire gift or none. Since the legatee died before accepting, the second paragraph of Article 954 applies: the legatee's heirs (your two children) may each accept or repudiate his or her respective share in the legacy independently. Can you explain what Article 1250 of the Philippine Civil Code says about payment in case of extraordinary inflation or deflation?

Article 1250 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that if an extraordinary inflation or deflation of the currency stipulated in an obligation occurs after the obligation is established, the value of the currency at the time the obligation was created shall be the basis for payment. Can you explain Article 770 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 770 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that the right to file an action for revocation or reduction of a donation is personal to the donor. If the donor did not file the action before his death, his heirs cannot file it, even if the donor could have filed it and even if he died within one year from the time he could have filed. Similarly, the action cannot be brought against the heirs of the donee unless the complaint was already filed against the donee before his death.

What does Article 800 of the Philippine Civil Code state about the soundness of mind of a testator?

Article 800 provides that the law presumes every person is of sound mind unless there is proof to the contrary. (1) If the heirs sells, donates, or assigns his right to a stranger, or to his co-heirs, or to any of them;

My father passed away and left a piece of land to me and my two siblings. I don't want my share, so I told my brother that I'm giving up my share in his favor for free. But if you sell your share to anyone, that act is deemed acceptance.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1050 of the Civil Code, your actions determine whether you have accepted the inheritance. If you sell your share to a neighbor (a stranger), that is considered acceptance of the inheritance because you are disposing of your right for value. On the other hand, if you gratuitously renounce your share in favor of your brother, the rule depends on whether your brother would have received your share by accretion. If you and your siblings are the only heirs and you renounce your share gratuitously in favor of one of them, and that sibling would have received your share by accretion (i.e., because the share would be divided among the remaining co-heirs), then such renunciation does NOT constitute acceptance. However, if the renunciation is for a price, or if it is in favor of a co-heir who would not receive by accretion, then it is considered acceptance. [Art. 1050].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, since you are giving it free to your brother, and assuming he and your other sibling are the co-heirs who would get your share by accretion, the gratuitous renunciation does not mean you accepted the inheritance.

STATUTORY TEXT: The good faith of the possessor consists in the reasonable belief that the person from whom he received the thing was the owner thereof, and could transmit his ownership.

I bought a second-hand motorcycle from a person who showed me a certificate of registration and a deed of sale from the previous owner. Later, someone else appeared claiming to be the true owner and said the seller had no right to sell. Under Article 1127 of the Civil Code, am I considered a possessor in good faith? Please explain.

Good faith affects your rights as a possessor, such as the right to retain fruits or claim prescription, but it does not by itself transfer ownership if the seller was not the true owner.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1127, good faith of a possessor is the reasonable belief that the person from whom the property was received was the owner and could transmit ownership. [Art. 1127].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you relied on documents like the certificate of registration and deed of sale. If these documents reasonably led you to believe the seller was the owner, and you had no reason to suspect otherwise, then you are considered a possessor in good faith. However, good faith must be based on reasonable diligence. If there were red flags or you failed to verify the seller's authority despite suspicious circumstances, your belief may not be considered reasonable, and good faith could be negated. The determination depends on the facts at the time you acquired the motorcycle.

What does Article 1036 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Can you explain Article 1225 of the Philippine Civil Code about divisible and indivisible obligations?

Article 1225 of the Civil Code explains how to determine if an obligation is divisible (can be performed in parts) or indivisible (must be performed as a whole). It states that obligations to deliver a specific, determinate thing are indivisible, as are obligations that cannot be partially performed without changing their nature. On the other hand, obligations that involve work measured by days or by units (like building a wall of a certain length) are divisible because they can be done in parts. However, even if an obligation is physically divisible, it will be considered indivisible if the law says so or if the parties clearly intended it to be indivisible. For obligations not to do (like not to build a fence), the question of divisibility depends on the specific circumstances of the obligation.

I have a situation. I lent money to my friend Juan, and his brother Pedro gave his land as collateral (mortgage) to secure Juan's debt. Later, Juan and I agreed to change the loan terms – we reduced the interest rate and extended the due date (a novation) without informing Pedro. ### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1296 of the Civil Code, when a principal obligation is extinguished by novation, the accessory obligations, such as a mortgage, are generally extinguished as well. [Art. 1296].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the novation between you and Juan extinguished the original loan, and consequently, the mortgage on Pedro's land is also extinguished as a general rule. However, the article provides an exception: the accessory obligation may subsist only insofar as it benefits third persons who did not give their consent to the novation. Here, Maria is a third person who did not consent to the novation, and she has an interest in the mortgage because you assigned your rights under it to her as security for her loan to you. Therefore, the mortgage does not completely disappear; it continues to exist to the extent necessary to protect Maria's interest. Pedro's claim that the mortgage is entirely extinguished is not entirely correct. The mortgage remains valid and enforceable, but only for the benefit of Maria, to secure the obligation you owe her. Pedro cannot use the novation to defeat Maria's right, because Maria's consent was not obtained.

In your case, the new Civil Code took effect in 1950 and requires only 10 years for prescription. By 1960, ten years had already elapsed since the new Code's effectivity. Therefore, Article 1116 allows the application of the new Code's shorter period. Since you have been in continuous, open, and exclusive possession since 1940, and as of 1965 the 10-year period under the new Code has long been completed, you can claim ownership by prescription. This is true even though the old law required 30 years and your total possession is only 25 years.

STATUTORY TEXT: No judgment annulling a marriage shall be promulgated upon a stipulation of facts or by confession of judgment.
In case of non-appearance of the defendant, the provisions of article 101, paragraph 2, shall be observed.

My husband and I have agreed to annul our marriage because of psychological incapacity. We both want to just sign a document saying we agree on the facts and have the court approve it without going through a trial. Is that possible under Philippine law?

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
No, that is not possible. Under Article 88 of the Civil Code, a judgment annulling a marriage cannot be promulgated based merely on a stipulation of facts (an agreement between the parties on the facts) or by confession of judgment (the defendant admitting the allegations and consenting to the annulment). The court is required to conduct a trial and receive evidence to determine whether the grounds for annulment actually exist. [Art. 88].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Even if both parties agree, the State has an interest in preserving marriages, so the court must be convinced by proof.

Can you explain Article 1035 of the Philippine Civil Code? What happens if an heir is excluded from inheritance due to incapacity but has children?

Article 1035 provides that if a child or descendant of the decedent is disqualified from inheriting because of legal incapacity (e.g., unworthiness), and that disqualified person has children or descendants of his own, then those children or descendants will inherit the legitime (the portion reserved by law) that the disqualified person would have received. However, the disqualified person himself cannot enjoy the property: he has no right to the usufruct (use and fruits) or administration of the property inherited by his children. The property goes to the grandchildren, but the disqualified parent cannot control or benefit from it.

Can you explain Article 87 of the Philippine Civil Code about who can file for annulment of marriage and within what time periods?

Article 87 of the Philippine Civil Code specifies who may file an action for annulment of marriage and the time limits for each ground under Article 85. For lack of parental consent, the party who was underage may file within four years after reaching 20 (for males) or 18 (for females), or the parent/guardian may file before the party reaches that age. For a marriage contracted during the absence of a spouse, the absent spouse may file during their lifetime, or either spouse of the subsequent marriage may file during the lifetime of the other. For insanity of a party, the sane spouse who had no knowledge of the insanity, or any relative or guardian of the insane party, may file at any time before the death of either party. For fraud, the injured party must file within four years after discovery. For force or intimidation, within four years from when it ceased. For the ground in number 6 of Article 85, the injured party has eight years after the marriage to file.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, under Article 1336 of the Philippine Civil Code, you may seek to annul the loan agreement. The law provides that violence or intimidation shall annul the obligation, even if it was employed by a third person who did not take part in the contract. [Art. 1336].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the threat came from a friend of the lender, not the lender himself, but that does not matter. As long as the intimidation was serious enough to produce reasonable fear in your mind and it caused you to give your consent, the contract can be annulled on the ground of vitiated consent. You should gather evidence of the threat, such as messages, witnesses, or any other proof, and file an action for annulment of contract in court. The burden is on you to prove that the intimidation was the reason you signed the agreement and that it was of such a nature to inspire a well-grounded fear of an imminent and grave harm to your family.

Can you explain Article 952 of the Philippine Civil Code about delivering legacies and devises?

Article 952 states that if a person is tasked to give a specific item as a legacy or devise (like a particular piece of property left in a will), they must deliver that exact item if they are able to do so, and they cannot just pay its cash value instead. For legacies of money, they must be paid in cash, even if the heir or the estate does not have any cash on hand. The costs necessary to deliver the specific item are for the account of the heir or estate, but this is without prejudice to the legitime (the mandatory share of forced heirs).

I ordered a custom-built industrial machine from a supplier. The contract said I would pick it up from their warehouse on March 1. I had some problems and only sent my truck on March 10. On March 5, a fire broke out in the supplier's warehouse and destroyed my machine. Who should bear the loss?

You would bear the loss of the machine.

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the delivery was scheduled for March 1, but you delayed sending your truck until March 10. The fire occurred on March 5, during the period of delay caused by your fault. Therefore, even if ownership had not yet transferred to you (since you had not taken possession), the risk of loss shifted to you because the delay was your responsibility.

I was granted a usufruct over a cattle herd. This year, two cows died from old age, one was killed by a wolf, and three died from a sudden disease outbreak. The rest of the herd survived. I have some calves born this year. What are my legal obligations? Do I need to replace all the dead cows, and what happens with the calves and the surviving herd?

If the animals subject to usufruct were sterile, the rules would be different, but that is not your situation.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 591 of the Civil Code, your obligations depend on the cause of death. For the two cows that died from old age (natural causes) and the one killed by a wolf (rapacity of beasts of prey), you are required to replace them with young animals from the herd, specifically the calves born this year. You must use the offspring to maintain the herd's number. However, for the three cows that died from a disease outbreak, if this was an accidental and uncommon event and you were not at fault, you are not obligated to replace them. Since only part of the herd perished, the usufruct continues on the surviving animals. You must preserve the remaining herd and the calves, but you do not need to compensate for the disease-related deaths. If the disease was considered contagious and wiped out a significant portion, you still only continue usufruct on the saved part. [Art. 591].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Any replacement of natural or predator losses should come from the young born during the usufruct.

It states that the owner of a property also owns everything that the property produces, as well as anything that is incorporated or attached to it, whether naturally or artificially. For example, if you own a piece of land, you also own the fruits or crops that grow on it, and you own any building or structure that is permanently attached to that land. This principle is subject to certain exceptions and specific rules found in other articles of the Civil Code.

What does Article 633 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 633 states that if the dominant estate (the property that benefits from an easement) is co-owned by several persons, the use of the easement by any one of those co-owners is considered use by all. Can you explain Article 468 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 468 provides a rule for determining which of two movable things that have been incorporated together is considered the principal thing. If the previous article (Article 467) cannot determine which is principal—for example, if one thing was not clearly intended as an ornament or for the use or perfection of the other—then the thing of greater value shall be considered principal. If their values are equal, the one with greater volume is principal. Moreover, for certain works like paintings, sculptures, writings, printed matter, engravings, and lithographs, the material on which the work is made (such as board, metal, stone, canvas, paper, or parchment) is always considered accessory. Thus, the artistic or literary work itself is the principal thing, and the physical material is accessory.

Can you explain Article 603 of the Philippine Civil Code about the extinguishment of usufruct?

Can you explain Article 1215 of the Philippine Civil Code about solidary obligations?

Article 1215 deals with solidary obligations where there are multiple creditors (solidary creditors) or multiple debtors (solidary debtors). It states that if any solidary creditor performs acts like novation (substituting a new obligation), compensation (setting off mutual debts), confusion (merging of debtor and creditor in one person), or remission (forgiving the debt), or if such acts are done with any solidary debtor, the entire obligation is extinguished. However, this is without prejudice to Article 1219, which deals with the internal reimbursement among the parties. The second paragraph provides that the creditor who performed the act or who collected the debt is liable to the other creditors for their share in the obligation. So, while one solidary creditor can extinguish the whole obligation, he must answer to the others for their proportionate shares.

Can you explain Article 905 of the Philippine Civil Code about renunciation or compromise of future legitime?

Article 905 states that any renunciation or compromise regarding a future legitime between a person and his compulsory heirs is void. This means that an heir cannot validly give up his or her right to inherit from a living person before that person dies. When the person dies, the compulsory heir can still claim his or her legitime. However, if the heir received something under the void renunciation or compromise (such as money or property in exchange for giving up the future inheritance), the heir must bring that to collation. Collation means that the value of what was received is considered an advance on the inheritance and will be deducted from the heir's legitime when the estate is settled.

STATUTORY TEXT: Obligations for whose fulfillment a day certain has been fixed, shall be demandable only when that day comes.
Obligations with a resolutory period take effect at once, but terminate upon arrival of the day certain.
A day certain is understood to be that which must necessarily come, although it may not be known when.

I borrowed money from a friend and we agreed that I will pay him when my mother passes away. My mother is currently alive and healthy. In your case, the agreement is valid, but payment is not due until your mother dies.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1193 of the Civil Code, your obligation to pay upon the death of your mother is an obligation with a suspensive period, not a conditional obligation. A 'day certain' is defined as an event that must necessarily come, even if the exact date is unknown. Death is certain to occur, so it is a day certain. Therefore, the obligation becomes demandable only upon your mother's death. Your friend cannot demand payment before that time. [Art. 1193].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the event were something that might not happen at all, such as winning the lottery, it would be a condition and subject to different rules.

As his legally recognized illegitimate children, you and your siblings collectively inherit all of his property, including the house and savings, to the exclusion of other relatives. [Art. 988].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The inheritance will be divided equally among the three of you, as the law provides that illegitimate children inherit the whole estate when there are no legitimate descendants or ascendants.

I received a donation of a piece of land from my uncle. He had some debts at the time. Now his creditors are coming after me to pay his debts because he has no other property left. Am I liable? What does the law say?

Under Article 759, you as the donee are not liable for the donor's debts unless the donation was made in fraud of creditors. Since your uncle did not reserve sufficient property to pay his existing debts at the time of donation, the donation is presumed to be in fraud of creditors. This means you may be held responsible for those debts up to the value of the donated property. [Art. 759].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, you can rebut this presumption by proving that the donation was not intended to defraud creditors, such as showing that your uncle had other assets or that the debts were unknown at the time.

Can you explain what Article 854 of the Philippine Civil Code means regarding preterition of compulsory heirs?

Article 854 deals with preterition, which is the omission of a compulsory heir in the direct line (such as children, whether legitimate, illegitimate, or adopted) from the will, whether living at the time of execution or born after the testator's death. The effect is that the institution of heir (the designation of a person as heir in the will) is annulled. However, devises and legacies (specific gifts of property) remain valid as long as they are not inofficious, meaning they do not impair the legitime (the portion reserved by law) of the compulsory heirs. If the omitted compulsory heirs die before the testator, the institution of heir becomes effectual, but without prejudice to the right of representation (meaning their own heirs may step into their place). In essence, a testator cannot completely omit compulsory heirs from the will; if they do, the main appointment of an heir fails, but specific gifts may still stand if they do not violate the legitimes, and if the omitted heirs predecease the testator, the appointment stands subject to representation.

This means the share that would have gone to the deceased illegitimate child is divided equally among his or her own descendants. The rule ensures that grandchildren through a deceased illegitimate child are not left out but inherit their parent's share.

Can you explain Article 951 of the Philippine Civil Code about legacies and devises?

Article 951 states that when a specific thing is bequeathed, it must be delivered together with all its accessions and accessories, and in the exact condition it is in at the time of the testator's death. Accessions are things that are attached or incorporated to the main thing, like a building on land or improvements on a car. Accessories are things that are meant to go with the main thing, like a spare tire for a vehicle or keys to a house. The condition of the thing at the testator's death is decisive: the heir or executor has no obligation to repair or improve it, and the beneficiary must accept it as it is.

Can you explain Article 35 of the Civil Code of the Philippines?

Article 35 of the Civil Code deals with situations where a person claims to be a victim of a crime, but the criminal case does not proceed because the prosecutor or the investigating judge decides there is no enough evidence to file a criminal charge. In such case, even if no separate civil action is allowed for that crime under the law, the victim may still file a civil case for damages. In this civil case, the victim only needs to prove the claim by 'preponderance of evidence' (meaning it is more likely true than not), which is a lower standard than the 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' required in criminal cases. To protect the accused from harassment, the court may require the plaintiff to post a bond to compensate the defendant if the case is found to be malicious. Also, if later the prosecutor decides to file a criminal case, the civil case is suspended until the criminal case is finished.

My husband passed away recently. We did not have children, but his parents are still alive. He left a will that gave almost all his estate to a friend. I want to know what my share is as his wife under the law.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 893 of the Philippine Civil Code, since your husband died without leaving legitimate descendants but left legitimate ascendants (his parents), you, as the surviving spouse, are entitled to a legitime of one-fourth of the hereditary estate. Since he gave almost all to a friend, the disposition is valid only insofar as it does not impair the legitimes of the compulsory heirs.

STATUTORY TEXT: To determine the legitime, the value of the property left at the death of the testator shall be considered, deducting all debts and charges, which shall not include those imposed in the will.
To the net value of the hereditary estate, shall be added the value of all donations by the testator that are subject to collation, at the time he made them.

My father passed away last year. He left a house and lot worth 5 million pesos, a car worth 1 million, and some bank deposits totaling 2 million. He had debts amounting to 1.5 million including funeral expenses and a loan. In his will, he gave 500,000 to his favorite charity. He also donated a parcel of land to my brother 10 years ago, which was worth 1 million then, but now it's worth 3 million. How do we compute the legitime of us children? We are three siblings.

However, your brother's donation of ₱1,000,000 will be collated, meaning it will be considered as an advance on his legitime, so his remaining share from the estate will be reduced accordingly.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 908, the first step in computing the legitime is to determine the net value of the hereditary estate. Take the total value of the properties left at death: house and lot (₱5,000,000) + car (₱1,000,000) + bank deposits (₱2,000,000) = ₱8,000,000. From this, deduct all debts and charges, but not those imposed in the will. The debts and charges here amount to ₱1,500,000 (funeral expenses and loan). The ₱500,000 given to charity in the will is a charge imposed in the will, so it is not deducted. Thus, net value = ₱8,000,000 - ₱1,500,000 = ₱6,500,000. Then, add the value of all donations subject to collation at the time they were made. The donation of land to your brother is subject to collation because it was made to a compulsory heir. The legitime of the children (assuming no surviving spouse) is one-half of this base under the law, which equals ₱3,750,000. [Art. 908].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Divided equally among the three siblings, each child's legitime is ₱1,250,000.

Since your siblings have not consented, the easement is not yet validly constituted on the entire property. Your consent alone is insufficient to grant the neighbor a full right of way over the property. However, your separate consent binds you personally and your successors. This means that although the easement is not effective against your siblings, you cannot prevent the neighbor from exercising the right of way insofar as it affects your share or your interest. Practically, the neighbor cannot use the easement over the whole property without your siblings' consent, but you are estopped from objecting to the exercise of the right as against yourself.

Can you explain Article 629 of the Philippine Civil Code about easements?

Article 629 states that the owner of the servient estate (the property burdened by an easement) cannot do anything that impairs the use of the easement. STATUTORY TEXT: The books in the Registry of Property shall be public for those who have a known interest in ascertaining the status of the immovables or real rights annotated or inscribed therein.

I am planning to buy a parcel of land in our province. I went to the Registry of Deeds to inspect the certificate of title and check if there are any liens or encumbrances. The staff told me that the registry books are not open to just anyone. Is that correct under Article 710? As a serious buyer, don't I have the right to see the records?

Your interest as a buyer is exactly the kind of known interest contemplated by the law, so you may request to see the title and all annotations affecting the property.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 710, the books in the Registry of Property are public for those who have a known interest in ascertaining the status of immovables or real rights annotated or inscribed therein. As a serious prospective buyer of the land, you have a clear and legitimate interest in knowing the status of the property, including any liens, encumbrances, or adverse claims. Article 1425 deals with natural obligations. If a debt is already prescribed, meaning the creditor can no longer sue because the time limit has passed, and someone else pays that debt without the debtor's knowledge or against the debtor's will, the debtor is not legally required to reimburse that third person. This is because the law considers it a fulfillment of a natural obligation—morally binding even if not legally enforceable.

Can you explain Article 1270 of the Philippine Civil Code about condonation or remission of debt?

Article 1270 states that condonation or remission is the act of a creditor forgiving a debt. It is essentially gratuitous, meaning the creditor gives up the right to collect without receiving anything in return. The debtor must accept the forgiveness for it to take effect. Condonation can be express (clearly stated) or implied (inferred from actions, like returning the promissory note). Both types are subject to the rules on inofficious donations, which protect the legitime of forced heirs—if the forgiveness reduces what heirs should legally inherit, it may be reduced or invalidated. Additionally, if the condonation is express, it must comply with the formalities required for donations (e.g., written form for certain values).

What does Article 1084 of the Philippine Civil Code say about voluntary heirs with conditions and partition of the estate?

Article 1084 of the Civil Code provides that if a voluntary heir (someone named in a will) is subject to a condition, such as having to fulfill a certain requirement before receiving their inheritance, that heir cannot demand partition of the estate until the condition is fulfilled. However, the other co-heirs (those who are not subject to conditions or whose conditions are already fulfilled) may demand partition, but they must give sufficient security, like a bond, to protect the conditional heir's rights in case the condition is later fulfilled. Until it is determined that the condition has not been fulfilled or can no longer be fulfilled, the partition is considered provisional or temporary, meaning it can be adjusted if the conditional heir eventually becomes entitled.

My grandfather passed away and left a piece of land to his heirs. According to a lawyer, one of the compulsory heirs has the right to choose whether to take the land itself or demand cash for his legitime. However, that heir is not making any decision. Can the other heirs make the decision instead? What happens if no one acts?

Therefore, in the scenario described, the other heirs may act if the original right-holder does not, and if no one acts, a public auction can be initiated by any interested party.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 913 of the Civil Code, if the heir or devisee who had the right to choose under the preceding article (e.g., the right to decide whether to take the property or demand cash) does not exercise that right, then any other heir or devisee who did not originally have such right may exercise it. This means that if the compulsory heir with the initial choice fails to act, the other heirs can step in and make that choice on behalf of the estate, such as deciding to take the property or demand its sale. If none of these secondary parties exercise the right, then any interested party (which could be any heir, creditor, or other stakeholder) may request that the property be sold at public auction. [Art. 913].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The purpose of this provision is to prevent the estate from being stalled indefinitely and to ensure that the property is liquidated and distributed according to the rules on legitimes.

Article 158 deals with improvements and buildings on the separate property of spouses during marriage. What is the meaning of Article 1296 of the Philippine Civil Code? I'm confused about how accessory obligations are affected by novation, especially the part about third persons who did not give their consent.

Article 1296 states that when a principal obligation is extinguished through novation (i.e., it is replaced by a new obligation), any accessory obligations attached to it, such as pledges, mortgages, or guarantees, are also generally extinguished. Can you explain Article 1295 of the Philippine Civil Code about novation and the insolvency of the new debtor?

Article 1295 of the Civil Code states that when a new debtor takes over the obligation of the original debtor with the creditor's consent, and that new debtor later becomes insolvent, the creditor generally cannot go back to the original debtor to collect. However, there is an exception: if the new debtor was already insolvent at the time of the substitution, and that insolvency was publicly known or known to the original debtor when he delegated his debt, then the creditor can still enforce the obligation against the original debtor. Can you explain Article 1230 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding penal clauses?

Article 1230 states that the nullity of the penal clause does not affect the principal obligation. This means that if the stipulated penalty for breach is void (for example, because it is illegal or contrary to morals), the main obligation still stands and must be performed. However, if the principal obligation itself is void, then the penal clause is also void, because the penal clause is merely an accessory to the principal obligation. In other words, the accessory follows the principal.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1125 of the Civil Code, any express or tacit recognition of the owner's right interrupts possession. [Art. 1125].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, sending a letter to the registered owner acknowledging that he is the owner constitutes an express recognition of his right. This act interrupts your possession, meaning that the 12 years you have been occupying the land no longer count toward acquiring ownership through prescription. The period of possession is effectively reset, and because you have acknowledged the owner's title, your possession is no longer considered adverse or in the concept of an owner. To acquire ownership by prescription, your possession must be adverse, continuous, and without recognition of the owner's rights. Since you have recognized the owner, the prescription period stops running, and you would need to start a new period of adverse possession only if you later clearly repudiate the owner's title.

STATUTORY TEXT: Rescission creates the obligation to return the things which were the object of the contract, together with their fruits, and the price with its interest; consequently, it can be carried out only when he who demands rescission can return whatever he may be obliged to restore.
Neither shall rescission take place when the things which are the object of the contract are legally in the possession of third persons who did not act in bad faith.
In this case, indemnity for damages may be demanded from the person causing the loss.

I bought a parcel of land from a seller, but I later found out that the sale can be rescinded because the price was very low (lesion). I want to rescind the contract, but the seller already sold the land to another person who did not know about the problem and is now in lawful possession. Can I still rescind under Article 1385? What are my rights?

Therefore, you cannot recover the land from the innocent third party, but you may file a claim for damages against the seller who transferred the property, as the seller is the one who caused the loss by selling the land despite the rescissible nature of the original sale.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1385, rescission of a contract requires mutual restitution: the party seeking rescission must be able to return what he received, and the other party must return what he received. [Art. 1385].

Since the new buyer is in lawful possession and appears to have acted in good faith (not knowing about the defect), rescission is barred. However, the law states that in such a case, indemnity for damages may be demanded from the person causing the loss.

My father passed away last year. In his will, he left me his house and lot, but there is a condition that I can only inherit it if I never get married. I am currently single but planning to get married next year. Is that condition valid? Can I still inherit the house even if I marry?

Additionally, note that the testator could have validly given you a right of usufruct, an allowance, or a personal prestation for as long as you remain unmarried, but that is not the situation here since the condition is an absolute prohibition on marriage.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 874 of the Philippine Civil Code, an absolute condition not to contract a first or subsequent marriage is considered as not written. This means that the condition imposed by your father prohibiting you from ever marrying is void and will be disregarded. You can still inherit the house and lot even if you get married. The only exception to this rule is when the condition is imposed on a widow or widower by the deceased spouse, or by that deceased spouse's ascendants or descendants. [Art. 874].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, you are not a widow or widower—you are the son of the deceased, and the condition was imposed by your father on you, not on a surviving spouse by the deceased spouse or their relatives. Therefore, the exception does not apply. The condition is void, and you will inherit the property without any restriction on marriage.

Can you explain Article 618 of the Philippine Civil Code about easements being indivisible?

Article 618 states that easements cannot be divided. If the servient estate (the property burdened by the easement) is divided among two or more persons, the easement remains unchanged, and each new owner must bear the easement on the part that corresponds to them. If the dominant estate (the property that benefits from the easement) is divided among two or more persons, each new owner may use the easement in its entirety, but they cannot change the place where it is used or make it more burdensome in any way.

Paki paliwanag po ang Artikulo 615 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa mga uri ng easement.

Ang Artikulo 615 ay nag-uuri ng mga easement sa apat na uri batay sa dalawang pamantayan: pagpapatuloy ng paggamit at pagkakita. Ang continuous easements ay yaong ang paggamit ay walang tigil o maaaring walang tigil nang walang pagkilos ng tao, tulad ng aqueduct na patuloy ang daloy ng tubig. Ang discontinuous easements ay ginagamit lamang sa mga pagitan at nakasalalay sa kilos ng tao, tulad ng right of way na kailangang lakarin o daanan tuwing gagamitin. Ang apparent easements ay nakikita sa pamamagitan ng mga panlabas na palatandaan na nagpapakita ng paggamit, tulad ng pinto o bintana. Ang nonapparent easements ay walang anumang panlabas na palatandaan ng kanilang pag-iral, tulad ng pagbabawal na magtayo ng mas mataas na gusali. Mahalaga ang mga klasipikasyong ito sa pagkuha, preskripsyon, at pagtatapos ng mga easement.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 301 of the Civil Code, the right to receive support cannot be renounced or compensated with what the recipient owes the obligor, but this rule applies only to current and future support. Support in arrears, however, may be compensated and renounced. [Art. 301].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the 100,000 pesos is support in arrears. Therefore, your ex-husband can validly compensate or offset the 50,000 peso loan against the arrears, leaving a balance of 50,000 pesos. You may also choose to renounce or forgive the entire remaining arrears if you wish, since arrears can be renounced.

STATUTORY TEXT: A contract is a meeting of minds between two persons whereby one binds himself, with respect to the other, to give something or to render some service.

I agreed with my neighbor to buy his old refrigerator for 5,000 pesos. We shook hands on it, and he said he would deliver it on Saturday. But now he says it's not a contract because we didn't sign any papers. Is there a valid contract under Philippine law?

If he refuses, he may be liable for breach of contract.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1305 of the Civil Code, a contract is a meeting of minds between two persons whereby one binds himself, with respect to the other, to give something or to render some service. [Art. 1305].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, there was a meeting of minds between you and your neighbor regarding the sale of the refrigerator at a specific price. Two persons were involved, and your neighbor bound himself to give the refrigerator. The law does not generally require contracts to be in writing unless a specific form is required by law for certain types of contracts, such as the sale of real property. For the sale of personal property like a refrigerator, an oral agreement is typically valid. Therefore, a valid contract exists, and your neighbor is obligated to deliver the refrigerator.

Paki-explain po ang Artikulo 900 ng Kodigo Sibil tungkol sa legitime ng asawang nakaligtas.

Ang Artikulo 900 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay tumatalakay sa legitime ng asawang nakaligtas kapag siya lamang ang sapilitang tagapagmana. Karaniwan, kung ang biyuda o biyudo lamang ang naiwan, sila ay may karapatan sa kalahati ng ari-arian bilang kanilang legitime, at ang testador ay maaaring malayang ipamahagi ang natitirang kalahati. Ngunit may eksepsiyon: kung ang kasal ay isinagawa 'in articulo mortis' (sa punto ng kamatayan) at ang testador ay namatay sa loob ng tatlong buwan mula sa kasal, ang legitime ng asawang nakaligtas ay babawasan sa isang-katlo ng ari-arian. Hindi ito nalalapat kung ang mag-asawa ay nagsama bilang mag-asawa nang higit sa limang taon, kung saan ang legitime ay babalik sa kalahati. Ang binawasang legitime ay naglalayong hadlangan ang mga kasal na ginawa lamang upang makakuha ng mana kapag malapit nang mamatay ang asawa.

Can you explain Article 1265 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the loss of a thing in the debtor's possession?

Article 1265 provides that if a thing is lost while in the possession of the debtor, the law presumes that the loss was due to the debtor's fault. The debtor can overcome this presumption by presenting proof that the loss was not due to his fault. However, this presumption does not apply when the loss is caused by natural calamities such as earthquakes, floods, storms, or similar events. In such cases, the debtor is not automatically presumed at fault, but he may still need to prove that the loss was indeed due to the calamity and not due to his own negligence. The article also states that this is without prejudice to Article 1165, which deals with the debtor's liability for fortuitous events in cases of delay or when the same thing has been promised to multiple persons.

Can you explain Article 1030 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1030 deals with wills that leave property to 'the poor' in general, without naming specific persons or a particular community. In such cases, the law presumes the testator intended to benefit the poor living in his or her domicile at the time of death, unless the will clearly shows a different intention. The article also provides for the designation of who qualifies as poor and the distribution of the property: the person appointed by the testator for that purpose; if none, the executor; if no executor, then the justice of the peace, the mayor, and the municipal treasurer, who decide by majority vote. All these acts require the approval of the Court of First Instance. The same rules apply if the testator left property to the poor of a specific locality.

Can you explain Article 1408 of the Philippine Civil Code? It says 'Unenforceable contracts cannot be assailed by third persons.'

Article 1408 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that unenforceable contracts cannot be assailed by third persons. Unenforceable contracts are those that cannot be enforced by a court action unless they are ratified. They are valid but defective because of lack of form, authority, or capacity of both parties, but the defect can be cured by ratification. This article means that only the parties to the unenforceable contract (or their successors-in-interest) can raise the defense of unenforceability to prevent its enforcement. Third persons, who are not parties to the contract, have no legal standing to challenge or question the validity of the contract on the ground that it is unenforceable. The rationale is that the ground of unenforceability is personal to the parties and does not affect third persons.

Can you explain Article 1033 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding unworthiness to inherit?

Article 1033 states that the causes of unworthiness (such as acts that would disqualify an heir) have no effect if the testator knew about them at the time he made his will, or if he later learned of them and condoned them in writing.
