Can you explain what Article 899 of the Philippine Civil Code says about the shares of the surviving spouse, legitimate parents or ascendants, and illegitimate children in inheritance?

Article 899 applies when a deceased person is survived by a legitimate parent or ascendant, a surviving spouse, and illegitimate children, but no legitimate children. In this situation, the estate is divided as follows: (1) the legitimate parents or ascendants are entitled to one-half (1/2) of the estate as their legitime; (2) the surviving spouse receives one-eighth (1/8) of the estate, taken from the free portion; (3) the illegitimate children collectively receive one-fourth (1/4) of the estate, also taken from the disposable portion; and (4) the testator may freely dispose of the remaining one-eighth (1/8) of the estate. This means that only 1/8 of the estate is truly within the testator's power to give away by will, as the rest is reserved by law for these heirs.

Ito ay ang mga sumusunod: (1) Yaong may mga lehitimo, lehitimado, kinikilalang natural na anak, o natural na anak sa pamamagitan ng legal na piksiyon; (2) Ang tagapangalaga (guardian), kaugnay sa kanyang inaalagaan (ward), bago ang pinal na pag-apruba ng kanyang mga account; (3) Ang taong may asawa, nang walang pahintulot ng kanyang asawa; (4) Mga dayuhang hindi naninirahan sa Pilipinas (non-resident aliens); (5) Mga dayuhang naninirahan sa Pilipinas na ang gobyerno ng kanilang bansa ay sinira ng Pilipinas ang diplomatikong relasyon; (6) Sinumang taong nahatulan ng krimeng may kinalaman sa moral turpitude, kapag ang parusang ipinataw ay anim na buwang pagkabilanggo o higit pa.

Under Article 115 of the Civil Code, the wife manages the household and may purchase things necessary for family support, which binds the conjugal partnership. However, the purchase of jewelry and precious objects is specifically made voidable unless the husband expressly or tacitly approved the transaction, or unless the price was paid from her paraphernal property (her own separate property). In your scenario, your wife bought a diamond ring—a precious object—using conjugal funds without your consent. Therefore, the purchase is voidable. You, as the husband, may take legal action to annul the transaction, unless you later approve it expressly (by clearly agreeing) or tacitly (by acting in a way that shows acceptance, such as knowingly allowing her to keep and use the ring without objection). Since the ring was paid with conjugal funds and not her paraphernal property, the exception for her using her own separate money does not apply.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.

Can you explain Article 1954 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean?

Article 1954 provides that if one person transfers ownership of non-fungible things (specific, identifiable items that are not interchangeable) to another, and the recipient is obligated to give things of the same kind, quantity, and quality in return, the contract is considered a barter, not a loan. This means the law treats the transaction as an exchange of goods rather than a loan. In a loan of fungible things (money or generic goods), the borrower can return an equivalent amount of the same kind and quality; but when the things transferred are non-fungible, the arrangement cannot be a true loan—it is a barter. This article clarifies the distinction between loan and barter based on the nature of the things transferred.

STATUTORY TEXT: The following shall be sufficient causes for the disinheritance of parents or ascendants, whether legitimate or illegitimate:
(1) When the parents have abandoned their children or induced their daughters to live a corrupt or immoral life, or attempted against their virtue;
(2) When the parent or ascendant has been convicted of an attempt against the life of the testator, his or her spouse, descendants, or ascendants;

(6) The loss of parental authority for causes specified in this Code;

I am preparing my last will and testament. My father left our family when I was a child and never provided any financial support. I want to disinherit him. According to Philippine law, can I do this? What are the grounds I can rely on?

The disinheritance must be made in a valid will, unaffected by any vice of consent, and the cause must be one of those enumerated in Article 920.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Yes, under Article 920 of the Civil Code of the Philippines, you may disinherit your father based on the ground of abandonment. Paragraph (1) states that it is a sufficient cause when 'the parents have abandoned their children.' Since your father left when you were a child and did not fulfill his parental obligations, this clearly falls under that provision. [Art. 920].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Additionally, if he refused to support you without justifiable cause, paragraph (7) also applies, which covers 'the refusal to support the children or descendants without justifiable cause.' To validly disinherit him, you must expressly state the specific cause in your will. The cause must be true and, if contested, you must be able to prove it.

Can you explain Article 1368 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1368 states that reformation of a written instrument may be ordered at the instance of either party or their successors in interest if the mistake was mutual. If the mistake was not mutual (i.e., only one party was mistaken), reformation may be ordered only upon petition of the injured party, or his heirs and assigns. In simple terms, when both parties made the same mistake in a written contract, either of them can ask the court to correct the document to reflect their true intention. But if only one party made the mistake, only the party who was harmed by that mistake can ask for correction.

Can you explain what Article 571 of the Philippine Civil Code says about the rights of a usufructuary?

Article 571 states that a usufructuary, the person who has the right to use and enjoy another person's property, is entitled to enjoy any increase the property acquires through accession (such as soil deposited by a river, or buildings added), any servitudes (easements) established in favor of the property, and generally all benefits inherent in the property. ### 💡 Application to Facts
Unless any of these properties fall under the exceptions provided by law (for example, if they were acquired by inheritance or donation with an express condition that they should not be part of the community), they are all considered part of the common property owned jointly by both spouses.

STATUTORY TEXT: The power to rescind obligations is implied in reciprocal ones, in case one of the obligors should not comply with what is incumbent upon him.
The injured party may choose between the fulfillment and the rescission of the obligation, with the payment of damages in either case. He may also seek rescission, even after he has chosen fulfillment, if the latter should become impossible.
The court shall decree the rescission claimed, unless there be just cause authorizing the fixing of a period.
This is understood to be without prejudice to the rights of third persons who have acquired the thing, in accordance with articles 1385 and 1388 and the Mortgage Law.

Scenario: I entered into a contract to buy a second-hand car from a seller for PHP 500,000. The contract says the seller will deliver the car to me within 30 days, and I will pay upon delivery. After 30 days, the seller did not deliver the car. I reminded him, but he still failed. Later, I found out he sold the car to another person who already took possession. What are my legal options? Can I cancel the contract and get my money back? Can I force the seller to give me the car? Please advise.

Instead, you can rescind the contract with the seller and claim damages for his breach.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1191 of the Civil Code, your contract is a reciprocal obligation: the seller is obligated to deliver the car, and you are obligated to pay the price. Since the seller failed to deliver within the agreed period, you, as the injured party, have the right to choose between fulfillment (demanding delivery) or rescission (cancellation) of the contract, plus damages in either case. However, because the seller already sold the car to a third person who took possession, fulfillment has become impossible. Therefore, even if you initially demanded delivery, you may now seek rescission. The court will decree rescission unless the seller can show a just cause for an extension. But note that this is without prejudice to the rights of third persons who acquired the car in good faith under Articles 1385 and 1388 and the Mortgage Law. [Art. 1191].

If the third person bought the car in good faith and has acquired ownership, you may not be able to recover the car from them.

If the transfer had been by donation instead of sale, you would not be liable to pay any indemnity.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 653 of the Civil Code, because you (the grantor) transferred a portion of your land by sale, and as a result your remaining land became isolated from the public road, you have the right to demand a right of way across the portion you sold. However, you must pay an indemnity to the buyer (the current owner of that land) for the use of the right of way. [Art. 653].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The indemnity is meant to compensate the buyer for the burden placed on his property.

Can you explain what Article 879 of the Philippine Civil Code means? I'm confused about the rule on negative potestative conditions for heirs.

Article 879 deals with conditional testamentary dispositions where the condition is potestative (depends on the heir's will) and negative (requires the heir not to do or not to give something). In such a case, the heir does not have to actually perform the negative condition immediately; instead, the heir must provide a security (like a bond or guarantee) that he will not do the prohibited act or give the prohibited thing. If the heir later violates the condition, he must return whatever he received from the inheritance, together with its fruits (produce, income) and interests. This protects the testator's wishes while allowing the heir to enjoy the inheritance under the condition.

Can you explain Article 1426 of the Philippine Civil Code about minors and annulled contracts?

Article 1426 deals with a situation where a person aged 18 to 21 (considered a minor under the old Civil Code before majority was lowered to 18) enters into a contract without parental consent. If that contract is later annulled, and the minor voluntarily returns whatever he received (the thing or the price), then he cannot later ask for it back, even if he did not actually benefit from the contract. This is because the return is considered a natural obligation – not legally enforceable, but once voluntarily performed, it cannot be undone. The law prevents the minor from recovering what he willingly gave back after the annulment.

Please explain Article 811 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding holographic wills.

Article 811 deals with how a holographic will is proven in court. A holographic will is one entirely written, dated, and signed by the testator's own hand. To probate such a will, at least one witness who knows the testator's handwriting and signature must testify that the will and signature are in the testator's handwriting. If the will is contested (someone challenges its validity), at least three such witnesses are required. If no such witness is available, the court may allow expert testimony to compare handwriting, if it deems it necessary.

Can you explain Article 1133 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1133 of the Philippine Civil Code states that if a person obtains possession of a movable (personal property) through a crime, such as theft, robbery, or embezzlement, that person (the offender) can never acquire ownership of that movable through prescription. Prescription is a legal way of acquiring ownership by possessing something for a certain period of time. However, this rule provides an absolute prohibition: no matter how long the offender possesses the stolen property, they cannot become its legal owner through prescription. The law does not allow a criminal to benefit from their illegal act.

Can you explain Article 1446 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean regarding acceptance by the beneficiary of a trust?

Article 1446 of the Philippine Civil Code states that acceptance by the beneficiary is necessary for a trust to be effective. However, if the trust does not impose any burdensome or onerous condition on the beneficiary, the law presumes that the beneficiary has accepted the trust, unless there is evidence showing otherwise. In other words, if the beneficiary would only receive benefits and no duties or obligations, acceptance is automatically assumed without any explicit act or declaration from the beneficiary. This presumption can be overturned if there is proof that the beneficiary actually rejected the trust.

My father died and left a small estate. His debts are more than the value of his properties. Some creditors are demanding payment. How should the estate be settled? I heard about preference of credits. What does Article 1059 mean for us?

If the assets are exhausted before all creditors are paid, the remaining unpaid debts are generally extinguished.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1059, when the assets of the decedent's estate are insufficient to pay all debts, the order of payment follows the preference of credits as provided in Articles 2239 to 2251 of the Civil Code. After these administrative expenses are paid, other preferred creditors such as the government for taxes and employees for unpaid wages are paid next. Only if there are remaining assets will ordinary unsecured creditors be paid proportionally to their claims. [Art. 1059].

In your situation, you should first settle the estate administration expenses, then pay taxes and other preferred claims, and if anything is left, distribute it proportionally among the ordinary creditors.

As a minor, you generally lack full capacity to act. Therefore, the lease agreement you signed is voidable; you may have it annulled or ratify it upon reaching the age of majority. The landlord's assertion that your mere juridical capacity makes the contract valid is incorrect because capacity to act is a separate requirement. [Art. 37].

### 💡 Application to Facts
You retain juridical capacity to inherit property from your parents, but to enter into binding contracts you need capacity to act.

PROVISION: Article 594 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE VI.—USUFRUCT > CH 3 - OBLIGATIONS OF THE USUFRUCTUARY > Art. 594
STATUTORY TEXT: If the owner should make the extraordinary repairs, he shall have a right to demand of the usufructuary the legal interest on the amount expended for the time that the usufruct lasts.
Should he not make them when they are indispensable for the preservation of the thing, the usufructuary may make them; but he shall have a right to demand of the owner, at the termination of the usufruct, the increase in value which the immovable may have acquired by reason of the repairs.

I have the right to use and enjoy a farm (usufruct) for 10 years. The owner recently spent a large amount to repair the damaged foundation of the farmhouse, which was necessary to keep the building from collapsing. Now he is demanding that I pay him interest on that repair cost for the remaining years of my usufruct. Is that legal? What if I had done those repairs because he refused? What would I be entitled to?

Therefore, because the owner made the repairs, you must pay legal interest for the time the usufruct lasts; you cannot avoid that by saying you would have done it yourself.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 594 of the Civil Code, since the owner made the extraordinary repairs (repairs of the foundation that were indispensable to preserve the property), the usufructuary is obligated to pay the owner legal interest on the amount spent for the duration of the usufruct. So the owner's demand for interest is valid. However, if the owner had refused to make those indispensable extraordinary repairs, you as usufructuary could have made them yourself. [Art. 594].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In that case, at the termination of the usufruct, you would be entitled to demand from the owner the increase in value that the property gained due to those repairs, not the total cost.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 594 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Can you explain Article 688 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 688 allows a property owner to create easements (also called servitudes) on his land as he sees fit, in any manner or form he deems best, provided that the easement does not violate laws, public policy, or public order. Can you explain Article 681 of the Philippine Civil Code? It states that fruits naturally falling upon adjacent land belong to the owner of said land. What does this mean?

Article 681 provides that when fruits (such as mangoes, etc.) fall naturally from a tree without any human intervention or external force (e.g., they drop because they are ripe), and they land on a neighboring property, the owner of that neighboring property becomes the owner of those fruits. This is based on the principle of accession—the fruits become part of the land where they fall. The tree owner loses any claim to them. This rule applies only to natural falling, not to fruits that are picked, shaken, or fall due to wind or other accidental causes.

Can you explain Article 1304 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 1304 states that if a creditor receives only partial payment of a debt, they can still demand the remaining balance. Moreover, if a third party paid that partial amount and was subrogated (stepped into the shoes of the creditor) to the extent of that payment, the original creditor has priority over that third party when collecting the remaining debt. This means the original creditor gets paid first for the balance before the subrogated party can claim anything from the debtor.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1278 of the Civil Code, compensation takes place when two persons are creditors and debtors of each other in their own right. [Art. 1278].

In your situation, you are a creditor of your neighbor for P50,000 (loan) and a debtor to him for P30,000 (repair services). Conversely, your neighbor is your debtor for P50,000 and your creditor for P30,000. Both of you are acting in your own right, not as representatives of others. Therefore, the legal conditions for compensation under this article are present. The two debts may be offset, meaning your obligation to pay P30,000 is extinguished up to that amount, and his remaining debt to you becomes P20,000.

Can you explain what Article 423 of the Philippine Civil Code means regarding the property of provinces, cities, and municipalities?

Article 423 classifies the property of local government units (provinces, cities, and municipalities) into two categories: property for public use and patrimonial property. Property for public use includes roads, parks, plazas, public buildings, and other assets intended for public service or common use. These cannot be sold or disposed of because they are held by the local government for the benefit of the public. Patrimonial property, on the other hand, is property owned by the local government in a private or proprietary capacity, such as income-generating assets or lands not devoted to public use. Patrimonial property can be sold, leased, or otherwise disposed of, subject to legal requirements. The distinction is important for determining how local government property can be managed, used, or alienated.

However, you should act promptly because the remaining time is only two years.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1094 of the Civil Code, an action to enforce the warranty among co-heirs must be brought within ten years from the date the right of action accrues. [Art. 1094].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your case, the right of action accrued when you were evicted from the property, as that is when the warranty against eviction became enforceable. Since only eight years have passed from the eviction, the ten-year prescriptive period has not yet lapsed. Therefore, you may still file an action against your co-heirs to enforce the warranty and claim compensation for the loss of your share. The warranty among co-heirs obliges each co-heir to guarantee the shares received by the others in the partition, and if one is evicted, the others must reimburse the value of the lost property.

Can you explain Article 1239 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1239 states that when an obligation is to give a specific thing, the payment or performance is only valid if the person paying has the free disposal of the thing and the legal capacity to transfer (alienate) it. If the person paying does not have the right to dispose of the thing (for example, they are not the owner and have no authority to transfer it) or lacks legal capacity (such as being a minor or mentally incapacitated), the payment is generally not valid. However, this rule is without prejudice to Article 1427 on natural obligations, which means that if the obligation is a natural obligation (like a moral duty that is not legally enforceable), a voluntary payment may still be considered valid even if the payor lacked capacity, because natural obligations cannot be recovered once voluntarily performed.

STATUTORY TEXT: All property of the marriage is presumed to belong to the conjugal partnership, unless it be proved that it pertains exclusively to the husband or to the wife. (1407)
Conjugal Partnership

My husband and I are married under the conjugal partnership of gains. He bought a house and lot during our marriage using money he inherited from his father. The title is under his name only. He insists it is his exclusive property because the money used was his inheritance. I believe that under Article 160 of the Civil Code, all property acquired during marriage is presumed conjugal, so the house should be considered ours. Who is right?

Therefore, unless your husband provides clear evidence, the house is presumed conjugal and belongs to both of you.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 160 of the Civil Code, all property acquired during the marriage is presumed to belong to the conjugal partnership, unless it is proven that it pertains exclusively to one spouse. [Art. 160].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The fact that the title is in your husband's name alone does not automatically make it exclusive; the presumption applies. Your husband claims the house is exclusive because he used inherited money. Inherited property is generally considered exclusive property of the inheriting spouse, and if he can prove that the entire purchase price came from his inheritance and that he did not use any conjugal funds, and that he took steps to keep the property as his exclusive property (e.g., the deed states it is his exclusive property or there is a clear intention), then the house may be considered his exclusive property. However, the burden of proof is on him. If he cannot sufficiently prove that the funds were exclusively his inheritance and that no conjugal funds were used, the presumption stands and the house is conjugal.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 160, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Family Court (Regional Trial Court designated under Republic Act No. 8369) having exclusive jurisdiction over family relations and matrimonial regimes.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Exempt from Katarungang Pambarangay if the action directly involves matrimonial validity, legal separation, or custody; otherwise, mandatory mediation before the Family Court.

Can you explain Article 918 of the Philippine Civil Code? What happens if a disinheritance is not valid?

Article 918 of the Philippine Civil Code states that a disinheritance is void if it was made without specifying a cause, or for a cause that is contradicted and not proven, or for a cause not allowed by law. As a result, the institution of heirs in the will is annulled only to the extent that it prejudices the person who was supposedly disinherited. This means the disinherited person will still be entitled to his or her legitime, which is the portion reserved by law for forced heirs. However, other testamentary dispositions such as legacies and devises remain valid as long as they do not impair that legitime. So the will is not totally void; only the part that would have excluded the forced heir from his legitime is set aside.

Can you explain Article 1068 of the Philippine Civil Code about collation of educational expenses?

Article 1068 provides that expenses incurred by parents in giving their children a professional, vocational, or other career education are generally not subject to collation. Collation is the process of returning to the estate certain gifts or advances given to heirs during the lifetime of the deceased to ensure equal division of the inheritance. However, educational expenses are considered part of the parents' obligation to support and educate their children, not an advance on the inheritance. There are two exceptions: (1) if the parents expressly provided that such expenses should be collated; or (2) if the expenses were so large that they impaired the legitime of other compulsory heirs. If collation is required, the amount to be returned is reduced by the sum the child would have spent if he had lived in the house and company of his parents, representing the ordinary living expenses the parents would have incurred anyway.

Please explain Article 321 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms.

The estate has the motorcycle but no cash, only a piece of land. Can I sell the motorcycle and give the friend the money instead? And for the charity, can I give them the land instead of cash?

The expenses necessary for delivering the motorcycle are for the account of the estate, but without prejudice to the legitime of forced heirs.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 952 of the Civil Code, you must deliver the specific vintage motorcycle to the friend if you are able to do so; you cannot discharge that obligation by paying its value. Selling it to give cash would violate the law. [Art. 952].

### 💡 Application to Facts
For the cash legacy of 500,000 pesos, you must pay it in cash, even if the estate has no cash on hand; you may need to liquidate other assets (such as selling the land) to raise the cash, but you cannot substitute the land for the cash legacy.

### ⚖️ Legal Action Summary
- **Governing Civil Code Article(s)**: Article 952, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines)
- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.
- **Pre-filing Requirement**: Mandatory Barangay Conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay under RA 7160) prior to court filing, unless the parties reside in different cities/municipalities or urgent provisional remedies (injunction/TRO) are required.
- **Possible Cause of Action to File**: Action under Article 952 of the Civil Code for enforcement of statutory rights with damages.

Can you explain Article 974 of the Philippine Civil Code about succession by representation and per stirpes division?

Article 974 states that when there is succession by representation, the estate is divided per stirpes. This means that the representative or representatives (such as children of a deceased heir) cannot inherit more than what the person they represent would have inherited if that person were alive or could inherit. In other words, the representatives step into the shoes of the deceased heir and collectively receive that heir's share, which is then divided among them equally.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 826 of the Philippine Civil Code, a codicil must be executed with the same formalities as a will. If the original will was holographic (entirely handwritten, dated, and signed by the testator), then a codicil to that will may also be holographic, provided it is entirely handwritten, dated, and signed by the testator. In your father's case, if the original will was notarial, the handwritten note would not be a valid codicil because it does not meet the required formalities. If the original will was holographic, the handwritten note might qualify as a holographic codicil only if it is entirely in his handwriting, dated, and signed, and clearly indicates it is an amendment to the will.

Article 622 states that continuous nonapparent easements (like a right to light or air that is not visibly obvious) and all discontinuous easements (whether apparent or not, such as a right of way that is used only occasionally) can only be acquired by a title. If it can be inferred from the nature of the obligation and the circumstances that a period was intended, the courts may fix the duration. The courts must also fix the period when it depends solely on the will of the debtor. In all cases, the court will determine the period that the parties probably contemplated. Once the court fixes the period, it cannot be changed.

Can you explain Article 1252 of the Philippine Civil Code about application of payments?

Article 1252 of the Civil Code provides that when a debtor owes several debts of the same kind to the same creditor, the debtor has the right to specify, at the time of payment, which particular debt the payment should be applied to. Additionally, if the creditor issues a receipt that states how the payment is applied, and the debtor accepts that receipt, the debtor is bound by that application and cannot later complain, unless there is a ground to invalidate the contract. This article ensures clarity and fairness in settling multiple obligations.

Can you explain Article 1451 of the Philippine Civil Code about implied trusts when land passes by succession?

Article 1451 provides that when a person inherits land through succession, but instead of registering the title in his own name, he causes the legal title to be placed in the name of another person, an implied trust is created by operation of law. This means that the person named in the title is considered a trustee holding the property for the benefit of the true owner—the heir who inherited it. The true owner retains beneficial ownership even though the legal title is in someone else's name.

Puwede po bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 418 ng Civil Code tungkol sa pagkakaiba ng consumable at nonconsumable na movable property?

Ang Artikulo 418 ng Civil Code ay naghahati sa mga movable property (personal na ari-arian) sa dalawang uri: consumable at nonconsumable. STATUTORY TEXT: When, there having been a meeting of the minds of the parties to a contract, their true intention is not expressed in the instrument purporting to embody the agreement, by reason of mistake, fraud, inequitable conduct or accident, one of the parties may ask for the reformation of the instrument to the end that such true intention may be expressed.

I agreed to buy a parcel of land from my neighbor for 200 square meters as we both intended. However, the Deed of Sale we signed states 150 square meters due to a typographical error. We both know the true agreement was 200 sqm. What can I do under Philippine law to correct the document?

In your situation, since the true intention was clear and only the written expression was erroneous, you can file an action for reformation of the instrument.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1359 of the Civil Code, because you and your neighbor had a meeting of the minds on the sale of 200 square meters, but the written Deed of Sale did not express that true intention due to a mistake (the typographical error), the proper remedy is reformation of the instrument. You may ask the court to reform the Deed of Sale so that it reflects the true area of 200 square meters. Reformation is appropriate because the mistake did not prevent the meeting of the minds; you both actually agreed on 200 sqm, only the document failed to state it correctly. [Art. 1359].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If, however, the mistake had prevented a meeting of the minds—for example, if one party believed the area was 200 sqm while the other believed it was 150 sqm—then the remedy would be annulment of the contract, not reformation.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

We are three siblings who inherited a parcel of land from our father. We partitioned it equally, and I received one portion. Recently, a third party successfully claimed ownership of my portion through a court case, so I lost it. My two siblings are supposed to compensate me according to our shares, but one of them has become insolvent and cannot pay. Can I demand that the other solvent sibling pay me the full amount? And what about the insolvent sibling's obligation later?

If the insolvent sibling's financial condition improves in the future, the solvent sibling has the right to seek reimbursement from him.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1093 of the Civil Code, the mutual warranty among co-heirs is proportionate to their hereditary shares. Since your share was lost due to a third-party claim, your co-heirs are obligated to indemnify you. In computing their liability, your own share is excluded because you are the one to be indemnified. Therefore, your two siblings are each liable for one-half of the loss (assuming equal shares). [Art. 1093].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If one sibling is insolvent, the other solvent sibling must cover the insolvent sibling's portion as well, meaning the solvent sibling must pay you the entire amount of the loss.

Mahalagang sundin ang proseso ng konsultasyon upang mapanatili ang pagkakaisa ng pamilya at maiwasan ang mga hindi pagkakaunawaan.

Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 312 ng Kodigo Sibil, ang mga lolo at lola ay dapat konsultahin ng lahat ng miyembro ng pamilya sa lahat ng mahahalagang usapin ng pamilya. STATUTORY TEXT: The ownership which the proprietor of a piece of land has over the waters rising thereon does not prejudice the rights which the owners of lower estates may have legally acquired to the use thereof.

I own a piece of land in a rural area. There is a natural spring on my property that I have always considered mine. ### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 510 of the Civil Code, you as the landowner have ownership over the waters rising on your land, including the spring. However, this ownership is not absolute and does not prejudice any rights that owners of lower estates (like your neighbor) may have legally acquired to use those waters. [Art. 510].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, if your neighbor has been using the water from your spring openly, continuously, and without your objection for the period required by law (which may be 10 or 20 years depending on the circumstances and applicable rules on prescription of easements), he may have acquired a legal easement or right to use the water. Article 510 expressly preserves such legally acquired rights, meaning you cannot simply rely on your ownership to stop him if he has indeed acquired that right. You should first determine whether your neighbor has met the legal requirements for acquiring a right of use through prescription or any other legal means.

STATUTORY TEXT: Subrogation of a third person in the rights of the creditor is either legal or conventional. The former is not presumed, except in cases expressly mentioned in this Code; the latter must be clearly established in order that it may take effect.

I paid my neighbor's debt to a lending company without any written agreement. The lender verbally told me I can now collect from my neighbor, but there is no document. Can I automatically step into the lender's shoes and demand payment from my neighbor?

You may have a right to reimbursement for the amount paid, but not the creditor's original rights and accessories.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1300, subrogation is either legal or conventional. Legal subrogation is not presumed and only arises in cases expressly mentioned in the Civil Code, such as when a person interested in the fulfillment of the obligation pays the debt without the debtor's knowledge. If your situation does not fall under those specific legal subrogation cases (e.g., you are not a co-debtor, guarantor, or otherwise interested party), then subrogation can only be conventional. Conventional subrogation requires a clear and express agreement between you and the creditor to transfer the creditor's rights to you. A mere verbal statement that you can collect is insufficient; the agreement must be clearly established, ideally in writing. [Art. 1300].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, without a clear conventional subrogation agreement, you do not automatically acquire the lender's rights to collect from your neighbor.

Can you explain Article 1428 of the Civil Code of the Philippines? What does it mean when after an action to enforce a civil obligation has failed the defendant voluntarily performs the obligation?

Article 1428 deals with natural obligations. A natural obligation is one that cannot be enforced by court action because the legal remedy has already been lost (for example, due to prescription or a final judgment that dismissed the case). However, if the debtor voluntarily performs the obligation after the court action has failed, he cannot later demand the return of what he delivered or the payment for the service he rendered. The law treats such voluntary performance as a valid fulfillment of a moral duty, and it has the same effect as fulfilling a civil obligation. For instance, if a debt has prescribed and the creditor can no longer sue, but the debtor still pays, the debtor cannot recover the payment.

Can you explain Article 754 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding donations?

Article 754 states that when a donated property is taken away (evicted) from the donee, the donee steps into the donor's shoes and can exercise any rights or actions the donor would have had against third parties. Generally, the donor does not guarantee the donee against eviction or hidden defects, except in two cases: (1) if the donation is onerous (i.e., imposes a burden on the donee), the donor is liable for eviction only up to the value of that burden; and (2) if the donor acted in bad faith (e.g., knew of the defect or lack of ownership), the donor is fully liable for eviction or hidden defects.

Can you explain Article 43 of the Philippine Civil Code about the presumption of simultaneous death?

Article 43 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with situations where two or more persons who are heirs of each other die in a common event and it is unclear who died first. If someone claims that one person died before the other (for example, to establish inheritance rights), that person must prove the order of death. If there is no proof, the law presumes that they died at the same time. As a result, no rights are transmitted from one to the other; each person's estate passes to their own respective heirs.

Please explain Article 628 of the Philippine Civil Code about easements.

Article 628 deals with the sharing of expenses for necessary works on an easement when there are multiple dominant estates. If several properties benefit from the same easement, each owner must contribute in proportion to the benefits they receive from the work. If one owner does not wish to contribute, he may exempt himself by renouncing the easement for the benefit of the others. Additionally, if the owner of the servient estate (the property burdened by the easement) also uses the easement, he must also contribute to the expenses in the same proportion, unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

Can you explain what Article 774 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 774 defines succession as a mode of acquiring ownership. When a person dies, their property, rights, and obligations are transferred to their heirs. The heirs receive the inheritance, but their liability for the deceased's debts is limited to the total value of the assets they inherit. Succession can happen either according to the deceased's will (testamentary succession) or, if there is no will, according to the rules set by law (intestate succession).

Can you explain Article 1342 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1342 provides that misrepresentation made by a third person (someone who is not a party to the contract) does not normally invalidate the consent of the contracting parties. However, there is an exception: if that misrepresentation by the third person caused a substantial mistake, and that mistake was mutual (i.e., both parties were misled by the same false information), then consent may be considered vitiated, and the contract may be voidable. Otherwise, misrepresentation by a third person alone does not affect the validity of consent.

STATUTORY TEXT: If the usufruct be constituted on the whole of a patrimony, and if at the time of its constitution the owner has debts, the provisions of articles 758 and 759 relating to donations shall be applied, both with respect to the maintenance of the usufruct and to the obligation of the usufructuary to pay such debts.

My father granted me the usufruct over his entire business and properties. At that time, he had outstanding loans from a bank. Now the bank is demanding payment. Am I, as the usufructuary, liable to pay his debts? Also, he is required to pay monthly support to his ex-wife. Do I have to cover that too?

It is advisable to review the terms of the usufruct agreement and the exact value of the patrimony to determine your precise liability.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 598, since the usufruct was constituted over the whole patrimony of your father, and he had existing debts (the bank loans) at the time of constitution, the rules on donations with reservation of usufruct and payment of debts apply. This means the usufruct remains valid, but you, as usufructuary, are obligated to pay his debts. However, your liability is limited to the value of the property you received in usufruct, unless there is a contrary stipulation. So if the value of the properties is less than the debts, you only need to pay up to that value. The same rule applies to his obligation to make periodical payments (the monthly support to his ex-wife), even though there is no known capital amount. [Art. 598].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, you are required to pay the support from the fruits or income of the property subject to usufruct, but only within the limits of the value of the property, unless otherwise agreed.

PROVISION: Article 490 (Republic Act No. 386 - Civil Code of the Philippines)
LOCATION: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE III.—CO-OWNERSHIP > Art. 490
STATUTORY TEXT: Whenever the different stories of a house belong to different owners, if the titles of ownership do not specify the terms under which they should contribute to the necessary expenses and there exists no agreement on the subject, the following rules shall be observed:
(1) The main and party walls, the roof and the other things used in common, shall be preserved at the expense of all the owners in proportion to the value of the story belonging to each;
(2) Each owner shall bear the cost of maintaining the floor of his story; the floor of the entrance, front door, common yard and sanitary works common to all, shall be maintained at the expense of all the owners pro rata;
(3) The stairs from the entrance to the first story shall be maintained at the expense of all the owners pro rata, with the exception of the owner of the ground floor; the stairs from the first to the second story shall be preserved at the expense of all, except the owner of the ground floor and the owner of the first story; and so on successively.

I own the second floor of a three-story house. The ground floor is owned by another person, and the first floor by someone else. The roof needs major repairs, the entrance floor is damaged, and both staircases need maintenance. Our titles do not specify how to divide these expenses, and we cannot agree. Who should pay for what according to the law?

Consequently, the ground floor owner does not pay for any stairs, the first floor owner pays only for the first set of stairs, and you pay for both sets of stairs in addition to your share of common elements and your own floor.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 490 of the Civil Code, since your titles do not specify the terms for contributing to necessary expenses and there is no agreement, the following rules apply: The roof, being a common element, must be repaired at the expense of all owners (including you, the ground floor owner, and the first floor owner) in proportion to the value of each one's story. The entrance floor, front door, common yard, and common sanitary works are also maintained by all owners pro rata. You must solely bear the cost of maintaining the floor of your own story (the second floor). For the stairs: the stairs from the entrance to the first story are maintained by all owners except the ground floor owner—so you and the first floor owner share that expense pro rata. [Art. 490].

### 💡 Application to Facts
The stairs from the first to the second story are maintained by all owners except the ground floor and first floor owners—so since you are the only owner above the first floor, you alone bear that expense.

Can you explain Article 1221 of the Civil Code about solidary obligations?

Article 1221 deals with solidary obligations when the thing to be delivered is lost or the performance becomes impossible. If the loss or impossibility occurs without any fault of the solidary debtors, the obligation is extinguished for all of them. However, if any one of the solidary debtors is at fault (e.g., through negligence), then all the debtors are liable to the creditor for the price of the thing, plus damages and interest. The innocent debtors can later seek reimbursement from the guilty or negligent debtor. Additionally, if the loss or impossibility happens due to a fortuitous event (like an accident or natural disaster) but after one of the solidary debtors has already incurred delay (meaning the creditor demanded performance and the debtor failed to comply on time), then the same rule as with fault applies — all solidary debtors become liable for the price and damages.

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 668 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa pagbilang ng panahon ng reseta para sa easement ng liwanag at tanawin.

Can you explain what Article 615 of the Philippine Civil Code says about the different kinds of easements?

Article 615 classifies easements into four types based on two criteria: continuity of use and visibility. Continuous easements are those whose use is or may be incessant without any act of man, such as an aqueduct where water flows continuously. Discontinuous easements are used at intervals and depend on human acts, like a right of way that requires walking or driving each time. Apparent easements are visible through external signs that reveal their use, such as a door or window. Nonapparent easements have no external indication of their existence, like a restriction on building height. These classifications matter for acquisition, prescription, and extinction of easements.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1253 of the Civil Code, if a debt produces interest, payment of the principal shall not be deemed to have been made until the interests have been covered. ### 💡 Application to Facts
Therefore, in your scenario, the P15,000 payment will be applied to the accrued interest first. At 5% monthly interest on P100,000, the interest for three months is P15,000 (5% x P100,000 x 3). Since your payment exactly covers the accrued interest, the entire P15,000 goes to interest and the principal remains P100,000.

Article 1356 states that contracts are generally valid and binding regardless of the form in which they were entered into, as long as all essential requisites for validity (consent, object, and cause) are present. Can you explain Article 1307 of the Philippine Civil Code about innominate contracts?

Article 1307 states that innominate contracts (contracts that do not have a specific name or are not regulated by special provisions of law) shall be governed by: first, the stipulations or agreements of the parties; second, the general provisions on obligations and contracts found in Titles I and II of Book IV of the Civil Code; third, the rules governing the most analogous nominate contracts (those with specific names and regulations, like sale, lease, etc.); and fourth, the customs of the place where the contract is made. This means that when parties enter into a contract that is not explicitly defined by law, they are free to set their own terms as long as they do not violate law or public policy, and in the absence of specific stipulations, the court will look to general contract principles, then to similar named contracts, and finally to local customs to fill in gaps.

Can you explain what Article 670 of the Philippine Civil Code says about windows and views?

Article 670 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that no windows, apertures, balconies, or similar projections that afford a direct view upon or towards an adjoining land can be made unless there is a distance of at least two meters between the wall containing them and the boundary of the neighboring property. For side or oblique views (views at an angle, not directly facing the neighbor), a distance of at least sixty centimeters is required. Importantly, the law also states that nonobservance of these required distances does not give rise to prescription. This means that even if someone violates these distance rules for a long time, they cannot acquire a legal right to keep such openings. The neighbor can always demand compliance.

Kabilang dito: (1) ang tagapangalaga (guardian), sa ari-arian ng kanyang inaalagaan; (2) ang mga ahente, sa ari-arian na ipinagkatiwala sa kanila para pangasiwaan o ipagbili, maliban kung may pahintulot ng punong-guro (principal); (3) ang mga tagapagpatupad ng testamento (executors) at tagapangasiwa (administrators), sa ari-arian ng estate na kanilang pinamamahalaan; (4) ang mga pampublikong opisyal at empleyado, sa ari-arian ng Estado o ng alinmang subdibisyon nito, o ng mga korporasyong pag-aari o kontrolado ng gobyerno, o institusyon na ang pangangasiwa ay ipinagkatiwala sa kanila; kasama rito ang mga hukom at eksperto ng gobyerno na nakikibahagi sa pagbebenta; (5) ang mga mahistrado, hukom, piskal, klerk ng mga korte, at iba pang opisyal at empleyado na konektado sa pangangasiwa ng hustisya, sa ari-arian at mga karapatan na nasa litigasyon o na-levy sa execution sa harap ng hukuman kung saan sila gumaganap ng kanilang tungkulin; kasama rin dito ang pagkuha sa pamamagitan ng assignment at ito ay nalalapat sa mga abogado hinggil sa ari-arian at mga karapatan na maaaring maging paksa ng anumang litigasyon kung saan sila ay nakikibahagi dahil sa kanilang propesyon; at (6) ang sinumang iba pang espesyal na diskuwalipikado ng batas. Ang layunin nito ay maiwasan ang mga salungatan ng interes, pandaraya, at pang-aabuso ng awtoridad.

STATUTORY TEXT: Minors and incapacitated persons may acquire the possession of things; but they need the assistance of their legal representatives in order to exercise the rights which from the possession arise in their favor.

My 15-year-old son inherited a piece of land from his grandfather. He is now in possession of the land and wants to sell it to pay for his education. Can he sign the sale documents by himself? What does the law say about minors having possession and exercising rights over property?

Without such assistance and approval, any sale executed solely by the minor would be voidable or unenforceable.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 535 of the Civil Code, your son, as a minor, can acquire possession of the land through inheritance. Possession refers to the actual holding or control of the property, and he is legally capable of having that possession. However, the article also states that he needs the assistance of his legal representative to exercise the rights arising from that possession. Selling the land is an act of exercising a right that comes from possession, not merely acquiring possession. Because your son is only 15 years old, he lacks full legal capacity to enter into contracts. Therefore, he cannot sign the sale documents by himself. His legal representative, which would be his parent or guardian, must act on his behalf. [Art. 535].

Additionally, since the sale involves disposition of property belonging to a minor, the legal representative must obtain court approval to ensure the sale is for the minor's benefit and in compliance with the law.

Can you explain Article 1468 of the Philippine Civil Code? It seems to cover contracts where the consideration is partly in money and partly in another thing.

Article 1468 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with contracts where the consideration (what is given in exchange) consists partly of money and partly of a non-money item. It says that the nature of the transaction—whether it is a sale or a barter—is determined by the manifest intention of the parties. If the parties clearly intended a sale, it is a sale; if they clearly intended a barter, it is a barter. However, if their intention is not clear, the law provides a rule: the transaction is considered a barter if the value of the non-money item given as part of the consideration is greater than the amount of money or its equivalent. Otherwise, if the money or its equivalent is greater, it is considered a sale.

Article 1536 of the Civil Code provides that in a contract of sale, if the buyer (vendee) was given a period or terms to pay (such as installment payments), but later the buyer loses the right to that period under Article 1198 (for example, by becoming insolvent, failing to provide promised security, violating the agreement, or attempting to abscond), then the seller (vendor) is no longer obligated to deliver the thing sold. This means the seller can withhold delivery until the buyer pays in full or gives adequate security. The seller's duty to deliver is conditional on the buyer's continued entitlement to the credit period.

What does Article 1439 of the Philippine Civil Code mean when it says that estoppel is effective only as between the parties thereto or their successors in interest?

Article 1439 of the Philippine Civil Code states that the principle of estoppel—which prevents a person from denying or asserting something contrary to what they have previously represented—only applies between the parties directly involved in the transaction and their successors in interest. Can you explain Article 37 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 37 distinguishes between juridical capacity and capacity to act. Juridical capacity is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations; it is inherent in every natural person from birth and is lost only upon death. Capacity to act, on the other hand, is the power to do acts with legal effect. It is acquired (e.g., upon reaching the age of majority) and may be lost (e.g., due to insanity, civil interdiction, or other legal disabilities). In essence, juridical capacity is passive, while capacity to act is active.

Can you explain Article 106 of the Philippine Civil Code about the effects of legal separation?

Article 106 of the Philippine Civil Code outlines the effects of a decree of legal separation. First, the spouses may live separately, but their marriage is not dissolved; they remain married to each other. Second, their conjugal partnership or absolute community of property is dissolved and liquidated, but the spouse who caused the separation forfeits any share in the profits earned by the partnership or community, subject to Article 176. Can you explain Article 864 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding fideicommissary substitution and the legitime?

Article 864 states that a fideicommissary substitution cannot burden the legitime. A fideicommissary substitution is when a testator leaves property to an heir (first heir) with the obligation to preserve it and pass it on to another heir (second heir) after a certain time or condition. The legitime is the portion of the estate that the law reserves for compulsory heirs, such as children or parents. This article means that while a testator can impose a fideicommissary substitution on the free portion of the estate, they cannot impose it on the legitime, because the legitime must go directly to the compulsory heirs without conditions or substitutions. The compulsory heirs are entitled to receive their legitime outright.

Please explain Article 1590 of the Philippine Civil Code. What does it say about a buyer's right to suspend payment of the purchase price when there is a threat to his possession or ownership?

Article 1590 of the Civil Code allows a buyer of property to suspend payment of the price if he is disturbed in his possession or ownership of the thing bought, or if he has reasonable grounds to fear such disturbance due to a vindicatory action (a lawsuit to recover ownership) or a foreclosure of mortgage. The suspension can last until the seller removes the disturbance or danger. However, the buyer cannot suspend payment if the seller gives security for the return of the price (in a proper case) or if there was an agreement that the buyer must pay even if such disturbance occurs. A mere act of trespass by a third person does not justify suspension of payment.

Please explain Article 596 of the Philippine Civil Code.

Article 596 provides that during the existence of a usufruct, the usufructuary (the person entitled to use and enjoy the property and its fruits) is responsible for paying the annual charges and taxes, as well as any other charges considered a lien on the fruits. This means that regular yearly taxes, such as the real property tax, are shouldered by the usufructuary because they are typically paid out of the income or fruits generated by the property. The owner remains responsible only for extraordinary taxes and expenses that affect the capital or structure of the property, not the annual operating costs.

Can you explain Article 1306 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1306 of the Philippine Civil Code embodies the principle of autonomy of contracts. It states that contracting parties may establish such stipulations, clauses, terms and conditions as they deem convenient, provided they are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy. This means that while parties have broad freedom to determine the contents of their agreement, this freedom is not absolute. Any agreement that violates a law, goes against societal morals or good customs, disturbs public order, or contravenes public policy will be considered void or unenforceable.

Paki explain po ang Artikulo 652 ng Civil Code. Kailan po ba libre ang right of way?

Ang Artikulo 652 ay nagtatakda ng espesyal na patakaran para sa easement o right of way kapag ang isang lupa na nakuha sa pamamagitan ng pagbili, pagpapalit, o paghahati-hati ay napapalibutan ng ibang mga lupa ng nagbenta, nagpalit, o kasamang may-ari. Kung ang lupa ay nakuha mo sa pamamagitan ng bilihan, palitan, o partisyon, at ito ay napapalibutan ng natitirang lupa ng nagbenta, nagpalit, o kasamang may-ari, sila ay obligadong magbigay ng right of way nang walang bayad na indemnity. Ito ay dahil ipinapalagay na kasama sa transaksyon ang pagbibigay ng daanan. Ngunit kung ang lupa ay nakuha sa pamamagitan ng simpleng donasyon (regalo), ang donor na may-ari ng nakapaligid na lupa ay may karapatang humingi ng indemnity mula sa donee (ang tumanggap) para sa right of way. Ibig sabihin, kailangan mong magbayad para sa daanan kung ang lupa ay ibinigay sa iyo nang libre.

Can you explain Article 56 of the Philippine Civil Code? Who are authorized to solemnize marriage?

Article 56 of the Philippine Civil Code specifies the persons authorized to solemnize marriage. These include: (1) The Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court; (2) The Presiding Justice and the Justices of the Court of Appeals; (3) Judges of the Courts of First Instance (now Regional Trial Courts); (4) Mayors of cities and municipalities; (5) Municipal judges and justices of the peace; (6) Priests, rabbis, ministers of the gospel of any denomination, church, religion or sect, duly registered as provided in Article 92; and (7) Ship captains, airplane chiefs, military commanders, and consuls and vice-consuls in special cases provided in Articles 74 and 75. STATUTORY TEXT: Legal or intestate succession takes place:
(1) If a person dies without a will, or with a void will, or one which has subsequently lost its validity;
(2) When the will does not institute an heir to, or dispose of all the property belonging to the testator. In such case, legal succession shall take place only with respect to the property of which the testator has not disposed;
(3) If the suspensive condition attached to the institution of heir does not happen or is not fulfilled, or if the heir dies before the testator, or repudiates the inheritance, there being no substitution, and no right of accretion takes place;

My uncle passed away recently. He had a will that left everything to his only daughter. But his daughter died two years before him. The will didn't name any alternate heir. Now my father, who is my uncle's brother, thinks he might be entitled to a share. Who inherits? Does the will still apply?

You may need to follow the rules on intestate succession to determine the exact shares.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
In your situation, the will named your uncle's daughter as the sole heir, but she died before your uncle. [Art. 960].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Under Article 960(3) of the Civil Code, if the heir instituted in the will dies before the testator, and there is no substitution and no right of accretion, legal succession takes place. Therefore, the will's disposition in favor of the daughter is ineffective. The estate will be distributed to the legal heirs according to intestate succession. If your uncle left no surviving spouse, no other descendants, and no ascendants (parents), then his siblings, including your father, would be among the legal heirs entitled to inherit.

Please explain Article 151 of the Philippine Civil Code.

Article 151 of the Philippine Civil Code states that if a spouse makes a donation with a burden or charge (an onerous donation), and the conjugal partnership pays for those charges, then the amount of those charges must be deducted from the donor spouse's exclusive property. For the wife, that exclusive property is called paraphernal property; for the husband, it is his capital. In short, the conjugal partnership must be reimbursed for any expenses it incurred in fulfilling the charges of an onerous donation made by one spouse from his or her exclusive property.

What does Article 1294 of the Philippine Civil Code mean?

Article 1294 deals with novation by substituting a new debtor. It states that if the substitution is done without the knowledge or against the will of the original debtor, then the original debtor is not liable if the new debtor becomes insolvent or fails to fulfill the obligation. In other words, the original debtor is released from responsibility once the creditor consents to the substitution, even if the original debtor did not agree to it.

I lent money to a friend in 2019 with a written agreement that he would pay me by December 31, 2020. He never paid. I filed a collection case on January 15, 2023. He now claims that my action is barred by prescription because more than three years have passed since I lent the money. Is he correct? When did the prescriptive period start?

Your friend's argument is incorrect; your claim is not barred by prescription.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1150 of the Civil Code, the prescriptive period for actions is counted from the day the action may be brought. [Art. 1150].

### 💡 Application to Facts
In your situation, the loan had a fixed due date of December 31, 2020. You could not have filed a collection case before that date because the obligation was not yet due. The cause of action accrued on January 1, 2021, when your friend failed to pay despite the maturity of the debt. Thus, the prescriptive period started on January 1, 2021, not on the date you lent the money. Since your case was filed on January 15, 2023, and the prescriptive period for a written contract is 10 years (or 6 years for an oral contract), your action is well within the period.

- **Competent Court / Jurisdiction**: Municipal Trial Court (MTC / MeTC / MTCC / MCTC) if monetary claim does not exceed ₱2,000,000 (Small Claims Court if ≤ ₱1,000,000 pursuant to SC Small Claims Rules); Regional Trial Court (RTC) if claim exceeds ₱2,000,000 or if incapable of pecuniary estimation pursuant to RA 11576.

Can you explain Article 1437 of the Philippine Civil Code about estoppel?

Article 1437 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with estoppel concerning immovable property. It states that if a person, in a contract between third parties, misleads one of them about the ownership or real rights over a piece of real estate, that person is barred from later asserting his own legal title or interest in the property. This applies only if four conditions are met: (1) there was fraudulent representation or wrongful concealment of known facts; (2) the person making the misrepresentation intended the other party to rely on it; (3) the misled party was unaware of the true facts; and (4) the defrauded party acted based on the misrepresentation. In simple terms, if you deceive someone about who owns land, you cannot later claim your own ownership to the detriment of the person who relied on your deception.

So you are entitled to one-fourth of the hereditary estate.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 898 of the Civil Code, if the decedent is survived by a spouse, legitimate children, and illegitimate children who are not acknowledged natural or natural by legal fiction, the surviving spouse's legitime is the same as provided in Article 897. Article 897 states that when the surviving spouse is with legitimate children and acknowledged natural children or natural children by legal fiction, the spouse's legitime is one-fourth of the hereditary estate. Can you explain Article 900 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding the legitime of a surviving spouse?

Article 900 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with the legitime of the surviving spouse when they are the only compulsory heir. Normally, if only the widow or widower survives, they are entitled to one-half of the hereditary estate as their legitime, and the testator may freely dispose of the other half. However, there is an exception: if the marriage was solemnized 'in articulo mortis' (at the point of death) and the testator died within three months from the marriage, the legitime of the surviving spouse is reduced to one-third of the estate. This exception does not apply if the couple had been living as husband and wife for more than five years, in which case the legitime goes back to one-half. The reduced legitime aims to discourage marriages entered into solely to secure an inheritance when the spouse is near death.

Can you explain Article 1191 of the Civil Code of the Philippines in simple terms?

Article 1191 deals with contracts where both parties have obligations to each other (reciprocal obligations). If one party fails to do what they are supposed to do, the other party (the injured party) has two options: they can either demand that the contract be fulfilled, or they can ask to cancel (rescind) the contract. In either case, they can also claim damages. Even if the injured party initially chose to demand fulfillment, they can change their mind and ask for rescission if fulfillment becomes impossible. The court will grant rescission unless there is a just reason to give the other party more time to comply. This is without prejudice to the rights of third persons who have acquired the thing in good faith, as provided in Articles 1385 and 1388 and the Mortgage Law.

Can you explain Article 1542 of the Philippine Civil Code about the sale of real estate for a lump sum?

Article 1542 states that when real estate is sold for a lump sum price (not priced per unit of measure or number), the price remains fixed regardless of whether the actual area or number is greater or less than what was stated in the contract. This rule also applies when two or more immovables are sold together for a single price. However, if the contract specifies the boundaries (which is always required in real estate sales) and also designates the area or number, the seller must deliver everything within those boundaries, even if it exceeds the stated area or number. If the seller cannot deliver the full area within the boundaries, the buyer is entitled to a proportionate reduction in price, or the buyer may rescind the contract if they do not agree to accept the deficiency.

Can you explain Article 733 of the Philippine Civil Code about donations with an onerous cause and remuneratory donations?

Article 733 states that if a donation is made with an onerous cause (meaning the recipient must do something or give something in return, like paying a debt or performing an obligation), it is not treated as a pure donation. Instead, it is governed by the rules on contracts. The reason is that such a donation is really a contract where both parties have obligations. On the other hand, if a donation is remuneratory (given to reward someone for past services rendered), the portion of the donation that corresponds to the value of the services is considered payment and is also governed by contract rules, while the excess over that value is treated as a true donation and is governed by the rules on donations.

Can you explain Article 605 of the Philippine Civil Code about usufruct in favor of towns, corporations, or associations?

This prevents a temporary right from becoming effectively perpetual when the beneficiary entity ceases to exist.

Article 617 states that easements are inseparable from the estate to which they actively or passively belong. This means that an easement is a right or burden attached to the land itself, not to the owner personally. Instead, they share Carlos's one-third equally, so each grandchild receives one-sixth of the total estate. [Art. 974].

Therefore, Ana gets one-third, Ben gets one-third, and Carlos's two children get one-sixth each.

Additionally, when computing the period, the first day (March 10) is excluded, and the last day is included. Thus, you start counting from March 11 as day 1. Article 48 of the Philippine Civil Code lists who are considered citizens of the Philippines. The choice of remedy affects procedure and prescription: if you choose to pursue the civil liability arising from the crime, you must generally wait for the criminal case to be resolved (unless you reserve the right to file a separate civil action). You may remove the fountain when the usufruct ends, but only if it can be done without damage to the property.

Can you explain Article 1145 of the Philippine Civil Code? What types of actions must be filed within six years?

Article 1145 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that actions based on an oral contract or a quasi-contract must be commenced within six years from the time the cause of action accrues. 'Oral contract' means a verbal agreement, while 'quasi-contract' refers to a lawful, voluntary, and unilateral act that obligates a person to compensate another to prevent unjust enrichment. If the creditor or aggrieved party fails to file the case within six years, the action is barred by prescription, meaning the court will no longer entertain it.

Can you explain what Article 1289 of the Philippine Civil Code means?

Article 1289 states that if a person has several debts that can be compensated (set off) against credits he has against the same creditor, the order in which those debts are compensated will follow the rules on application of payments. Under those rules, the debtor may choose which debt to apply the compensation to, but if he does not, it will be applied to the most onerous debt, and if all are equally onerous, proportionately.

My father passed away and left a will. In his will, he disinherited me without stating any reason. He gave all his properties to my brother and also donated a piece of land to a friend. I am his legitimate child. What are my rights? Can the will still be followed?

Under Article 918 of the Civil Code, your disinheritance is void because it was made without specifying a cause. This means you are still entitled to your legitime as a compulsory heir. The donation to your father's friend is a legacy or devise and remains valid, but only if it does not impair your legitime. [Art. 918].

### 💡 Application to Facts
If the donation reduces your legitime, it may be reduced accordingly.

STATUTORY TEXT: The title for prescription must be true and valid.

I bought a parcel of land from someone 20 years ago, but it turned out that the seller was not the real owner and the deed of sale is void. I have been occupying the land and paying taxes since then. Can I still acquire ownership of the land through prescription? The title I have is apparently invalid.

But for purposes of this article, the void title cannot be used as basis for prescription.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1130 of the Civil Code, the title for prescription must be true and valid. This means that if you are claiming ownership through acquisitive prescription based on a title (just title), that title must be genuine and legally effective. A void deed of sale, such as one executed by a person who was not the owner, cannot serve as a valid title for prescription. Therefore, you cannot acquire ownership through ordinary prescription because your title is void. [Art. 1130].

### 💡 Application to Facts
However, you may still be able to acquire ownership through extraordinary prescription, which does not require a title, provided you possessed the property in the concept of an owner, publicly, peacefully, and continuously for the period required by law (30 years for immovables under Article 1137).

Article 422 states that property of public dominion, which is property intended for public use (like roads, parks, plazas) or public service (like government buildings, municipal halls), when it is no longer intended for such public use or public service, automatically becomes patrimonial property of the State. STATUTORY TEXT: Unless otherwise agreed, where goods are delivered to the buyer, and he refuses to accept them, having the right so to do, he is not bound to return them to the seller, but it is sufficient if he notifies the seller that he refuses to accept them. I ordered 100 sacks of rice from a supplier. They delivered the rice, but upon inspection, I found that it was of inferior quality and not what we agreed upon. I told the delivery personnel that I refuse to accept the goods. However, they just left the sacks at my warehouse. Now I'm worried: do I have to return the rice to the supplier? Am I responsible if the rice gets damaged while it's in my warehouse? I don't want to be liable for something I didn't accept.

You are not required to ship or return the goods yourself, but you must avoid negligence if you keep them on your premises.

### 📚 Governing Statutory Basis
Under Article 1587 of the Civil Code, since you have a valid right to refuse acceptance because the goods do not conform to the contract, you are not obligated to return the goods to the seller. It is sufficient that you notify the seller of your refusal. However, if you voluntarily act as a depositary—meaning you take charge of the goods and exercise control over them—you assume the obligations of a depositary. This means you must exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in caring for the goods, and you may be liable for loss or damage caused by your negligence. [Art. 1587].

### 💡 Application to Facts
Simply leaving the goods in your warehouse without your active consent to act as custodian may not automatically make you a depositary, but if you take any steps to protect or manage the goods, you could be considered a voluntary depositary. Therefore, you should promptly notify the seller of your refusal and request them to retrieve the goods.

Article 643 imposes three obligations on anyone who wants to exercise the right granted in the preceding article (Article 642, which allows the use of water from springs, brooks, or rivers on another's land for certain purposes).
